0f6e30fb13eb.text: By — Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/signs-of-fraying-loyalty-emerge-in-netanyahu-stronghold-before-israeli-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Signs of fraying loyalty emerge in Netanyahu stronghold before Israeli election World Oct 23, 2026 7:31 PM EDT KIRYAT SHMONA, Israel (AP) — Kiryat Shmona has long been a bastion of support for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party. But that loyalty is no longer ironclad. Once a bustling commercial center, Israel's northernmost city was temporarily evacuated three years ago after being battered by rockets from nearby Lebanon, and it still feels half-empty even though the attacks have mostly subsided. Although the town remains staunchly conservative, there are rumblings of displeasure with Netanyahu's handling of the latest war against the militant group Hezbollah, and that could bode poorly for him in Israel's election Tuesday. READ MORE: Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection Vowing to stop Hezbollah's attacks, Netanyahu led a bombing campaign in Lebanon and invaded the country twice since 2023. More than 4,000 Lebanese have been killed, and Israeli troops have occupied a swath of southern Lebanon, leveling multiple towns and displacing an estimated 1 million people. Still, Hezbollah remains active. Some in Kiryat Shmona say Israel should have been even tougher; others say they no longer trust that Netanyahu cares about them. Eti Ben Shabat, 64, says in previous elections she had always followed her family in voting for Likud, almost without thinking. But in recent years, she said, something snapped. She pointed in part to Netanyahu's broken promises to bring security to the north and dismantle Hezbollah. "I don't want the lies to continue," she said. In previous elections, support went heavy for Netanyahu Netanyahu is unlikely to lose Kiryat Shmona entirely. But even a small dip in its support — and that of other traditional strongholds — could spell trouble for him. It could tip a very tight election to the man aiming to replace him, Gadi Eisenkot. Or it could strengthen far-right parties, which would likely back Netanyahu to remain prime minister but would then have even greater power in a ruling coalition. Kiryat Shmona has always supported right-wing parties, particularly Likud. In the last elections held in 2021 and 2022, around 50% of voters there chose Likud, compared to a quarter of voters nationwide, according to the Central Elections Committee. "Kiryat Shmona, the way the city is socioeconomically and religion-wise, it is made for the right and specifically Likud," said Sami Malul, 72, a retired Likud city councilor who served as the town's acting mayor in 2008. But the town is reeling from the war. The government evacuated Kiryat Shmona and dozens of other towns and villages along the Lebanese border for more than a year – from the time Hezbollah began firing on Israel after Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel until a ceasefire with Hezbollah was reached in late 2024. Netanyahu claimed to have subdued Hezbollah. So trust in him shattered among some in Kiryat Shmona when Hezbollah missiles again started hitting in March after Israel and the U.S. launched their war on Iran. Israel's subsequent occupation of southern Lebanon has reduced but not stopped Hezbollah fire. Efforts by the Lebanese army to remove Hezbollah from southern Lebanon have made little progress. Kiryat Shmona claims that nearly 80% of its 22,000 residents have returned, but locals say the real figure is closer to 50%. Streets feel empty and abandoned. On the main commercial drags, several shops remain shuttered. Others are open but devoid of customers. Malul insists the government handled the war and the evacuation well, prioritizing residents' safety. He argued Kiryat Shmona has faced attacks since its founding and Netanyahu isn't to blame for the current situation. Many others feel the same. "We really love Bibi, and we can't choose anyone else, but he should see the needs of his people," said Maimon Amsalem, using Netanyahu's nickname. "Keeping our security is the most important thing, we don't want anything else." For some, three years of war triggers a dramatic shift Nissan Zeevi, a third-generation resident of northern Israel who lives in a town adjacent to Kiryat Shmona, has voted for Likud as long as he can remember. But this year he is running for a seat in parliament with the Beyachad opposition party, furious over what he calls Netanyahu's "abandonment of the north." During the most recent war with Hezbollah, Zeevi founded Lobby 1701, an activist group advocating for better security in the north. He wants the Israeli military to increase its attacks against Hezbollah and maintain its buffer zone in southern Lebanon until the Lebanese government identifies Hezbollah as a terror organization. "Residents in the north have been in a war for three years that hasn't ended," said Zeevi. "You can see the people's great frustration and great disappointment in Netanyahu." "Netanyahu still has his base here, who will go with him through fire and water. But people have much more political awareness now," said Zeevi. "After 20 years, he needs to make way for new leadership." In a small town, voting along family lines Around town, there's little evidence that elections are just days away, and little outward excitement for Likud or Netanyahu. A few scattered campaign posters for the smaller right-wing parties flutter at intersections or are glued onto mobile bomb shelters. Few residents wanted to speak about politics, citing a general feeling of hopelessness and frustration. No candidates have offered a concrete plan for the conflict with Hezbollah, beyond offering vague promises of "strong defense." 90ec80047af2.text: By — Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Paul Wiseman, Associated Press By — Didi Tang, Associated Press Didi Tang, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/treasury-proposes-rule-to-curb-high-tech-investments-in-china-and-other-adversaries Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Treasury proposes rule to curb high-tech investments in China and other adversaries Politics Oct 23, 2026 7:19 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Treasury Department proposed a rule Thursday to crack down on American high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence in China, Russia, North Korea and other "countries of concern." The U.S. government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power. That program began in 2023 when then-President Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound U.S. investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence going into China. Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program. In December 2025, Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia. The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin. REAAD MORE: Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen The rule announced Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, though Treasury used Trump's favored term for AI, "superintelligence" or SI. The proposed rule "sends an important signal to markets that Washington is tracking where U.S. capital is flowing and what capabilities it is helping build," said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies. The screening of outbound investments "recognizes that capital can accelerate military-relevant capabilities just as surely as technology transfer can," Singleton said. Jason Chipman, a former Justice Department lawyer who specializes in cybersecurity, investment rules and export controls as a partner at the law firm WilmerHale, said the new rule "will require more substantial compliance programs to manage risk." Treasury's rule to implement the 2025 law — the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — would only apply to investments that exceed $50,000 and would exclude many financial investments, including stock purchases. Treasury will hear public comments on the proposal before issuing a final rule. "It's just the first step in a fairly long process to get to changes which presumably will be more enforcement-minded, to put more teeth behind the outbound investment program," said former U.S. trade official Ryan Majerus, now a partner at King & Spalding law firm. In Beijing, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said the U.S. should abide by the principles of a market economy and stop interfering in normal economic and trade cooperation between businesses. Asked about Washington's proposal to add biotechnology to the list, ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said that "Overstretching the concept of national security, taking discriminatory measures against specific countries, and artificially restricting trade, economic and investment activities serve no one's interests." She added that China will closely monitor relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its interests. Since Trump's first term, the United States and China — the world's two biggest economies — have been locked in an economic and tech rivalry. They've restricted the export of sensitive technology and critical products — such as China's rare earth minerals and America's advanced computer chips — to each other and slapped tariffs on each other's products. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed last year to ease tensions while they engaged in talks, a temporary truce they last month extended into January. But the sparring continues. In July, the Treasury Department issued a $200,000 fine against a U.S.-based company for failing to report to the department a $92,500 investment in a Chinese artificial intelligence and robotics company by one of its subsidiaries. 0c9a48bd2c49.text: President Trump is making a final push to help Republicans maintain control of Congress as some of the most closely watched races remain competitive. But the battle for the Senate is also playing out in court. In Alaska, the Trump administration sued to potentially block certification of the election if the Republican incumbent loses. White House correspondent Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: President Trump is making a final campaign push to help Republicans maintain control of Congress, as some of the country's most closely watched races remain competitive. But the battle for the U.S. Senate is also playing out in court. In Alaska, the Trump administration has filed a lawsuit seeking to potentially block certification of the election if the Republican incumbent loses. Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, has been following both developments and joins us now. So, Liz, let's start in Alaska, where the Justice Department has filed this unusual lawsuit. Why is the DOJ getting involved? Liz Landers: The Department of Justice has taken a series of potentially political actions really close to Election Day now. What was filed here in Alaska is, they're trying to block the certification of the vote there, but only if the Democrat, Mary Peltola, wins and beats the incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The issue here is that there is a-another candidate named Dan J. Sullivan, who's also on that ballot. And Republicans are worried that voters could get confused by this. But this has already been litigated by the Alaska Supreme Court, who said that Dan J. Sullivan could stay on this ballot. Department of Justice is bringing this lawsuit, they say, to protect the integrity of the Senate election there. They say in their lawsuit that the federal government could be harmed by this election certification if it is -- quote -- "tainted by a frivolous candidacy because that undermines confidence in the makeup and workings of the federal government." President Trump was asked about this earlier today. President Donald Trump: I'm the one that said do it. They have two guys run -- named Dan Sullivan running. So the Democrats put up a guy. I don't think he ever voted before. All of a sudden, he decides to run for the Senate, and his name is Dan Sullivan. One is Daniel S. One is Daniel J. The Daniel J. is the fake. Liz Landers: Daniel J. Sullivan has voted in Alaska races before, just to be clear. But I asked the former Department of Justice civil rights attorney David Becker, who's also an election expert about this, and he said this is purely a matter of state law, and the Department of Justice has no authority and no role here. He said that this kind of litigation is unprecedented to try to block the certification of an election 11 days before the vote. Geoff Bennett: The Justice Department also announced charges today against two former FBI officials over their testimony about Hunter Biden's laptop. What are they accused of doing? Liz Landers: The Department of Justice is claiming that these two FBI officials lied in congressional testimony that they gave in 2023. And this was about their involvement in a specialized foreign influence task force in these investigations into Hunter Biden's laptop and that they knew about the laptop. The attorneys for one of the former FBI officials who was charged here, Nikki Flores, said in a statement to the "News Hour" that: "The government's reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust to push a false narrative for a shot at political points." Hunter Biden's laptop story broke just a few weeks before the 2020 election. I'm sure you remember covering this. The laptop contained e-mails that appeared to show discussions of Hunter Biden's foreign business dealings. And at the time, Democrats questioned whether that was Russian mis- and dis-information. Geoff Bennett: And so finally, with Election Day approaching, you have got some of the biggest names in politics, to include President Trump, hitting the campaign trail. Who's heading where? Liz Landers: President Trump goes to Georgia tomorrow to help in that Senate race there. Also, he's headed to Michigan on Sunday. Mike Rogers is in a tough election there, the Republican against the Democrat, Abdul El-Sayed. Also, former President Barack Obama will be in Michigan as well tomorrow campaigning with Abdul El-Sayed, and he will also be going to Ohio as well. The former president has also cut a bunch of radio ads for other downballot candidates. Geoff Bennett: Liz Landers, a busy week for you. Next week's going to be busier. Liz Landers: Indeed, yes. (LAUGHTER) Geoff Bennett: Thanks, as always. Liz Landers: Of course.

70cbcb36a7d9.text: In our news wrap Friday, the White House says Melania Trump brokered a localized ceasefire deal in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky, Romania's president blamed Russia for a drone strike that sank a cargo ship in the Black Sea and Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu ordered the army there to prepare for a full closure of the occupied West Bank. Geoff Bennett: We start the day's other headlines with the latest on the war in Ukraine. The White House says first lady Melania Trump has brokered a localized cease-fire deal in Oleshky, the Ukrainian city captured by Russia early on in the war. The cease-fire would allow for humanitarian aid and evacuations from the town, which Mrs. Trump said is -- quote -- "on the brink of disaster." Following today's announcement, officials on both sides welcomed the agreement. President Trump told reporters today it was the first lady's initiative. President Donald Trump: What she wants to do is save children. And that's her focus. And both sides are cooperating with her, so doing a very good job. Geoff Bennett: The cease-fire is set to begin next week. Meantime, Romania's president has blamed Russia for a drone strike today that sank this cargo ship off its coast in the Black Sea, calling it a new example of Russian aggression beyond Ukraine. At least one sailor was killed. Three others were missing. That's as Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his military's access to Starlink satellite systems is still being interrupted, despite U.S. assurances that it's running again at full speed. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President: This is a real problem for us because the Russians attack us almost every day. Geoff Bennett: Zelenskyy also said negotiators from the U.S., Ukraine and Russia have agreed to hold technical level talks in Abu Dhabi in early November. Those would not involve political leaders. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army there to prepare for a full closure of the occupied West Bank after suspected gunmen shot and killed two Israeli soldiers. Video from the Israeli army showed the firefight at a military checkpoint. The two attackers, both Palestinian, were killed in the exchange of gunfire. The army said it prevented the men from advancing towards civilians. Following the shoot-out, Netanyahu blamed Hamas for the attack and vowed that Israel would retaliate. Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister (through translator): We will act, first of all, to demolish this place, to change it completely. We will evacuate the residents. We will go house by house. We will also remove the weapons there, and all the terror infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed. Geoff Bennett: After his comments, construction equipment could be seen starting to demolish homes near the site of the shooting. All of this comes just days before Israeli elections, when voters will decide whether to give Netanyahu another term in office. In China's Tibet region, first responders are racing to rescue survivors after a magnitude-7 earthquake struck the remote city of Nagqu. State media says at least 16 people are dead and more than 50 others were injured. Security camera footage showed the moment the quake struck as people fled into the streets. Hundreds of homes were destroyed, leaving many people there displaced. Local officials said multiple rounds of search-and-rescue have been complicated by the region's high altitude, low temperatures, and concern about further building collapses from aftershocks. Here at home, a police officer in Mississippi has resigned days after state authorities cleared him in the fatal shooting of a 1-year-old boy during a suspected shoplifting incident. Newly released body camera footage shows officers approaching a car in a Walmart parking lot in June guns drawn. As the vehicle moved forward, Sergeant Hunter Foster fired into it, killing 1-year-old Kohen Wiley, who was sitting on his mother's lap. Mississippi's attorney general ruled this week that the shooting was justified because the vehicle had moved toward an officer. But Wiley's family disputes that finding and is calling for a federal investigation. Kohen would have celebrated his second birthday on November 1. President Trump signed an order today removing 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian goods, including those in agriculture and forestry. The move is a bid to help Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is facing a tough reelection race. Many of Mr. Trump's tariffs have put particular strain on businesses in Maine. The changes become effective next Friday. Meantime, stocks ended the week down as oil prices rose to their highest level since 2022. The Dow Jones industrial average tumbled more than 600 points. The Nasdaq had a more modest drop, and the S&P 500 slipped by half-a-percent.

2c37848f6fa5.text: Kaylub Giamanco is the father who stopped a school shooter in Bend, Oregon, a week ago. The teen gunman entered the school and killed three students and a teacher before Giamanco stopped him. In a new interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting, Giamanco describes the moments leading up to his heroic actions, how he felt after he took down the shooter and that day's larger tragedy. Geoff Bennett: There's a new interview today with the first detailed comments from the man who stopped a school shooter in Bend, Oregon, one week ago. Three students and a teacher were killed before the suspect was shot and killed by a father who has children of his own at the Silver Rail Elementary School. That man is Kaylub Giamanco, who is a carpenter. He told our colleagues at Oregon Public Broadcasting in this exclusive interview that he was heading home for lunch and driving by the school when he saw the shooter carrying a shotgun. Kaylub Giamanco, Stopped School Gunman: And then I proceeded into the parking lot, and I saw him walking all the way across the school, and I just was in full panic. Like, no, there's children, there's babies in there. And I told my Siri to call 911. And the dispatch had picked up. And I was reporting the incident. But she was asking questions that they frustrated me, and I understand there's protocol, but she was asking me, do I know the person, all these things. And I said: "I'm sorry. I have to go in. People are going to die." And then I peeked through the window, and, at this point, I found my opportunity, and I seen a teacher on the left struggling with the gunman on the right with the rifle. And I knew that they were -- they were both side to me, and I knew that he did not know that I was there. And so at that point, I swung the door out and open, and I stepped in and I fired. And they dropped to the ground, and the teacher sprang out of the building, thinking that I was a second shooter, and I could see the fear in her eyes, and that did hurt a lot. But I could see the fear in her eyes. She left the room, and this happens in seconds. And then I looked down at the gunman, and he was scrambling for his weapon. And I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn't move, because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else. Geoff Bennett: Giamanco also spoke of how he felt after he took down the shooter and of that day's larger tragedy. Kaylub Giamanco: Felt like I was having a heart attack almost the entire time. I have never had so much chest pain. I mean, I can't tell you what it feels like to take a life. It's really not -- that's not how I thought that my Thursday was going to go. But I can tell you that I genuinely feel like I was supposed to be there. And if I wasn't there, I just don't know what would have happened. The teacher that was wrestling with the gun with the gunman, I just -- I want to recognize her. She gave me the opportunity to make my shot without losing my life. I saw a clear shot to where I did not have to take her life. Without her and that little spur-of-the-moment delay, I very much feel like I would have been facing the shooter head on, and we could have both died, or I could have died, and I felt like I was the last line of defense between me and the rest of the children in the school. I don't know her name. I would love to know her name. I would love to give her a hug, because that's a real true hero to not have a weapon and to put yourself in between your babies and a firearm. It's a lot, you know? I really did want to speak with the families and the victims and just cry with them and hold them. I want to apologize for not saving their babies. That's probably the biggest thing for me right now, because the gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there's ones that I didn't save, and that's probably the hardest thing for me right now. Geoff Bennett: Thank you again to our colleagues at Oregon Public Broadcasting for that interview.

de9ef8c251a6.text: By — Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/seeking-to-help-collins-in-maine-trump-exempts-some-canadian-imports-from-his-50-tariffs Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Seeking to help Collins in Maine, Trump exempts some Canadian imports from his 50% tariffs Politics Oct 23, 2026 6:48 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump, seeking to help Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a tough reelection battle in Maine, is exempting some imports — including plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery — from the 50% tariffs he slapped on $20 billion worth of Canadian products over the summer. The changes will take effect Oct. 30. The White House said the president was seeking to offset "the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest.'' Collins, locked in a tight race with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, issued a statement saying she'd spoken with Trump's top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "about the toll tariffs are taking on Maine families, businesses, farmers, and growers.'' WATCH: What Maine voters are saying about the Collins-Jackson Senate race "Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense," Collins said. She said she asked for tariff relief for such products "and stressed the burdens additional costs impose on Maine businesses and families." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Collins said she'd seek "additional relief from tariffs and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner." Trump started a trade war with America's longstanding ally and northern neighbor, reaching back to a Depression-era trade law to impose tariffs on Canadian imports. He charged that Canada discriminates against U.S. dairy, auto and alcoholic beverage producers. Canada promptly lashed back with tariffs of 15% to 50% on American products, matching Trump's import taxes dollar for dollar. Trump ratcheted the dispute up from there last month by imposing a flat-out ban on $1 billion worth of Canadian imports, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles. The U.S. president has claimed that foreign countries pay his tariffs. In fact, U.S. importers do. And they often face the tough choice of having to pass along the higher costs to their customers or absorb them. As the Nov. 3 midterm elections approach, many Americans are furious about the cost of living. An Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll of 2,140 U.S. adults, conducted Sept. 24-28, found that 65% now blame Trump's policies for persistently high prices more than factors outside of his control, signaling weariness over his aggressive use of tariffs and unhappiness with the war with Iran, which has driven up the price of gasoline. Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement, "Trump's desperate, 11th hour attempt to save Susan Collins' political career is an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies." Collins complained that Trump's levies were hurting Maine farms and businesses that rely on Canadian imports when U.S.-made alternatives are not available. Her office cited the example of Maine wild blueberry growers who need specialized harvesting boxes from Canada that work with their processing equipment. A father who shot dead a gunman at his two daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described "hearing children pleading for their lives" and his anguish over those he could not save.
Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by parent Kaylub Giamanco.
"I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday.
"The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."
Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them".
He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life.
"I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said.
The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was also killed, another child and a teacher were wounded.
Giamanco told OPB the day of the attack began with breakfast and packed lunches. He and his wife spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day.
The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began.
He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school.
Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services.
"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,'" he told the broadcaster.
He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building.
"I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said.
Giamanco crawled through a shattered window and reached the classroom, where a teacher was struggling with the gunman. He opened the door and fired.
Giamanco told OPB he fired again when the attacker reached for his weapon. He then placed his own gun on the ground and raised his hands as an officer appeared.
He described feeling like the "last line of defence" between the children and the gunman and said he "was supposed to be there" that day.
Afterwards, he called his wife to say he would not be home for lunch and that she needed to get to the school immediately. He then called his mother to tell her what had happened.
"Mum, I just had to take the life of what I think is might be a child because he ran into my daughter's school with a gun," he said.
Police identified the gunman as Griffin J John II - a former pupil who had attended special education classes at the school. His motive remains under investigation.
Police said the teacher who confronted the attacker had thrown her phone at him, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
The youngest victim was Rhoam Summer, 5. His father said the family was "broken and lost".
Megan Lambert, 25, the teacher who was killed, was working in what her family described as her "dream job".
"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.
The other two boys have not been publicly named at their families' request.
The injured teacher has been named as Becky Drury, 54. She said in a statement shared with US media that the gunman shot her as she tried to shut her classroom door.
Giamanco's name became public less than a day after the shooting. His mother, Kenda Freeman, read a family statement saying he was not seeking recognition and asking for privacy.
Shortly after the attack, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised his intervention while acknowledging its emotional cost.
"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she said.
Giamanco told OPB he now lies awake after his family goes to bed, replaying the attack.
"I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams."

abc0eb191c27.text: It's been more than a decade since Iowa has had a Democratic governor or senator. But this year, with the incumbents retiring, both races are competitive. As Peter Tubbs at Iowa PBS reports, record-high diesel prices have hit the state's agriculture industry particularly hard and could influence the midterm elections. Geoff Bennett: It's been more than a decade since Iowa has had a Democratic governor or senator, but this year, with the incumbents retiring there, both races are competitive. As Peter Tubbs of Iowa PBS reports, record high diesel prices have hit the state's agricultural industry especially hard and could influence the results. Peter Tubbs: The ongoing war in Iran may be influencing the midterm elections in the Corn Belt. Over the last eight months, farmers have seen the price of inputs go up, including a doubling of diesel fuel prices. The increases are squeezing producers already up against tight profit margins. Aaron Lehman, Iowa Farmers Union: Whether that is seed, whether it's chemicals, whether it's repair costs, labor costs, right after the war, the prices for fertilizer and diesel spiked dramatically, and we have seen that continue all the way through to our inputs for harvest and what -- the fertilizer for next year. Peter Tubbs: Aaron Lehman is president of the Iowa Farmers Union. He's spending an additional $1,000 day to harvest and transport his crop, double his costs from 2025. The fertilizer that fed his corn crop this season now costs 75 percent more than a year ago. The topic of diesel prices and the pressure on farmers led off a debate between Iowa's U.S. Senate candidates. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-IA): You talk about farmers and how we can help them. It is about their bottom line and doing whatever we can to reduce energy costs, input costs across the board. So I have proposed a several point energy plan, diesel prices being the top of mind there. Josh Turek (D-IA): When I'm out there with farmers, and especially at harvest time, talking about an all-time high of diesel, this is because of this war in Iran, and a war that Ashley Hinson has voted in favor of seven times. It is hurting Iowans and it's hurting Iowa's in a unique way, and we need to provide some relief to Iowans. Peter Tubbs: Lehman believes the jump in diesel and fertilizer costs are direct result of President Trump's war in Iran. The White House announced this week an $8 billion bailout for farmers experiencing high diesel costs. But high fuel prices could be a reason rural Americans, many of whom have supported Trump's policies, will vote against the Republicans on this year's ballot. After being a swing state for decades, Iowa has voted for Republicans at the federal level the last two election cycles. In a break from tradition, the Iowa Farmers Union has endorsed all the Democrats running for Congress. Aaron Lehman: That's unusual for us, but our farmers are facing such a huge crisis. We really expect to have an Iowa response to that. And this is meant to say we need a stronger response to what we're feeling here out on the ground. Peter Tubbs: The Iran war and the rising price of diesel is being felt by farmers across the heartland. In Kansas, the U.S. Senate race is a toss-up, with incumbent Republican Roger Marshall facing a strong challenge from Pastor Adam Hamilton. If Hamilton wins, he'd be the first Democrat to represent the state in nearly a century. Despite the impact on his farm, Ron Suppes says he supports the Trump administration's war in Iran and will vote for Marshall. Ron Suppes, Wheat Farmer: I'm going to tolerate it until the end. I don't think it'll last that long. I think it'll be over pretty soon. I'm surprised that all of this happened before the election, but I think they ran into a situation where we need to do something now or never. Peter Tubbs: Back in Iowa, agriculture represents only 3 percent of the state's economy, but farm business sets the political and emotional tone. Low profits on Iowa's farms have a ripple effect to the economy as a whole. It's part of the reason economic growth in Iowa has lagged behind its six neighboring states and the country at large for a decade. Aaron Lehman: I think people are really starting to have a conversation. And a lot of people are saying, I need to reconsider. Peter Tubbs: For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Peter Tubbs in Alleman, Iowa.

cc72669372ad.text: Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW and National Review editor Ramesh Ponnuru join Geoff Bennett to discuss the week in politics, including the Trump administration's legal fight over a closely watched Senate race in Alaska, reports that Elon Musk restricted Ukraine's access to Starlink and Vivek Ramaswamy's personal ad attacking his opponent in the Ohio governor's race. Geoff Bennett: For more on the Trump administration's legal fight over a closely watched Senate race in Alaska and the latest tensions surrounding the war in Ukraine, we turn to the analysis tonight of Capehart and Ponnuru. That's Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW and Ramesh Ponnuru, editor of "The National Review." David Brooks is away this evening. Always great to see you both. Jonathan Capehart: Hey, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: So, the Justice Department is now suing to potentially block certification of Alaska's Senate election if the Republican, Dan Sullivan, loses. We have not had an election yet, to be clear. Jonathan, what do you make of this president directing his DOJ? He said that he's the one who told him to do it, to lay the legal groundwork to challenge a possible defeat. Jonathan Capehart: This disrupts, breaks, whatever word you want to use, all sorts of precedent, all sorts of new ground. One, the president of the United States should not be directing the Department of Justice to do anything. I mean, he's the first president to turn the Department of Justice into his own personal law firm. That is not its role. They are supposed to be about the laws of this country on behalf of the American people. That's one. Two, the executive branch and federal government have nothing to do with elections, period, anywhere. And three, you showed -- I'm so glad you showed the ballot for everyone to see. It is not going to be difficult to determine which Dan Sullivan, if you want to vote for which one, either one, which one you want to vote for? Because incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan, it's right there in parenthesis. So this is a lawsuit in search of a crisis or chaos, and it is my hope that, whatever happens with this, it is dispatched before the election, before Election Day. Geoff Bennett: Is this -- and we see the ballot there that you were referencing? So, Ramesh, is this a legitimate concern about election integrity with the competing Sullivans, or is this an effort to cast doubt on a election result before voters have even spoken? Ramesh Ponnuru, Senior Editor, "The National Review": Well, the lawsuit is asking for a non-certification in the case that Sullivan, Senator Sullivan, loses by a margin small enough that the votes for the other Dan Sullivan made the difference. So that would be a very unusual kind of circumstance. I think it's unlikely to happen that way. It could be, frankly, that Mary Peltola, the Democrat running, just wins by a larger margin, given the way that the polling is looking. Look, Republicans think that this is a dirty trick that the Democrats have played to sour the election, to taint the election. The thing is, though, the Alaska Supreme Court said in June, he stays on the ballot. Both of these Sullivans stay on the ballot. Now, we don't know the court's rule -- the reasoning, because it hasn't released that reasoning. It says that's coming out later. But that's sort of the end of the matter legally. As far as I can tell, there's no actual federal hook for the federal government to get involved. So it's hard to see this lawsuit going very far. Geoff Bennett: What precedent would it set if a president could use the Justice Department to delay certification of an election by simply alleging that, hey, voters might be confused? Jonathan Capehart: It would be a terrible precedent. And also let's not forget this is yet one more action that he has taken to sow confusion about this upcoming midterm election, but this is in keeping with a practice he has done since January 6 of 2021, when he tried to overturn a free and fair election. This is just one more gambit. And I don't think it's going to work. Ramesh Ponnuru: It's interesting too. Senator Sullivan's campaign said, we think our voters are going to be able to tell the difference. Geoff Bennett: More to come on this on this story, for sure. So we have been reporting throughout this entire week on this story first reported by The Wall Street Journal that Elon Musk ordered restrictions on Ukraine's access to his Starlink satellite communications network. The Trump administration has been offering conflicting accounts of who authorized these restrictions. President Trump says Musk has since restored the access, but you have Zelenskyy and Ukrainian military officials reporting that these disruptions continue. When you look at this, I mean, we're talking about technology that is being used in an active war. Has the U.S. in many ways effectively outsourced part of its foreign policy to Elon Musk? Ramesh Ponnuru: Absolutely. It seems as though we have got a partly privatized foreign policy. And, look, the private sector has done enormously wonderful things in developing technology, but you do have to wonder about the wisdom of letting so much control of our policy be set by a private individual, one with his own political interests, his own political views, which are, frankly, not always perfectly grounded in reality. Geoff Bennett: Musk is one of the Republican Party's biggest financial benefactors. How do you see all of this? Jonathan Capehart: Look, I don't know if the administration has outsourced its foreign policy. To me, it looks like we have a private citizen who is taking unilateral action in a war, one. Two, I'm reminded of something that an old friend and mentor of mine, Alberto Ibarguen, when he was president of the Knight Foundation, I remember him saying to me about the Internet, Congress shall make no law that will infringe on the rights of the American people writ large. But then he asked the question, what happens if it's not Congress that is infr

6a82c003a673.text: This weekend, voters in Brazil head to the polls in a high-stakes presidential runoff that could reshape that country's political future. Will Brazil join a rightward shift across parts of the Americas, or stick with its left-wing leadership? Voting is compulsory for most adults, and the race has deepened political divisions across the country. Stephanie Sy reports. Geoff Bennett: This weekend, voters in Brazil head to the polls in a high-stakes presidential run-off that could reshape that country's political future. Will Brazil join a rightward shift across parts of the Americas or stick with its left-wing leadership? Brazil is South America's largest country, home to more than 200 million people. Voting is compulsory for most adults there, and the race has deepened political divisions across the country. Stephanie Sy has more. Stephanie Sy: The Rocinha favela is a sprawling, sloping community of 100,000 people overlooking a lesser-known part of Rio de Janeiro. The serenity from an aerial view betrays the hardships of the working-class slum and the vicious political battleground it's become. Brazilians will face a stark choice this Sunday, to either hand leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula Da Silva a fourth term or replace him with Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of a former far-right president who was convicted for leading an attempted coup. Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazilian Presidential Candidate (through interpreter): Brazil is without a president, but stay calm, because not for long. Flavio Bolsonaro is coming. Luiz Inacio Lula Da Silva, Brazilian President (through interpreter): I am convinced there is no reason why we shouldn't be elected president of the republic in the run-off. There is no reason, economic, social, or political. Stephanie Sy: Both men are plagued by corruption claims, and both have their gloves off, as seen in this fiery debate. At stake, the largest country in Latin America's political and economic direction, its relationship to the United States, and some say no less than the Amazon rain forest. In the Rocinha favela, Brazil's divisions are laid bare. Fabio Rosario, who's lived here for 40 years, says he's lost faith in 80-year-old Lula. Fabio Rosario, Rocinha Favela, Rio de Janeiro, Resident (through interpreter): I realized it was all a lie, pure deceit. He would say one thing and do another. He was there for 16 years and didn't manage to accomplish anything. Stephanie Sy: But Tamara Moreira continues to support Lula for his social policies, which include cash transfers through his Bolsa Familia, or family allowance program. Tamara Moreira, Secretary, Rocinha Residents Association (through interpreter): As a mother, I need access to social benefits, health care, schools, programs like Bolsa Familia, and food assistance. Lula's administration has always focused on the community, on single mothers and those with fewer privileges. Stephanie Sy: He's also focused on the rights of Brazil's indigenous tribes and protection of the Amazon, says Marina Silva, Lula's former environmental minister. Marina Silva, Former Brazilian Environment Minister (through interpreter): Under Jair Bolsonaro's government, the Cerrado, which is one of the biomes most pressured today in terms of deforestation, saw a 47 percent increase. He didn't create a single conservation unit. He didn't demarcate any indigenous land. Stephanie Sy: But for the majority of Brazilians, this election is about the cost of living and violent crime. Gilberto Thomaz works as a driver in Sao Paulo. He backs the Bolsonaros, both father and son. Gilberto Thomaz, Bolsonaro Supporter (through interpreter): When Jair Messias Bolsonaro came along, demonstrating that not everything in government was defined by corruption, we gained more power and strength to break away from what had been taught in schools, universities and elsewhere. Stephanie Sy: And like many on Brazil's political right, he sees the Bolsonaros' alignment with the Trump administration on what they call narco-terrorism as vital to clamping down on drug trafficking. Patricia Campos Mello, Editor at Large, Folha de S.Paulo: And now we have the tightest contest ever in Brazilian history, electoral history. I mean, it's virtually tied. Stephanie Sy: Patricia Campos Mello is editor-at-large at Folha de S.Paulo. She says Sunday's election may prove more contentious than the 2022 contest, when Lula challenged Jair Bolsonaro. Weeks after that election, Bolsonaro's supporters ransacked Brazil's presidential palace in a raid inspired by the pro-Trump activists who stormed the U.S. Capitol. While Jair serves a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup, his son Flavio has carried on the torch. The 45-year-old former senator won a first-round vote on October 4 against Lula by 2 percentage points, setting up Sunday's run-off. Patricia Campos Mello: What we do know is that never the candidate who finished second in the first round went on to win in the second round. Stephanie Sy: But Flavio's advantage is not assured. Mello's investigation into the role social media may have played in the first round results has thrown a wrench into the race. Patricia Campos Mello: The ad account of Lula Instagram was blocked. They say it was a mistake, a technical problem due to a mistake. But this was just for one hour. And before that, there were reports of the views getting affected, but there's a lot of anecdotal evidence. The only concrete things we have is the internal messages admitting to these problems. Stephanie Sy: Mello's report revealed that Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, experienced technical errors that may have disadvantaged Lula, including less visibility for his paid online ads. Lula accused Meta of algorithmic manipulation, which the company denies. This week, both candidates tried to have the other disqualified by a Brazilian court. But the contest is still very much on, and the results should be known by late Sunday. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Stephanie Sy.

577850aeeb59.text: Health care costs are climbing, putting new pressure on millions of Americans and raising questions about the coverage they can afford. The challenges extend to Medicare Advantage. We hear from seniors struggling to navigate those changes, and Geoff Bennett discusses more with Dan Weissmann. Geoff Bennett: Health care costs are climbing, putting new pressure on millions of Americans and raising questions about the coverage they can afford. According to KFF -- that's a health policy research organization -- premiums for employer-sponsored family health insurance rose 9 percent this year, with the average annual cost now exceeding $7,000 for workers. And the challenges extend to Medicare Advantage, the private insurance plan that more than 30 million Americans choose as an alternative to traditional Medicare. With Medicare's annual open enrollment period now under way, seniors are weighing their options. But in some parts of the country, insurers are pulling out of markets or eliminating plans that Americans have come to rely on. We spoke with several seniors struggling to navigate those changes and an increasingly complicated health care system. Susan Hayse, Medicare Advantage Customer: I'm Susan Hayse, and I have been on the Medicare Advantage program for four years. Bob Heffernan: Medicare Beneficiary: I'm Bob Heffernan in Vermont, and I was on the Medicare Advantage plan, actually two of them for three years, and when they both withdrew from that system, I switched back successfully to original Medicare. Diane Payne, Medicare Advantage Customer: I'm Diane Payne. And my biggest challenge for picking a plan next year is the cost of dental plans and vision are going up. Deductibles are going -- out of pocket is going up. And I just want to try to get the best deal for what I'm paying for. Bob Heffernan: Medicare Advantage was truly superior, in my view, to original Medicare. It covered the doctor's visits, the lab costs, the prescription drugs, the hospital expenses. Diane Payne: I realized last November that I got diagnosed with breast cancer and I had an agent come to the house to talk to me. It was hard to figure out what to do. Susan Hayse: This particular year, it was a big shock. Every year, you get the notification from your insurance company that there's going to be changes to your policies. There were things that had copies that were dollar amounts, like $50, changing to 50 percent. Diane Payne: I saw that chronic illnesses and things like cancer can impact, even on our Advantage plans, how much you're going to pay per office call and visit. Oh, I'd like to know what I might be getting into. Am I going to be charged more? Am I still going to be able to see my oncologist? Susan Hayse: I have developed a condition that will probably keep me from being able to switch back to original Medicare and a supplemental policy, or it'll be exorbitantly expensive. Bob Heffernan: Now, of course, we're back to paying for Medigap, which is expensive, and paying for prescription job coverage, which is expensive, and paying for the eye doctor and paying for the dentist. Diane Payne: Because of the chemo and the radiation, suddenly, dental is really important to me. And if they're just going to cover the checkups and not cover fillings or any problems, and they cut it, my current plan, I started looking elsewhere. Bob Heffernan: They all have deductibles now. So I'm not even adding that in that you're paying up until you hit a deductible, that you have to pay out of pocket before they will even start covering. Susan Hayse: If I'm unable to switch to original Medicare and a supplemental program because of a preexisting condition, I will switch to a different Advantage program that aligns more closely with the medical network I prefer here in my area. Diane Payne: It's a legwork for something that should be much simpler. Just tell us. Just put it on your plan and just say what will cost. Geoff Bennett: Lots to discuss. Luckily, we have with us Dan Weissmann, creator and host of the health care podcast "An Arm and a Leg." It's great to speak with you. So your team recently examined the changes sweeping through Medicare Advantage. What did you find? What accounts for all of these changes and, in some cases, insurance companies dropping the plans that seniors have come to rely on? Dan Weissmann, Host: Yes. And there's no single answer to it, except the biggest picture one, which is the insurance companies are private companies, they're responsible to shareholders, and they have been deciding in a lot of cases these plans that we're offering, it's not going to make us enough money, so we're not going to offer it any more, or we're going to change the terms to be more advantageous to us and less advantageous to you. Geoff Bennett: And for folks who have not yet had to rely on these programs, we should explain or you should explain, what's the difference between Medicare and Medicare Advantage? Dan Weissmann: Traditional Medicare, as people call it, is run by the federal government. It's kind of what we think of as Medicare. Unless you're checking into the hospital or getting something at the pharmacy counter, everything else, physical therapy, outpatient surgery, doctor visits, traditional Medicare only covers 80 percent of the bill. So you're left responsible for 20 percent, which can be, listen to all those things I just said, untold thousands of dollars, depending on your health. And unlike other insurance these days, there's no out-of-pocket maximum. So you could be on the hook for almost anything, unless you pay out of pocket for what's called a supplemental plan or a Medigap plan. And that fills in that gap. It follows Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted founder of Theranos, just weeks before she goes to prison. The intimate access and the questions it raises are the talk of this fall movie season. Jeffrey Brown sat down with Alissa Wilkinson for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Geoff Bennett: Screenings of the new documentary "You Can See Everything" are selling out across the country, and it's opening at more theaters today. The film is co-directed by Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder, and follows Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted founder of the blood testing company Theranos, just weeks before she goes to prison for conspiracy and fraud. But the intimate access and the questions it raises are big reasons why it's the talk of this fall movie season. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown has more for our arts and culture series, Canvas. Elizabeth Holmes, Former CEO, Theranos: I don't have anything to deceive you on. Of course I'm not deceiving you. Jeffrey Brown: "You can see everything," it was a promise made by Elizabeth Holmes to comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder. And the result is a highly unusual and provocative film. In 2023, just 34 days before she was set to begin serving an 11-year prison sentence, Holmes and her family invited Fielder and a film crew to their San Diego beach rental. At one time, Fielder even moved in. Elizabeth Holmes, seen in the film, joined by her partner, Billy Evans, and two young children, is very different from the public persona many remember, the woman with black turtlenecks and red lipstick who promised to revolutionize health care through her start-up Theranos that claimed it could use a single drop of blood to run hundreds of tests. Holmes was touted as the youngest ever self-made female billionaire. But it all came crumbling down after the company's device turned out not to work, and she was convicted of defrauding investors. For their part, Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim have produced an entirely unconventional documentary. Nathan Fielder, Filmmaker: I hope you're hungry for nothing. Jeffrey Brown: Before this, Fielder was best known for playing a deadpan version of himself in projects that blend reality and fiction, like "Nathan For You" and "The Rehearsal." Nathan Fielder: I think we're going to get along pretty well. Jeffrey Brown: "Off-the-charts bonkers, a movie that defies categorization," just some of what critics are saying of a film filled with plot twists, unexpected turns, no spoilers here, and questions of truth and perception. Elizabeth Holmes: Why would I deceive you? There's no -- there's no reason for me to do that. Nathan Fielder: OK. All right. OK, good chat. Jeffrey Brown: And joining me now is Alissa Wilkinson, film critic for The New York Times. Thanks for being with us. So why do you think this film is resonating so much? Is it the subject, the filmmaker, the nature of the film itself, all of the above? Alissa Wilkinson, Movie Critic, The New York Times: I think there are a couple of reasons. I think the subject obviously really is of interest to people, because she's been represented in pop culture so much. Nathan Fielder is also someone that a lot of people love, including myself. The kind of some things that he makes are unusual. But I think that, when you go see the film, you understand that it's actually playing with your sense of reality and how you watch documentaries. And I think for a lot of people that's really provocative and interesting. Jeffrey Brown: All right, so let's walk through some of those briefly. Nathan Fielder himself, as we said, he's not a traditional documentary maker. He's not a journalist. What is -- what do you think he's up to here? What do you see him doing? Alissa Wilkinson: I think of Nathan Fielder as kind of a performance artist who is interested in how audiences watch things. He started his career as a producer on "Canadian Idol," and so has been thinking about reality TV and the ways that we interact with what we think is real and what might not be real on television. And this is moving it over into a film context. And I think that his attempt in here to make us think about how we're watching things and what we believe to be true and how we're manipulated in those things is very relevant to the Elizabeth Holmes story, but also more broadly relevant to the way that we watch basically anything that's presented to us on a screen these days. Jeffrey Brown: All right, so then there's Elizabeth Holmes herself, who, as you said, has fascinated people for a long time, been the subject of docudramas, investigations, and so on and so forth. What portrait of her emerges? Alissa Wilkinson: Honestly, I went into seeing this movie assuming I knew everything about Elizabeth Holmes. I'd watched the documentaries. I'd watched "The Dropout," which was the Hulu television show about her. I kind of thought I knew who this person was. And I think I was constantly second-guessing my perception of her as I watched the film. And that for me is kind of a novel experience. The film is much bigger than just Elizabeth Holmes, but I think the first half really gives you a sense of why people might have been taken in, and maybe makes you question whether you think you -- they were taken in or whether she was doing something else entirely. Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky says unexplained limits on Starlink and Starshield services continue to affect Ukrainian forces, while US officials and Elon Musk offer conflicting accounts of who controls the restrictions.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed.
The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.
The BBC's Washington correspondent Daniel Bush looks at what officials have said about the technology.

A second storm in as many days is set to batter parts of the UK, as hundreds of homes remain without power following powerful winds and heavy rain on Friday.
Storm Boelo is forecast to hit on Saturday, with an amber weather warning issued from 21:00 BST across much of Scotland as well as parts of Northern Ireland and northern England where gusts of up to 80mph (128km/h) could lash exposed areas.
Travel chaos, power cuts and localised flooding are all possible as the storm sweeps in on Saturday. Engineers were continuing to work to restore power to a number of areas still without electricity.
The warning comes just one day after Storm Austen unleashed wind gusts in excess of 75mph, resulting in toppled trees, transport disruption and thousands of power outages.
Strong winds and heavy rain will persist over the weekend as Storm Boelo moves across parts of the country.
An amber weather warning for wind has been issued for across much of Scotland, excluding the Northern Isles, as well as the far north of Northern Ireland and England from 21:00 BST on Saturday to 21:00 BST on Sunday.
Wind gusts of 60-70mph are forecast, with exposed coastal areas potentially seeing speeds of up to 80mph.
The Central Lowlands could also experience periods of disruption as strong winds funnel through the region.
Travel disruption is expected - with ScotRail has confirming that some train services will be cancelled after 21:00 on Saturday - while damage caused by the winds could lead to additional power cuts.
The second bout of bad weather comes after Austen, the first named storm of the season, brought strong wind gusts to large parts of southern England and Wales throughout Friday. Bad weather disrupted travel with fallen trees blocking railway lines and roads.
In Brighton, part of the iconic West Pier - an abandoned structure that first opened in 1866 - collapsed into the sea.
The National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 60,000 properties since Storm Austen began - but on Saturday morning there were still hundreds of homes without power.
Yellow weather warnings for wind on Saturday cover Orkney, the rest of Northern Ireland and northern England.
Gusts of 55-75mph are possible in these areas, with isolated gusts potentially reaching 80mph.
While the worst of Saturday's weather is forecast to be felt in areas covered by warnings, heavy and persistent rain is expected across larger parts of the UK.
Spray and surface water could make driving conditions hazardous, while further downpours increase the risk of localised flooding.
Strong winds are forecast to continue into Sunday, although rain should gradually ease across most of the country.
Sunny spells and blustery showers are expected elsewhere, while north-east Scotland is likely to see the most persistent rainfall.
Stormy weather to continue early next week
Once the weekend's stormy weather has passed, forecasts suggest another area of low pressure will develop over the Atlantic before deepening as it approaches the UK from the south-west.
This could bring a further spell of wet and potentially very windy weather to much of the country on Monday and into Tuesday.
Whether the system will be strong enough to be named remains uncertain.
Later in the week, high pressure is expected to build over the near continent, bringing a return to drier, calmer and more settled conditions.
Are back-to-back storms unusual?
It is not unusual for storms to arrive one after another â in fact, they often develop in clusters, particularly during periods of unsettled weather across the Atlantic.
A strong jet stream is needed to help rapidly develop powerful windstorms. The process involves warmer air being pushed northwards and colder air moving southwards across large areas of the Atlantic, creating a sharp contrast in temperatures.
These temperature differences provide favourable conditions for new low-pressure systems to form and strengthen.
If these systems are then steered beneath a developing, powerful jet stream, they can intensify rapidly, potentially becoming named storms capable of bringing damaging winds, heavy rain and widespread disruption as they move towards the UK.

France is on high alert ahead of a new day of nationwide protests on Saturday, a week after the country saw some of its worst unrest in decades.
Sweeping restrictions have been imposed on demonstrations across France but hundreds of thousands of protesters are still expected to gather in Paris and elsewhere for a second round of protests organised by students, trade unions and wider anti-government groups.
The interior ministry has said it will deploy 70,000 police officers, ramping up the security presence in French cities, after the government was accused by opposition parties of failing to foresee the scale of the unrest on 17 October.
"We will not let anything go unchallenged," said Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez.
"We will be uncompromising with the vandals, with the looters, and all those who commit acts of violence," he added, explaining that separate from the planned protests, numerous calls for violence had been seen on social media from the "far left and radical extreme left".
Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.
Disillusionment is high among the French public, who have seen cost-of-living pressures increase and who are faced with increasingly dire warnings that any future government will likely come with deep spending cuts.
The protests began with demands from high school students to improve school conditions and fix staff shortages, before violence took hold in places.
President Emmanuel Macron met high-school students' representatives on Friday ahead of Saturday's protests, and although they said he had made clear commitments to them, they said students should "continue to mobilise".
Macron told them his government would make a series of commitments to improve high school education from Monday, his advisers told French TV.
Macron decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted to take place on Saturday. Several key cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier have gone further by announcing blanket bans on gatherings.
Official announcements appear to have done little to deter organisers, with hundreds of large and small demonstrations planned across France.
After a week in which some cities have lived under partial curfews, there is an inconsistent picture as to what level of protest will be permitted by authorities.
While some mayors have pressed ahead with broad bans, others have agreed to allow demonstrations registered with authorities - for example, in Marseille, a previous order barring all protests was swiftly reversed to allow a trade union-organised march to go ahead.
In Paris, a march organised by the student trade union and supported by labour groups has been ordered to stick to a route that does not go through the city centre - though preparations for potential unrest in some of the city's most recognisable parts are under way regardless.
The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums will all be closed, a scheduled home match for football team PSG has been moved to Monday, while some businesses have boarded up their windows.
In a sign of how a student-led protest movement expanded to become a wider anti-government outpouring, protesters associated with a revived gilet jaunes (yellow-vest) movement could be out in force across France on Saturday.
The protest movement, which has attracted support from both the left and right, led huge disruptive demonstrations during Macron's first term in office.
A website associated with the group listed more than 500 planned demonstrations and 200 other actions on Saturday, and demanded that Macron resign.
The group said "we refuse to add our voices to the chorus of outrage" over the violence on 17 October and accused police of attacking protesters.
France is still reeling from last week's unrest, which saw police vastly outnumbered by protesters and rioters, shops looted and buildings torched - perhaps most emblematically, the ornate 19th-Century town hall in Limoges.
French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said while visiting Limoges on Friday that the national government would pay for the building to be reconstructed "exactly as it was" rather than local taxpayers having to foot the bill.
Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin said 232 people had been imprisoned for their role in the 17 October riots and more than 1,100 others had appeared in court. Around 260 of those cases involves "charges of organised gang activity", he added.
Darmanin has ordered prosecutors to seek punitive measures against people convicted of looting or attacking police officers, including banning them from taking part in demonstrations, removing their right to vote and barring them from accessing social media.
The recent unrest has played out against a backdrop of a polarised political landscape and with France preparing for what could be the most divisive and unpredictable election period in a generation.
Macron will leave office next spring and polls suggest a candidate from his centrist movement could fail to make it through to a run-off vote in May.
That would likely leave French voters to choose between the hard-right National Rally and radical-left La France Insoumise (France Unbowed).
Leading figures from both parties have levelled the blame for the disorder at Macron and his ministers, sensing fertile ground among the French public after a period in which his centrist party has struggled to form functioning governments and pass legislation.

A project is aiming to help restore one of the UK's rare native trees across the Thames Valley using DNA testing.
Conservation groups have warned numbers of black poplar trees have fallen due to decades of felling, land drainage and habitat loss.
The Swindon to Oxford: Regenerating the Thames and Tributaries nature recovery programme is working with local conservation groups to regenerate the population along the River Thames and its flood plain.
Catrina Bass, from the Long Mead Foundation in Swindon, is involved in the project and said while the trees were "extraordinary survivors", there were just 50 recorded in Oxfordshire currently.
Describing black poplars as "Lord of the Rings" looking trees with "great gnarled trunks", she said they support other wildlife, including the poplar hornet moth.
The project secured initial funding from West Oxfordshire District Council and the Vale of White Horse Council but is now aiming to raise Â£20,000 for the work, which involves DNA analysis of existing trees, propagating new cuttings and planting them in suitable sites.
Oxfordshire County Council's Local Nature Recovery Strategy has committed to match fund the fundraiser up to Â£10,000.
Also involved in the project is the Trust for Oxfordshire's Environment, which works with community groups to fund local environmental projects.
Chief executive Benjamin Heaven Taylor said black poplars play an important role in reducing flood risk, by lining rivers and floodplains, holding water back.
He said the population that remained was "extremely fragmented", adding that it "needs a helping hand to recover".

- Published
Plans have been made for a historic swimming pond to be restored.
A new partnership between the Carew Pole Garden Trust, Torpoint Artists Collective and Rooted Futures said it was "taking the first steps" towards restoring a historic bath house swimming pond on the Antony Estate, in Cornwall, funded through the National Lottery Community Fund.
It said it hoped it would bring it into community use and improve access to nature.
In a joint statement, the partners said specialists at the garden trust had started to look at how the bath house pond "could be cleared, identify tree maintenance needs and better understand the tidal inlet and the movement of water through the site".
The bath pond and bathing house were built in the late 18th Century after being designed by Thomas Parlby.
Reginald Pole Carew, who had inherited Antony, wanted somewhere to swim in the stretch of woodland on the bank of the tidal River Lynher.
Sir Tremayne Carew Pole, who currently resides on the estate, said, when it was first built, it was used to swim in and the bath house, where the ladies would swim, had a sunken pool fed by the pond.
He said, over the years, it started to be used as a decorative pond for the garden as surrounding trees shed leaves into the pond and humus (soil organic matter) and mud formed at the bottom, making it not a great place to swim.
"I've always wanted to restore it to be swimmable and to share the benefits with those in the local community," he said.
'Creativity and community'
In the statement, the organisations said this would help shape the next steps of restoration and it aimed to "create a welcoming community resource where people can connect with green and blue space, discover the natural environment and contribute to the long-term care of a valued local landscape".
It added "education, creativity and community participation" would be central to the project.
It said Torpoint Artists Collective would develop a programme of artist-led workshops including wildlife recording, photography and nature journalling.
Open-water swimmers, nature lovers and anyone interested in the pond's future have been invited to share feedback and volunteer by emailing Antony Woodland Garden.
The partners said a Friends of the Pond group would be set up to "help shape the next steps, bringing together local knowledge, practical skills and ideas for the site's long-term care and use".

a21218cbcd14.text:
- Published
While most people are preparing to stay indoors as another storm approaches, others are getting ready to head straight into it.
Storm Boelo is expected to bring strong winds and disruption to parts of Northern Ireland this weekend.
For those tasked with keeping people safe and dealing with the damage, severe weather can bring long hours, dangerous conditions and calls for help at any moment.
In preparation for the storm, the Department for Infrastructure said their teams have been checking and clearing road gullies, monitoring river levels and tidal surges, and deploying a portion of temporary flood defences.
"Regional Community Resilience Groups have also been advised of weather patterns and to make appropriate preparations," a spokesperson said.
From rescue volunteers to tradespeople, being on standby means preparing for situations they cannot always predict.
With equipment checked and vehicles ready, they are prepared to respond whenever their help is needed.
The rescue service
Darren Harper is the Belfast area commander for the Community Rescue Service, whose volunteers are preparing to respond to emergencies.
He said severe weather can bring heavy rainfall, rising water levels and flooding, with volunteers placed on standby to respond if needed.
"Our main concern is the safety of the public," he said.
Harper explained that preparations involve checking vehicles and equipment to ensure volunteers are ready for any call out.
"Being on standby, our volunteers are ready to mobilise at a short notice," he said.
"They're checking over vehicles, checking over equipment and they're ready to assist their partner agencies and emergency services as and when the call comes."
He said the risks associated with severe weather should not be underestimated, particularly around rivers and areas prone to flooding.
"Take weather warnings seriously, avoid flooded roads and paths. Stay away from swollen rivers and never put yourself at risk by entering any flood water," he said.
"Don't underestimate the weather - and stay away from riverbanks," he added.
Harper said taking simple precautions could prevent people from getting into dangerous situations.
The roofer
For roofer Charles Howard, storms can bring an overwhelming number of calls from people needing emergency repairs.
"Normally years ago you would have loved the storms, because obviously you got the influx of work," he said.
"But now because the storms are so regular, I kind of hate it."
During a storm early last year, Howard said he received about 800 messages from people seeking help.
"It's hard to actually keep control of it," he said.
He explained that preparing for particularly bad weather usually involves stocking his van with spare roof tiles and clearing his schedule to deal with emergency calls.
"If it's going to be a bad, bad storm, you just pretty much go and load the van up with all the salvage tiles and stuff like that," he said.
He said his work can begin even before the worst of a storm arrives, with strong winds already causing damage to roofs, advising homeowners to inspect their homes before and after storms, particularly for loose or damaged tiles.
He added that dislodged ridge tiles can fall onto driveways and gardens, potentially damaging vehicles.
The tree surgeon
Tree surgeon Callum Kirk, who works in the Newtownabbey area and covers much of Belfast, said storms bring a different kind of working day.
Instead of scheduled jobs, he must be prepared to respond to fallen trees and potentially dangerous situations.
"Whenever there's a storm, we have to be on standby for any trees that could come down over someone's driveway or their property," he said.
He said preparing for severe weather involves checking and sharpening equipment, even when there is no guarantee of being called out.
"You haven't got planned work, you don't know, it's sort of a surprise, you're just more or less going to help people," he said.
Kirk explained that much of his work comes after the worst of the weather has passed, when fallen trees need to be removed from roofs, garages and other properties.
He said that work can be particularly hazardous.
"If you see a tree that looks like it's going to fall, get in contact with someone before it's too late."
He encouraged homeowners to keep an eye on potentially unstable trees throughout the year, particularly as the storm season approaches.
