The Scoop
The New York Times article appeared on September 24, 2025, under the headline The Billionaire, the Psychedelics and the Best-Selling Memoir.
The 4,980-word investigation by Katherine Rosman and Elisabeth Egan captured a wave of discomfort that had rippled from New Yorkâs publishing world to Amarillo, Texasâ police department about a bestselling memoir by a billionaire pillar of Manhattan society. Amy Griffinâs The Tell told the story of a woman whose perfect exterior masked childhood trauma, and how the drug MDMA helped her remember and ultimately move past childhood sexual abuse.
The Times story turned her success into a parable about class and Americaâs new ultrarich. Most damagingly, the Times discussed the possibility that Griffinâs memory of sexual abuse might have been borrowed from a classmate who attested that stories in The Tell were âeerily similar to the abuse she herself enduredâ in middle school from a different teacher.
Some of Griffinâs friends suggested she shrug off the bad press. But she was livid, consumed by it, friends said. It was intensely personal: In the days after the story, there had even been an exchange of Snap messages between Rosmanâs son, a student at the University of Southern California, and a friend of one of Griffinâs children. The messages, reviewed by Semafor, were heated but respectful.
The weekend after the story published, Griffin and her husband John Griffin, whose hedge fund was the source of their billions, were in the safe space of the superagent Ari Emanuelâs annual Aspen retreat, âThe Weekend.â A person seated with Griffin in Aspen recalled her saying the Times had sought to destroy her life and her familyâs.
Then Griffin said something that shocked her interlocutor, the person recalled: By calling into question Griffinâs account, Rosman had made her and her childrenâs life miserable â and she would do the same to the Times reporterâs son.
Griffin, through a spokesperson, heatedly disputed the claim: âAmy Griffin has never threatened Katherine Rosmanâs children or taken any action to harm Ms. Rosman or her family. These allegations are categorically false,â the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson cited the exchange of Snap messages after the story published. âAt an event shortly after publication, Mrs. Griffin was upset about the impact on her daughter and expressed those feelings in a conversation with a friend. Her words were later taken out of context and mischaracterized as a threat she never made.â
The person who heard Griffinâs comments in Aspen understood them as a threat, and said they felt obliged to act.
The person asked a mutual contact to warn Rosman, according to three people familiar with that exchange.
Rosman, in turn, alerted her employer. Then The New York Timesâ general counsel, David McCraw, spoke to Griffinâs lawyer, Tom Clare, though the two men offered somewhat different versions of what was said.
Thereâs no indication Griffin ever took any action against Rosmanâs son.
But Griffinâs focus on the Times story and other fallout has, acquaintances say, continued. The classmate, Joleene Altum, sued Griffin for emotional distress and invasion of privacy, and Griffin countersued for defamation in a bitter, ongoing legal battle. Itâs been covered breathlessly on Instagram and by celebrity media â led by the former Access Hollywood host Billy Bush, who last Monday on his podcast described being confronted by Griffin at a wedding on the Hawaiian island of Lanai.
âIn my opinion,â he said, Griffin âis a woman who has become unhinged, tearing down innocent people, trying to ruin lives and careers,â he said. âShe has attempted to blackball people from schools. Sheâs threatened to bankrupt media publications and individuals, including me.â
Griffin has also continued to focus her ire on Rosman, who didnât provide a comment to Semafor for this story. Months after the disputed exchange at Aspen, Griffin spoke to a person in a position to influence admissions at a major American university, a person with direct knowledge of their conversation confirmed.
In the conversation, Griffin asked the person to use that influence to deny admission to Rosmanâs children, the person with direct knowledge of their conversation said. Rosmanâs daughter is a senior in high school. The person did not act on the request, they said.
âMrs. Griffin has never contacted anyone associated with any university or school regarding Ms. Rosmanâs children,â Griffinâs spokesperson said.
âIf these troubling reports are accurate, this is a stunning abuse of power and influence wielded against the family of a journalist doing her job to report the news and follow the facts, simply because the subject of that reporting didnât like the coverage,â New York Times spokesman Charlie Stadtmiller said in a statement. âThe Timesâs reporting of Sept. 2025 was a careful, fair and above all accurate pursuit of the facts that probed important questions about memory, the past, traumatic events and the state of memoir publishing.â
Benâs view
Itâs tempting to see this story âÂ as the Times did âÂ as a parable of a billionaire class that has lost all moral moorings. But as I spoke to people in and around Griffinâs gilded circle, it was the opposite: Members of her social world were shocked by the suggestion sheâd take revenge on a journalistâs children, and most found it wildly out of character. Some I spoke to said they couldnât believe she meant what she said. One sought to warn Rosman, and the other did not act on Griffinâs alleged suggestion to attempt to intervene in Rosmanâs daughterâs college application.
Indeed, even as Americaâs emotional and capricious billionaires inspire terror in its professional and middle classes, they seem at times more vulnerable to negative media attention than anyone else. For the second time in three weeks, Indian cartoonist Satish Acharya found himself effectively invisible on Instagram in his own country.
The 55-year-old discovered on Tuesday that his account had once again been briefly blocked in India, allegedly with no explanation from the platform.
Just a few weeks ago, another cartoonist, Manjul, had found that Instagram had restricted a post criticising India's election commission over its controversial revision of voter rolls. His profile remained accessible.
The cases have raised concerns about the use of legal orders to restrict political satire in India, with cartoonists saying they are often given little explanation for why their work has been blocked.
Acharaya's account was first restricted from 28 September to 6 October, when users in India could neither find his profile through search nor access it through a web link.
Anyone trying to access his profile saw a message saying it was unavailable under India's Information Technology Rules.
The rules allow authorities and courts to order social media platforms to remove or restrict content.
The government says they help tackle unlawful material, but artists and free-speech advocates warn they can stifle India's rich tradition of political satire.
"Meta platforms have been restricting the reach of my cartoons for some years," Acharya told the BBC. "But when my entire profile was restricted in India, I was a little sad."
He wrote to Meta, Instagram's parent company, but received no reply. He says he was preparing to go to court when his account became accessible again in early October, only to be blocked again earlier this week for three days.
In a statement, Meta told the BBC that it may temporarily restrict accounts to comply with India's IT Rules but did not explain the specific reasons for restricting Acharya's account or Manjul's post.
Critics say the restrictions come as humour and satire play an increasingly visible role in political dissent in India, particularly among younger people.
Memes and Gen-Z humour helped fuel protests over education and jobs in July, which led to the resignation of India's education minister. Online debate has also intensified over a controversial revision of voter rolls that removed 130 million names.
The political significance of social media has not been lost on the government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has urged ministers to strengthen their online presence and connect with younger audiences.
At the same time, technology policy expert Prateek Waghre says the government is increasingly using legal orders to regulate online content.
The Indian Express reported, external that government agencies sent nearly 195,000 blocking and content-restriction orders to platforms including Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July through the federal government's Sahyog portal.
The figures, obtained through a right-to-information request, do not show how many posts were ultimately restricted or removed. The BBC has not seen the original response.
Waghre says that some platforms, particularly Meta, "seem more willing to comply", he says, while X appears more willing to push back. But limited public data makes comparisons difficult. Meta declined to comment on his assessment.
The government has also reportedly sought greater scrutiny of how social media platforms recommend content.
Earlier this week, several media outlets reported, external that authorities had asked Meta to ensure its systems did not steer users towards "a single or limited set of narratives" and strengthen checks on content that could "cause public disorder or incite violence".
The BBC has sought comment from India's IT ministry on the restrictions and reported instructions to Meta but has not received a response.
Of course, political satire has a long history in India - as do attempts to curb it.
Cartoons have been a fixture of Indian journalism since independence, with RK Laxman's Common Man becoming one of its most recognisable characters.
But cartoonists have also faced censorship. During the Emergency in the 1970s, when civil liberties were suspended and the press was tightly controlled, Abu Abraham continued drawing, even as dozens of his cartoons were stamped "not passed by censors".
In 2012, cartoonist Aseem Trivedi was arrested on sedition charges over cartoons allegedly mocking the Indian constitution. The charges were later dropped.
Today, concerns about restrictions on political expression extend beyond cartoonists. India ranks 157th in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, while critics accuse the government of putting growing pressure on independent media. The government rejects the criticism, saying India's media remains free and vibrant.
Comedians have also faced controversy over political satire. Kunal Kamra, known for his jokes about Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his party, has faced threats, cancelled shows and legal action.
For cartoonists, however, challenging those in power is central to their work.
"We are among the default opposition," says Sandeep Adhwaryu, a cartoonist at a leading Indian newspaper.
"The nature of the craft is to oppose," he says, adding that cartoonists, like journalists, must question whoever holds power.
Acharya says he has followed that principle throughout his career. Before 2014, many of his cartoons targeted the Congress-led government and were shared by BJP leaders.
"I never faced official restrictions on my cartoons during the previous governments, though there would be some trolling occasionally," he says.
Now, with the BJP in power, much of his satire is directed at Modi's government.
Social media has allowed independent cartoonists like Acharya to reach audiences without relying on newspapers or other traditional outlets.
"We are not associated with newspapers or any mainstream media. That's why we can draw," says Manjul.

Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.
These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.
They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.
But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.
In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.
It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.
Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.
They are growing rapidly
There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map, external, a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.
That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000, external operational sites.
As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.
Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.
But when it comes to actual capacity, the US is ahead by a much larger margin, with China in second place and Europe lagging far behind.
This gap is set to widen in the coming years, leading some to warn Europe risks missing out on the potential economic benefits of the AI boom, external.
They are getting bigger
Data centres vary wildly in size, ranging from ones that fit inside a garden shed to others covering vast expanses of land.
The world's largest operational data centre is widely reported to be one run by China Telecom in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, covering an area of approximately one million square metres (10.7 million sq ft). That is equivalent to about 140 Fifa football pitches.
However, much larger sites are under construction as the graphic below shows.
All these sites are being built exclusively to provide the immense computing power needed to run AI services.
For instance, Colossus 2, which is part of the wider Colossus campus, will house hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips made by tech giant Nvidia.
It will also be used to train xAI's chatbot Grok. Elon Musk's company will use 41 methane gas turbines to help power the site, which activists say could "significantly increase" local air pollution, external. Local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards.
They use more electricity than France
The pressure data centres put on local resources has sparked increasing concern. These facilities can use significant amounts of water to cool their systems, which could lead to water shortages, some experts say.
Data centres worldwide are also thought to consume more electricity than the whole of France, as the chart below shows.
This growing hunger for power is driving up carbon emissions, analysis shows, while putting pressure on local grids, which some fear could push up energy prices.
With others worried about the noise data centres make and the space they take up, a public backlash is gathering steam.
Some 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and it could be a key issue in November's midterm elections.
Outside the US, opposition to data centres has emerged in countries like Mexico, France, Indonesia and the UK.
But they can boost jobs
But supporters say data centres are critical to national security, and the development of AI.
They also say they are good for the economy, external, attracting investment, generating tax revenue and creating jobs in areas like construction.
A recent report by the Brookings Center, external suggests data centres do create local jobs, although fewer than industry advocates claim.
The type of data centre matters too. So-called hyperscale facilities - massive sites owned and run by tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft - have a bigger positive effect on jobs, it found.
But "colocation" facilities, which lease space to remote tenants without a local presence, brought fewer benefits.
As the debate over their merits intensifies, the data centre rollout continues.
This year, the tech industry is expected to spend a combined $765bn, external ($544bn) on AI infrastructure in 2026, with this topping $1tn next year.
But as concerns about the environmental impact grow, the tech industry is exploring alternatives.
One idea is to put data centres in space, external or on the Moon, where they could harness abundant solar energy.
Others predict that more AI processing could eventually be carried out by the hardware already inside our computers and smartphones, reducing the need for vast data centres altogether.
Additional reporting and design by Erwan Rivault, Matt Faraci and Dominic Bailey.

Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships - the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022.
The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced its decision on Sunday, four months after confirming Russian athletes would again be eligible to compete in its events.
In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifted a suspension on the Russian Olympic Committee.
That suspension had been imposed following the country's invasion of Ukraine.
The IOC's subsequent decision potentially opened the way for Russian athletes to compete for their country at the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.
The IWF announced the host cities of four world championships at junior, youth and senior levels, awarding the 2029 senior event to Ahmedabad in India.
"All the bids we received were excellent and we are sure that the championships in your respective countries will be a huge success," said IWF general secretary Jose Quinones.
No world championships in an Olympic sport, summer or winter, have been held in Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine.
The 2025 World Aquatics Championships, initially awarded to the Russian city of Kazan, were instead moved to Singapore.
Moscow has not held the World Weightlifting Championships since 1983.
The Russian Weightlifting Federation said: "[We are] the first Olympic sports federation to succeed in bringing a top-level official competition back to the country in many years."
Federation president Aleksandr Vinokurov thanked the IWF in a post on Telegram "for their trust", with the championships also serving as a qualifying event for the 2032 Olympic Games in Brisbane, Australia.
"Russia has all the necessary experience and capabilities to host competitions of the highest level," he said.
"Moscow has repeatedly staged major international sporting events and has modern infrastructure."
In announcing its decision in July to provisionally lift Russia's suspension, the IOC said that no decision had been taken on whether Russia could display their flag, colours and anthem at the Olympic âGames.
The IOC said it would continue to "not organise IOC events in Russia or invite Russian government or state officials to its events".
Some Russian athletes competed at the 2024 Paris Olympic Games and this year's Winter Olympics in Milan as neutrals.
Ukraine filed an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) requesting that the IOC decision to lift its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee be annulled.
The IOC's move decision came after the International Paralympic Committee had already ended Russia's exile from global sports events, with the country's athletes allowed to compete under their national flag at the Winter Paralympics.
Five Ukrainian athletes are listed to compete in the 2026 IWF World Championships in Ningbo, China, which are scheduled to take place from 27 October to 8 November.

c610f742ab55.text:
- Published
US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.
The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.
Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay Â£1,500 costs.
Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense".
The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension.
The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries.
In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained."
CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder.
Sentencing Brown, Judge Baumgartner said: "This was not planned violence. It was nevertheless serious violence by two people in a crowded nightclub."
The judge told Brown: "Violence of this kind in a crowded nightclub is serious, it creates an obvious risk, not only to the person against whom it is directed, but also to others nearby."
He added that Brown's conduct was "particularly dangerous" and that he had to be "physically pulled away" from the attack.
The judge said Brown's fame, commercial success and professional standing "do not entitle you to special treatment - the law applies equally to everyone".
But judge Baumgartner also said he had noted Brown's guilty plea, compliance with bail conditions, and the impact a custodial sentence would have on Brown's children, and said the singer's "risk of further offending is low".
Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to a charge of affray at Southwark Crown Court in July.
The singer had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied, and which were subsequently dropped.
These were assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon.
Following Brown and Akinlolu's guilty pleas, the CPS released a statement outlining that Brown had approached Diaw on the dance floor, hitting him over the head with a glass bottle twice, before Akinlolu then punched Diaw in the head.
"They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the CPS said. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor."
On Monday, the court was shown three pieces of CCTV footage from inside Tape nightclub on the night of the attack.
The attack lasted no more than 20 seconds, but Brown could be seen hitting the victim four times with a tequila bottle, twice to the head.
Prosecutor, Heidi Stonecliffe KC, described the weapon as a "heavy square-shaped tequila bottle" and said Diaw was approached by Brown at around 03:00.
The footage showed that the nightclub was very small and packed at the time.
The defence described Chris Brown as a "dedicated and a loving father of four children," someone who is "positive and present".
The singer is described as having lived "a good and law-abiding life" since his last conviction in 2013.
The events in Tape nightclub were described by the defence as a "short and deeply regretted incident".
Brown's defence lawyer told the court that he apologises to all those present at the club at the time of the attack.
"This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Sallie Bennett-Jenkins KC said.
"It is, however, an incident which was very short-lived, lasting something more than 17 seconds but no more than 20.
"It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr Brown... offers a profound apology to all those present."
The court heard Akinlolu "genuinely believed" that Brown was "under attack" when he joined the attack, punching Diaw.
Brown was described as being like a "brother" to Akinlolu, his lawyer Laurie-Anne Power KC told the court.
She added: "He genuinely believed him to be under attack and became involved, and thereafter accepts his initial involvement very quickly evolved into the events he has pleaded guilty to."
Diaw was taken to St Mary's Hospital in London after the attack. Ms Stonecliffe KC said he was discharged with "pain relief and a diagnosis of head injury and superficial injury of the knee".
An MRI scan taken in early March showed a "high grade injury to a ligament on the inner side of the left knee", the court heard.
Defending Brown, Ms Bennett-Jenkins KC said there was a "relatively low level of force" and disputed how significant the injuries were.
The defence argued that the attack left no fractures or broken skin and there was an absence of serious injuries.
Diaw, the victim, was "not supportive of the prosecution" and "withdrew" his support some time after the incident, the court heard.
Brown and Akinlolu stood up and faced one another and clasped hands after the judge concluded his sentencing remarks before walking out of the glass dock.
There were loud cheers outside the court as Chris Brown left the building as he appeared to stop to sign an autograph.
After the sentencing, Brown shared a video from inside his car on his Instagram story, showing him looking out the window before turning to the camera and giving a thumbs-up.

Anthropic has said artificial intelligence could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.
The company behind AI chatbot Claude revealed losses of more than $80.7bn (Â£60.5bn) in the first half of the year. It said it generated revenue of $16.3bn over the same period.
The number of shares to be released and their price range is yet to be determined.
Anthropic's valuation when it goes public has been expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which this summer was the biggest-ever stock listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion.
Ahead of its public listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.
It said that advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Anthropic, which was founded just five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, announced its intention to go public in June.
Its most significant rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit, saying it, too, intended to go public. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.
After the companies had decided on such plans, a wave of cyber-security and other types of technological breaches occurred involving their AI agents, or AI bots that are designed to operate somewhat autonomously.
Current and former staff of both companies also gained public attention with new warnings that AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect the whole of humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.
In its financial filings, Anthropic detailed losses that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.
Anthropic said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT. It will be the first true AI company to go public, marking a test for the future of the technology.
Tech companies have been heavily investing in costly AI infrastructure and tools, like data centres and the informational models that underly all AI technology, pouring more than $1tn into the efforts over the last year alone.

Brazil's President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro.
Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since the return to civilian rule in 1985 to win an election after losing the first round of voting.
Lula told celebratory crowds this election is a "loss for negativity, lies", later adding "long live democracy".
FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, who is the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled, which experts say is unlikely.
In an unprecedented move, polls were also extended for two hours on Sunday evening after both candidates made requests for different reasons.
Lula's team had argued that voters in SÃ£o Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Senator Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in SÃ£o Paulo as the reason for their request.
The decision - issued by the Supreme Court just as polling stations were due to close - meant that some had already shut and were not able to re-open.
Supreme Court President Kassio Nunes Marques - appointed by the older Bolsonaro - confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voting extension did not cause issues for the count or the electoral process.
Lula secured 51.79% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.21% - a difference of 4.4 million votes between the two candidates.
The result came as a surprise after Bolsonaro - who has the backing of his father - won the first round of voting on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%.
But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one.
Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the first and second rounds of a presidential election since 1989.
As disconsolate Bolsonaro supporters left the house in BrasÃlia where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in SÃ£o Paulo to celebrate and address his supporters.
"This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country", the former metal worker said. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people."
Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin told him: "You, for the second time, have saved Brazilian democracy."
Bolsonaro, who had been poised to give a victory speech, said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable" and "impossible".
But electoral law experts have told BBC Brasil that the chances of the results being annulled are remote.
Fernando Neisser from the Institute of Lawyers of SÃ£o Paulo (Iasp) said it would be "difficult from a legal standpoint" given that the margin of victory was relatively large, and would depend on the "narrative" his lawyers put forward.
Expert Alberto Rollo said that dates for presidential elections in Brazil are fixed and determined by the constitution, which would add another complication to getting it annulled.
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.
His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.
But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.
Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" - which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".
Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.
Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.
While Trump has yet to react, other world leaders have been congratulating Lula on his win.
Ecuador President Daniel Noboa Azin said the region had "common enemies, shared challenges, and much to gain when we work together."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory", saying "the comeback of global progressivism has just begun". French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world".
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world".
Additional reporting by VinÃcius de S. Mendes, BBC Brasil

e1209836ac27.text: Anthropic's IPO filing includes an extensive list of extreme warnings — including the chance its own technology could put humanity at risk. Why it matters: These are the wildest IPO risk factors in history, a jarring collision of Wall Street legalese and what some see as Silicon Valley sci-fi, including catastrophic threats to humanity, blackmailing AI models, and $750 billion in computing commitments. Driving the news: Anthropic's prospectus includes over 90 pages of risk factors, which make up about a third of the paperwork overall. Among the most eye-popping, the company warns: 💥 AI could post "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," and could try to manipulate humans; 🔎 Models are becoming harder to monitor as they're getting better at circumventing oversight, and the pace of autonomous work alone could exceed the ability of human reviewers to monitor actions; 💰 AI models generally, including its own, have exhibited behavior resembling blackmail, including attempts to resist being shut down. Zoom in: Anthropic also disclosed that four of its models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations. In one incident, a model used a discovered password to gain administrator access, collected additional credentials, changed system settings and accessed an individual's personal information. Anthropic said it found no evidence that the models pursued goals beyond their assigned tasks or attempted to evade oversight. The big picture: Every company has to lay out risks for their investors to consider when they go public. But Anthropic is the first in modern history to go to such existential extremes. Friction point: The company also acknowledged that its success depends in large part on its ability to develop the best frontier intelligence. It admits that could butt up against safety practices, adding that model capabilities may then "advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement" corresponding safety measures. That underscores a fundamental tension critics have warned about: As Anthropic scales and faces pressure from public market investors to build better models than its competitors, its commercial ambitions could increasingly clash with its safety commitments. By the numbers: The risk factors also include the more typical financial cautions. Anthropic has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to cloud computing and equipment leases, even as customers can reduce their usage relatively quickly. Some agreements require minimum payments regardless of demand, and the company warns that failing to meet certain obligations could trigger defaults elsewhere, potentially accelerating debt repayments and jeopardizing access to computing infrastructure. Anthropic also acknowledges that it previously underestimated its compute needs. But overestimating future demand could leave it paying for expensive, underutilized infrastructure. The bottom line: Anthropic's IPO paperwork is an unusually candid warning about the risks of building a business around technology that its creator acknowledges may become increasingly difficult to control.

Then the students came World Oct 26, 2026 9:52 AM EDT BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbia's populist strongman Aleksandar Vucic dominated the Balkan country's politics for 14 years. Then came the students. The long-ruling authoritarian leader on Sunday conceded the defeat of his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party to a grassroots movement of university students in a parliamentary election. The students had led protests for almost two years before unseating him in a historic change of government. READ MORE: From France to Albania, how social unrest is fueling protests across Europe The 56-year-old political veteran easily outplayed political opponents in the past and thought he could do it again. Ahead of Sunday's ballot he pulled a maneuver in the style of his ally Russian President Vladimir Putin when he resigned the presidency to pursue a bid to become the prime minister. Vucic then launched a fierce campaign involving favorable around-the-clock coverage on state media and attacks on opponents. He handed out cash to voters and promised higher pensions, new roads and cheaper medicines. It didn't work. The diverse youth movement's message that rampant corruption, cronyism and organized crime under Vucic were eating away at the country resonated widely with voters. The student protests first started in 2024 after a collapsed canopy at a renovated train station in Serbia's north killed 16 people, triggering claims that graft-fueled negligence led to poor construction work and eventually to the crash. Defiant, Vucic on Sunday blamed his defeat on foreign interference. "I want people to know," he said. "This was the verification of a revolution that they carried out directly with support of different European countries and the deep American state, the one that is also against President (Donald) Trump." Vucic began his career as an ultranationalist During a political career spanning more than 30 years, Vucic morphed from being an extreme nationalist who supported aggression against non-Serbs in the former Yugoslavia to a populist who shifted his preferences to balance between global powers and influences. During the wars in the 1990s, Vucic was one of the radical party leaders who advocated the creation of a "Greater Serbia" that would include territories in Croatia and Bosnia where minority Serbs live. Those policies are widely blamed for bloody conflicts that killed over 100,000 people and displaced millions. Vucic was known for fiery speeches, including one in Serbia's parliament where he said that for each Serb killed in the Bosnian war, 100 Bosnian Muslims must die. He later said that he didn't mean it literally. As information minister in the late 1990s, Vucic oversaw media critical of then-President Slobodan Milosevic slapped with heavy fines or shut down. He shifted away from ultranationalism to a proclaimed pro-EU stance on the eve of his party's electoral win in 2012. He embraced Europe for a time In office, Vucic positioned himself as pro-European and pro-Russian, and as an admirer of Trump. Ahead of the decisive ballot, however, Vucic re-embraced his hard right roots and turned to Putin again as he struggled to restore his shaken voter base. Vucic defied the EU last month by allowing a hero's funeral in Belgrade for Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb army commander convicted of genocide by a U.N. court in the Netherlands. "It is no coincidence that Vladimir Putin said he hopes that I will be the prime minister," Vucic boasted days ahead of the ballot, ditching the proclaimed pro-EU position that helped his populist party come to power in 2012. Vucic's fall draws varied reactions in Russia Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov expressed hope Monday that the post-Vucic government will retain friendly relations with Russia. Vucic had refused to join EU sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine despite formally seeking membership for Serbia in the 27-nation bloc. READ MORE: Serbians protest real estate project linked to Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner "We highly value the contribution Mr. Vucic has made to the development of our bilateral relations," Peskov said. "We intend to continue doing everything possible to help the development of our relations with Belgrade," Peskov said. "But, as you know, it takes two to tango." Konstantin Kosachev, a deputy speaker of the upper house, the Federation Council, said that the Serbian elections' outcome could signal that "there would be one sovereign country less in Europe." But Konstantin Malofeyev, a hawkish tycoon who sponsors a virulently nationalistic media outlet, welcomed Vucic's defeat, denouncing him as a hypocrite who has tried to maneuver between Russia and the West. "The Serbian people have delivered a historic verdict on the Vucic regime," Malofeyev said on his Telegram channel. "The era of political hypocrisy and duplicity is drawing to a close." Vucic controlled Serbia for 14 years In the past 14 years, Vucic served as a deputy prime minister, the prime minister and president. As president for nearly 10 years, Vucic turned the largely ceremonial post into the center of power in the country. He was known for frequent addresses to the nation and appearances in pro-government media. "He is a competitor who has mastered a technology of governing that is based on stick and carrot, and the idea that nobody but him is right," Dejan Pavlovic, a professor in the Faculty of Political Sciences at the University of Belgrade, told The Associated Press recently. The EU goal of reducing global deforestation could have damaging consequences for Ethiopiaâs coffee sector and wider economy, a think tank said. Some 15 million people in the country widely considered to be the birthplace of coffee are involved in the industry, which sends 30% of its output to the EU, according to London-based ODI Global.
The blocâs new rules, due to come into force at the start of next year, will require exporters of certain commodities â including coffee and cocoa â to prove they are deforestation-free. The change is placing tough traceability and mapping burdens on producers. Coffee growing in Ethiopia is dominated by smallholders, whose beans are mixed together and sold on. Difficulties in tracing their origin could result in 60% of these growers being excluded from the European market, ODI Global estimated.
Ethiopiaâs coffee authority is compiling data, but the process is not complete. In order to reverse historical deforestation, the country has also committed to planting 8 billion new trees this year, though the project has faced questions over verification and survival rates.

Kodal Minerals plans to expand its lithium business across West Africa, betting the gold-rich region can become a major supplier of the battery metal, Reuters reported.
The London-listed miner began producing lithium last year in Mali, in a joint venture with Chinese mining company Hainan Mining. Kodal has now agreed to acquire up to 80% of the Asamankese lithium exploration project in Ghana.
Africa is attracting investment from major miners as China and Western governments compete to secure minerals for clean energy and advanced technologies. Lithium, used in rechargeable batteries for electric vehicles, electronics, and electricity storage, has drawn more than $2 billion in Chinese investment to Zimbabwe, Africaâs largest producer, since 2021.

A US solar energy provider plans to grow its Africa operations by adding facilities in Nigeria that will serve more than 30,000 people in the oil-rich, but electricity-poor, Niger Delta region. Deployment of grids backed by battery storage systems is ongoing, with a full launch slated for next year.

Solar minigrids have presented African households and businesses with a viable alternative to unreliable fossil-fuel-powered national grids strained by under-investment. Swazi chef Sanza Sandile is using food to combat anti-migrant sentiment in South Africa. His Yeoville Dinner Club, found on the main street of the immigrant-rich inner Johannesburg neighborhood, is now in its 10th year.
The menus for the family-style meals unapologetically embrace the cultures and cuisines from across the continent and beyond, challenging the xenophobia stoked by some politicians, which has resulted in many migrant-owned restaurants seeing trade plummet.
Sandile, whose mother fled the apartheid regime, and who was raised partly by an uncle who took part in the armed struggle against the white-minority government, has spent years gathering recipes from around the world, believing food can invoke memory and inspire integration.

160643e67406.text: By — Eléonore Hughes, Associated Press Eléonore Hughes, Associated Press By — Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press By — Anna-Catherine Brigida, Associated Press Anna-Catherine Brigida, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/incumbent-lula-is-declared-winner-of-brazils-election-as-bolsonaro-rejects-results Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Incumbent Lula is declared winner of Brazil's election as Bolsonaro rejects results World Oct 26, 2026 9:19 AM EDT RIO DE JANEIRO (AP) — Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of widening U.S. influence in Latin America. WATCH: Brazil's high-stakes presidential runoff could reshape country's future With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote. Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours. Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated to take the presidency in 2022. Lula's triumph bucks a regional trend of victories for right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Trump. It also means Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, will likely continue defying Trump's demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs. Lula says Brazil is 'not anyone's backyard' A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with First Lady Rosângela da Silva and allies after his runoff victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Speaking to his supporters, thousands of whom gathered on Sao Paulo's main artery and in Rio de Janeiro's Cinelandia Square, Lula expressed his gratitude to the Brazilian people, and pledged to respect all Brazilians, regardless of gender or religion. He also attacked Bolsonaro. "This was a defeat for denialism and lies. I must confess that every time I attended a debate, I felt embarrassed," he said. He also doubled down on his commitment to Brazil's sovereignty. "Either the homeland remains free, or we die for Brazil," he said. "This country will not accept being anyone's backyard." In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the color of Lula supporters — shouted "You lost! Cry harder!" to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed. Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula. "I don't understand how people can vote for Lula," he said. "The country is collapsing." Lula is set to begin his fourth non-consecutive term as president on Jan. 5, 2027. Bolsonaro rejects results after confusion at polling places The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates. Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in Sao Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favor the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he is favored. The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time. Polling stations in Brasilia and Rio de Janeiro closed shortly after the original 5 p.m. deadline, reporters for The Associated Press observed. READ MORE: Brazil's Lula warns against foreign interference in elections, urges leaders to respond to global conflicts Bolsonaro, whose father is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after he lost the 2022 presidential election to Lula, pointed out that Zanin is Lula's former lawyer and criticized him for "changing the rules of the game in the middle of the game." "It's impossible to recognize the results of the election in the context of these things that happened," he said. It's not clear if Bolsonaro's complaint could meet the legal threshold to annul the results. Bolsonaro also has the right to request a recount if he has evidence of fraud, but that might not change the results. The president of the electoral court, Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Court by former President Bolsonaro, said that the extension of voting hours did not impact results. Joao Pedro Padua, a law professor at the Fluminense Federal University, said that Bolsonaro can file a lawsuit directly with the country's electoral authorities or the Supreme Court, asking for the elections to be declared null and void. "But there isn't much legal basis for that," Padua said. "The extension of voting hours is unusual, but for it to invalidate the elections, the candidate would have to prove that it affected voters' ability to freely express their will. There doesn't seem to have been any such impact." Lula overcame concerns about security and cost of living Bolsonaro bested Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. Sunday night's victory by Lula marked the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency. Lula faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro mad

Senegalâs government is locked in a budget standoff with parliament as the oil price crisis triggered by the war in Iran strains the heavily indebted West African countryâs finances. The revised 2026 budget, which sets spending at about $13 billion, would cut public investment while increasing energy subsidies. The bill is due before lawmakers on Tuesday, after the finance committee rejected it.
Parliament Speaker Ousmane Sonko, who leads the largest party in the legislature, said the budget sacrifices essential investment and demanded greater transparency over government finances. Sonko, who was fired as premier in May, has clashed with his successor over how to manage the countryâs debt. Prime Minister Ahmadou Al Aminou LÃ´ said the government would use âinstitutional and constitutional toolsâ to end the impasse if the deadlock persists.

The UAE is contending with an oil spill off its shores, the most visible example of the risks of attacks on tankers and a threat to an already fragile tourist season. Beaches are closed across the northern UAE, including in Ras Al Khaimah, where the Wynn Al Marjan Island is set to open next year. This was not the first oil spill of the war: A tanker ran aground near Omanâs southeastern coast, leaving a slick covering about 6.5 times the land area of Manhattan, and Iran had an oil spill off Qeshm Island near a breeding ground for endangered hawksbill sea turtles, Bloomberg reported.

For years, Qatar has faced accusations of supporting Hamas, the Muslim Brotherhood, and Iran, and using Al Jazeera and American universities to spread its agenda. While Doha has influence among Islamist movements, it has consistently rejected nefarious intentions, pointing to its role as a mediator and US defense partner. Still, the charges are used as political ammunition in the US and Israel, where key elections will be held over the next two weeks, with some Israelis in particular repeating claims that Qatari funding helped enable Hamasâ Oct. 7 terror attack.
The charges have always been short on evidence. A recent Time investigation uncovered secret correspondence showing that Israel encouraged and coordinated nearly $2 billion in Qatari payments to Gaza over more than a decade. In a 2020 letter, Mossadâs director at the time praised Dohaâs humanitarian efforts for âensuring stability and safety in the region.â
The accusation that Qatar uses university funding to promote antisemitism has also been debunked by a former US ambassador to Qatar who is affiliated with Georgetown, which has a branch in Doha. He noted that 97% of the $6.25 billion Qatar provided to American universities since 2001 went to six institutions, all of which have campuses in the country.

Gulf states are closely watching as Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday, in the first national election since the Oct. 7, 2023 terror attack. A victory for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would mean an increasingly assertive military posture from Israel; his defeat could âbe an opportunity to move towards a more stable regional order,â Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at Chatham House, told Semafor.
Broadly, a Netanyahu win would mean more of the same for the region, too: The Abraham Accords would hold, and Saudi normalization would stay out of reach without a credible path to Palestinian statehood, Vakil, who is also a lecturer at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, said. A new government wouldnât necessarily shift course on Iran or the Palestinians, but it could âcreate some diplomatic spaceâ for Gulf engagement on Gaza and the West Bank, according to Vakil. âA Netanyahu defeat would be welcomed by most Gulf capitals.â
Polls point to a deadlocked parliament, with the opposition â an anyone-but-Netanyahu bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot â on track to win the most seats, but short of a majority. That means the potential for protracted coalition talks (Netanyahu took 58 days to form a government after the 2022 vote). Eisenkot supports military action to stop Iranâs nuclear program if necessary, but in recent weeks he has called regime change in Tehran militarily unachievable.

e09ff748fe6b.text:
Saudi Arabia reopened Riyadhâs international airport on Sunday even as Yemenâs Houthis vowed to continue attacking the facility, which they had forced to close after deadly strikes two weeks ago. Operations resumed with limited flights by Saudi carriers from half the airport. The capital faced renewed attacks on Sunday, with authorities reporting the interception of Houthi ballistic missiles.
Foreign airlines have not yet resumed flights to Riyadh, and some traffic shifted to Al Qassim airport, more than 350 kilometers from the capital. Riyadh Air, the recently launched Saudi sovereign fund-controlled airline, has moved its entire operations to Al Qassim. The strikes in Riyadh have killed at least 13 people and wounded hundreds â some of the survivors were allowed to speak about their ordeal to Saudi state TV over the weekend.

Anthropic’s Claude AI chatbot helped a scientist plan potentially risky bird flu experiments.
The researcher relied on Claude to plan studies, analyze data and choose experiments involving highly pathogenic avian influenza, the company reported September 10 in a threat intelligence report. The work sought to identify and introduce mutations that could help bird flu viruses adapt to mammals and transmit more easily between them. Anthropic says that, to its knowledge, no private company had previously publicly shared evidence of potential misuse of its platform for biological weapons development. But the company did not provide enough detail to determine whether Claude simply sped up work the researcher could already do or gave the researcher a new capability, experts say.
Learning how avian influenza viruses might pose a pandemic risk “is absolutely a normal part of virology research,” says influenza researcher Thomas Friedrich of the University of Wisconsin–Madison School of Veterinary Medicine. Such research can help scientists assess whether emerging bird flu viruses pose a greater risk to humans.
But experiments that deliberately aim to boost pathogen traits such as transmissibility or disease severity draw scrutiny, Friedrich says, because of concerns about accidents or misuse.
Though the report comes amid broader debates about the security of AI models, arguments over this “gain-of-function” research predate generative AI. In 2012, studies involving H5N1 bird flu and airborne transmission in ferrets prompted an international debate over whether the scientific benefits outweighed the risks. Some H5N1 transmission experiments were put on hold for a year while researchers and officials worked out how to handle the risks.
In Anthropic’s case, discovered in May 2026, the bird flu researcher accessed Claude from a region where the service was not supported or available. Anthropic says the researcher used workarounds to access Claude anyway. Material shared with Claude suggested the group probably had physical access to relevant virus samples. Anthropic banned the researcher’s account in May for evading restrictions on access.
Anthropic says it could not tell whether the researcher intended harm because legitimate and dangerous biological research can look similar. The company did not respond to questions from Science News about why it considered the case significant, how it assessed Claude’s role in the research or whether any proposed experiments had actually been performed.
Anthropic released too little information to determine the purpose of the work, says biodefense researcher Gregory Koblentz. “There is no evidence that any of this research was connected to the development of biological weapons,” says Koblentz of George Mason University in Fairfax, Va.
The same kind of biological research can serve very different purposes, from civilian science to military defense. Even work done at a military-affiliated institution does not, on its own, show that researchers are developing a biological weapon, Koblentz says.
Anthropic also did not provide enough detail to show exactly how much Claude helped, Friedrich says. The company’s own account suggests the AI model “did not meaningfully add scientific capability,” he says. In other words, it may simply have sped up the researcher’s work, rather than enabling something they could not have done otherwise.
Even if Claude’s role was only to speed up the work, that can make a big difference in a scientist’s workflow, says virologist David O’Connor of the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Systems such as Claude can help researchers find papers, synthesize results and parse data more quickly, he says. “Work or analyses that would have taken me months can now be done in an afternoon.”
As a result, existing scientific information, including about avian flu viruses, may become easier to find and use, O’Connor says. O’Connor says frontier AI models could let scientists tackle questions they might not have attempted before. “The frontier models will change the ambition of research questions that are asked,” he says.
The bird flu research was one of five instances in Anthropic’s report involving uses of Claude that the company says could support biological weapons development. None of the five look technically sophisticated or particularly concerning to biologist Kevin Esvelt of the MIT Media Lab. Esvelt is more suspicious of the researchers’ motives; he says the five cases showed signs of ill intent. But none “represented a competent attempt at weaponization.”
The poor quality of these particular attempts does not show what a more capable user might be able to do with AI-assisted biology, Esvelt says. AI can help with research and analysis, but turning an idea into a biological threat takes additional work, Koblentz says. “Even if AI is used to design a potentially dangerous pathogen, it is not a threat until the organism can be modified in a lab or synthesized.”
That requires facilities, measures for keeping viruses contained, funding, trained personnel and hands-on experience. Those barriers vary depending on who is doing the work, O’Connor says. They would be a major obstacle for an inexperienced person working alone, but less so for scientists with specialized training and access to a well-equipped laboratory.
Regardless, the remaining laboratory steps are substantial, Friedrich writes in an email. “There is a big gap between identifying mutations that could potentially adapt an avian influenza virus to humans and a ‘harmful biological outcome’.”

If Nvidiaâs Jensen Huang is the business worldâs Bugs Bunny, playing every position on the baseball field by himself, Elon Musk is its Forrest Gump, materializing at the center of events both strange and consequential.
In just the past 10 days, Musk has cut a $1 billion check to help the Ellisons build a right-leaning media empire; tested market jitters with a gargantuan SpaceX bond offering; set in motion the largest-ever corporate merger and the largest-ever philanthropic gift; and set a new standard for all corporate demo days with an actual flying car. Further from Wall Street, he reset US foreign policy by cutting Ukraine off from Starlink â a move that says enough about whoâs in charge that President Donald Trump claimed credit for reversing it â and dominated the midterm-elections homestretch with spending that will near $450 million this cycle.
After his post-DOGE meltdown last year, many had thought Musk had been neutered. He lost his lawsuit against OpenAI. SpaceXâs grandiose IPO prospectus drew titters from an investment community generally prone to believe outlandish promises. But like X, Musk has emerged stronger and more central to finance, politics, and culture.

- Published
A nurse has been killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack as they were responding to an Ebola alert in north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The two were targeted by local youths who accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the Ebola virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi. The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack.
In an attempt to prevent the virus spreading, neighbouring Uganda has banned all non-essential travel to and from DR Congo and says its citizens returning from there will be quarantined for 21 days.
More than 4,800 people have died and nearly 10,000 been infected in DR Congo since this outbreak began in May.
Reacting to the attack in DR Congo, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said health workers "must be able to carry out their duties in safety and dignity", adding that healthcare personnel should always be protected.
The UN agency also extended its condolences to the family and colleagues of the nurse who was killed and wished the injured worker a swift recovery.
The BBC has contacted the Ebola response team for comment on the circumstances surrounding the attack in DR Congo.
Earlier this month, two countries - Kenya and Nigeria - reported their first cases of Ebola linked to the current outbreak.
The patient in Nigeria was on Monday flown from Abuja to Switzerland for further treatment.
She is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya. She was evacuated alongside her husband, who has shown no symptoms.
Nigeria's health ministry said she was stable, conscious and able to communicate.
Authorities are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus.
The new restrictions announced in Uganda come after questions were raised over her case and that of a Kenyan businessman. Both tested positive for Ebola after travelling through Uganda, even though no cases have been reported there since August.
The Kenyan had arrived from DR Congo where he had business interests.
Only essential travellers, including aid workers, truck drivers and security personnel, will be allowed to cross the border from DR Congo to Uganda, subject to strict health screening, the health ministry announced.
In addition, all travellers entering Uganda, regardless of their country of origin, will be required to complete locator forms to facilitate contact tracing where necessary.
It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost".
About 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan patient have all been discharged, it added.
"All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola," Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme.
Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August.
The two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day.
Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients.
The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi, and the country has since confirmed eight other cases of Ebola. A second woman, related to the businessman died over the weekend.
Ugandan officials had previously said the patient in Nigeria had travelled to eastern DR Congo, only transiting through Uganda. On Sunday, however, the health ministry said Uganda and Nigeria were both working to establish her movements, complete travel history and possible routes of exposure.
The Ugandan health minister said the recent cases meant the risk had not ended and further underscored the need to "remain vigilant".
"We share a border with [DR Congo], where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties," Baryomunsi said.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind this outbreak is relatively rare and there is still no vaccine or specific treatment - though trials are under way.
Additional reporting by Swaibu Ibrahim in Kampala

6957095ef0a2.text:
Lizâs view
How does Wall Street quantify fear? Political boogeymen get names (Red Menace, death panels); financial ones get numbers. The VIX captures the marketâs twitchiness, while credit-default spreads calculate the odds of a company going bust.
When it comes to AI jitters, the price of fear is settling somewhere around 200 basis points.
When SpaceX issued its first corporate bonds â back in the giddy, futuro-optimist days ofâ¦ four months ago â it paid 6.65% for the most expensive piece. The most expensive slice of the $40 billion of private credit borrowing itâs finalized in recent days will cost as much as 8.75%, a person familiar with the matter said, having shot higher since we reported on price talks last week.
Breaking down that gap: At least 25 basis points can be attributed to the Fedâs September rate hike and expectations of another one by the end of the year.
The rest comes down to pure nerves. Those 200 basis points translate into hundreds of millions of dollars of extra borrowing costs that canât be pinned on the Fed or the overdue sobering-up among lenders. It owes squarely to the growing doubts about the ROI of AI and whether borrowers will be good for the money.
Elon Musk touted the deal as a sign of SpaceXâs strength, gliding over its eye-watering cost. âAs of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesnât have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,â he posted on X Sunday. âWeâre investment grade and have Starlink & launch revenue.â And yet the market is pricing a BBB company like itâs two rungs lower.
Thereâs also, as one executive at an AI infrastructure fund put it to me last week, the âsupply-demand imbalanceâ â finance-speak for AI needs a lot of money and investors need to catch their breath. For now, the AI anxiety appears confined to credit investors, by nature a more dour and pessimistic bunch than stockholders. But fear is contagious, and if it spreads to stockholders, things could get ugly quickly.
Notable
- âThe credit market is getting jammed right now because it hasnât figured out a good way to offloadâ AI-related risks, Citadelâs co-CIO Pablo Salame told Bloomberg. âAIâs rising tide will sink some boats, and itâs a wavy tide.â

Meta is issuing new stock for the first time since 2013, announcing a $95 billion offering to fund its AI buildout. About $60 billion will come in the form of new, nonvoting shares that the company created last week, a move that telegraphed its rapacious need for cash and CEO Mark Zuckerbergâs desire to raise it without diluting his control stake (and pay his tax bill).
The offering tops Googleâs $85 billion and Oracleâs $25 billion announced stock sales this year.
All three show how the AI boom is stretching corporate balance sheets: The biggest cash-cow businesses in the world can no longer support it, and borrowing can no longer fill the gap. Hyperscalers are expected to spend $800 billion on AI this year and more than $1 trillion next year. Meta shares are up 2% premarket, suggesting that while credit investors are scared, stockholders are still sanguine.

cec1d59763c9.text: Top Democrats poised for powerful roles next year are demanding that major banks and ports preserve any records they have tied to potential imports or other deals involving Russian diesel . Why it matters: Probing President Trump's agreement with Moscow will be a priority if Democrats regain control of either or both chambers of Congress. The new demand shows that inquiries will extend beyond the White House and into C-suites. Driving the news: "[A]ny importation of Russian diesel into the U.S. raises significant legal questions and may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations," a new letter obtained by Axios states. It's signed by Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.). They're in line to lead the powerful Foreign Relations, Banking, Finance and Judiciary Committees, respectively, if Democrats regain the Senate. Rep. Greg Meeks (D-N.Y.), who's in line for the Foreign Affairs Committee gavel if House control changes, also signed. It's led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the top Foreign Relations Democrat who is not seeking reelection. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who is also retiring, signed as well. State of play: The Wall Street recipients of Saturday's letter are J.P. Morgan, Bank of America, Citi, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. The same letter went to port authorities for the ports of Houston, Beaumont, and Corpus Christi, Texas, and New York/New Jersey. Catch up quick: Earlier this month Trump claimed an agreement to bring escalating Russian exports to global and U.S. markets, and the Treasury Department waived sanctions to help enable it. Friction point: The lawmakers and other critics say it runs afoul of a bipartisan 2022 law barring imports of Russian oil, gas, and petroleum products. "The potential arrangement to import Russian diesel also raises significant national security concerns, given that it would finance Russia's brutal and illegal war against Ukraine," the letter states. Yes, but: The Treasury Department has repeatedly claimed the agreement is legal. The big picture: The new letter urges the banks and ports not to enable "purchase, transportation, importation, unloading, storage, financing, or distribution" of Russian diesel in the U.S. It also goes further, urging the parties not to facilitate any transactions for Russian diesel to other markets under the recent sanctions waiver. Zoom in: Citing "anticipation of further congressional oversight," it calls on recipients to preserve a wide range of potential records and communications related to "proposed or actual" transactions. Think contracts, shipping documents, vessel records and plenty more. The demand extends to any communications with suppliers, intermediaries and U.S. government officials. The lawmakers want confirmation by Wednesday that records are being preserved, plus details of any potential or actual Russian diesel transition. What we're watching: It's unclear how much Russian diesel, if any, will reach U.S. shores. Reports Friday in S&P Global , Reuters and elsewhere identify a tanker that initially signaled a New York destination, while the shipping intelligence firm TankerTrackers on Friday said three tankers had signaled U.S. destinations. But ships' planned destinations frequently change for one reason or another. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.
The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 90,000 properties are still without power as of Monday.
Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old in Mid Kelton, Dumfries and Galloway.
The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for strong winds from 18:00 on Monday to 03:00 on Tuesday across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland.
The Met Office has warned that further power cuts in areas covered by the warning are likely and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.
Coastal communities could also be affected by spray or large waves, while travel delays are expected.
Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.
Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.
"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," Slade told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.
Marcus Reed, the operations director at a home fragrance manufacturer, said his factory and shop in Lyndal, Cumbria would be without power until Tuesday evening.
He told the Today programme that he has had to turn away employees and customers.
"To lose two days manufacturing and distribution is going to be really disruptive," he said, adding that it was bad timing as it was "the busiest time of the year" for his business in the lead-up to Christmas.
"This is probably the worst situation I've experienced in my time here; we've had ad hoc issues over weekends where we've lost power, but it's been contained within a 12-hour period. It's the first time anything like this has happened, it's very serious."
Wendy McKinney, whose bathroom shop in the seaside town of Largs in North Ayrshire was flooded on Sunday, told the Today programme the storm had been "devastating to local businesses".
She said the local council only handed out sandbags after flooding had already started:"[They] were just left in the middle of the street yesterday afternoon on pallets just for everybody just to try and help themselves, but it was too little too late."
North Ayrshire Council told the BBC that it had distributed almost 300 sandbags in Largs and Saltcoats and would continue to "respond where it has been safe and appropriate to do so".
A spokesperson said council teams "followed established resilience procedures" but would review flooding reports and "consider any lessons that can be learned".
Disruption to travel has continued on Monday, and some schools in Scotland have been shut either due to lack of power, heating, water or damage.
Another yellow warning of wind, external has been issued by the Met Office, covering much of Scotland, as well as parts of northern England and Northern Ireland from 03:00 to 23:59 on Tuesday.
Monday morning has seen rain in many parts of south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and this is moving north-eastwards reaching central, eastern and northern England, as well as most of Scotland, by around lunchtime.
Winds will also strengthen throughout Monday, and it will turn even windier overnight as the area of low pressure passes close to Northern Ireland and north-west Scotland with gusts peaking on Tuesday.
Additional reporting by Ben Rich, lead weather presenter.
