On the face of it, Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva has done the impossible one more time - within three weeks he overturned defeat in first-round voting to gain re-election as Brazil's president.
It was no mean achievement for a man who before his first successful run at the post in 2002 had tried three times unsuccessfully.
When he became president in 2003, he came to office as the first leftist leader of Brazil in nearly half a century.
Now aged 80 and with plenty of experience at governing as large a democracy as Brazil, he has bucked the trend of electoral victory for right-wing leaders in Latin America whose policies mirror that of US President Donald Trump.
Who is Lula and what are his policies?
Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.
The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.
He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near SÃ£o Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.
Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.
Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.
In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.
The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.
Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.
He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.
In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.
By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.
However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.
He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.
Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.
Why was Lula previously jailed?
Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.
Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.
Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.
He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated.
In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.
When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday.
Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office.
And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.
His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.
What is Lula's relationship with Trump?
Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.
The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.
Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, FlÃ¡vio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off.

The Scene
China is key to global manufacturing across a range of sectors, but foreign capitals â increasingly worried about domestic industry being hollowed out in the face of cheap, high-quality goods from the country â are cracking down.
Few are doing so more aggressively than India, which has set deadlines for local firms to source more of its solar power supply chain domestically, even as it seeks to add a whopping 200 gigawatts of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030.
Beijing is mounting its defense against that strategy: This month, it proposed export controls on several technologies used to make solar equipment, and has reportedly restricted Indian firmsâ access to key parts of the solar supply chain.
âThereâs nowhere else for us to go but to go to China and to get equipment from them that allows us then not to buy the end product from them,â Sumant Sinha, the chairman and CEO of Indian renewables firm ReNew, said in an interview. âOf course, theyâve wised up to this fact.â
Ultimately, though not directly comparable to the Strait of Hormuz crisis, overreliance on China is its own bottleneck, Sinha warned. âWe all talk about increasing electrification â¦ But itâs fully based on dependence on China. And thatâs not a healthy thing.â
So, as a result, countries such as India can only wean themselves off China if China allows them to, he noted. And so, âwhy would they?â
Q&A
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Prashant Rao: Can you describe the kind of broader pressure, either from yourself, your offtakers, whoever, to get off the Chinese supply chain? How much does the Chinese supply chain loom over you?
Sumant Sinha: Itâs more of a sovereign issue than it is an individual company issue. For us, if you tell us to buy from China, we buy from China. Does that increase our dependence on China as a country? Of course it does. I think the sovereign, that is the Indian government, took a view that we did not want to have that reliance. And I donât disagree with that because, why should you have that?
Especially when your own domestic market is big enough. And there are all sorts of geostrategic issues that are going on as well with China.
What theyâve done is actually pretty interesting, which is that they give you a forward notice. And thatâs what they did for solar modules. They said two years from now, theyâre going to stop imports of Chinese modules or any other modules from outside India. So, you have two years to set up capacity.
Lo and behold, at the end of that time period, we now have close to 200 gigawatts of solar module manufacturing. Which is great.
Now theyâve also done the same thing for cells. So that cell restriction is coming into place this December. And from two years from now, theyâre going to do the same thing for wafers and ingots. So theyâre slowly, slowly going further up the value chain. They may do it for polysilicon as well at some point in time, or they may give some other incentives.
I would say that three to four years from now, theyâll have a fully domestic supply chain for solar. And theyâre trying to do similar things for batteries and the battery components and so on as well.
How does that affect your costs?
Obviously our costs are higher than Chinaâs costs. Because letâs say the cost of production in Chinaâs here, our cost of production is slightly higher.
What would you say the ratio is? Like 1.2?
Itâs 20%. But they are selling at a price of 80% to 90%. So, theyâre selling at massive discounts, which they can, by the way, increase if they want to make sure that no Indian manufacturing comes in. And we are selling at whatever is the regular margin to sell at.
So, on a sales price to sales price basis, weâre probably 30% more expensive than that. But that is because Chinese [companies] are making massive losses.
Bottom line is our costs are a little bit higher. But as long as it applies to everybody in the industry, it doesnât matter. Because what that then means is that we just pass on the cost to the end consumer.
Therefore, the end consumer ends up paying that cost. Now, you may argue why should the end consumer pay a higher cost? The end consumer pays a higher cost because ultimately that allows us to localize the supply chain.
How would you characterize your current reliance on Chinese technology?
We are still importing equipment. So, even if we start making cells ourselves, which we are doing right now, we will still have to buy wafers until such time that we start manufacturing wafers in India, which will take us another two years.
A lot of the equipment to manufacture all these items comes from China. And so, we need to import from China. So that reliance is there. Because over the years, whatâs happened is that China not only started making modules and cells and all of these clean tech equipment, but they also started making the capital equipment to make all of these things. And then over time, the R&D to make the capital equipment, and so on.
Theyâve done that very intelligently. Thereâs nowhere else for us to go but to go to China and to get equipment from them that allows us then not to buy the end product from them. Of course, theyâve wised up to this fact.
So, itâs functionally impossible to wean yourself off the Chinese green supply chain?
If they allow us to transfer technology from China, [but] why would they? Thatâs the point. We have to see what to do about it. Itâs not that straightforward.
The thing that I find very surprising is that the rest of the world is fully dependent on China for supply chains in clean tech. Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.
When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico for of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.
Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.
But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.
Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.
He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.
But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.
His signature policy has played out in five key ways.
1. A border that is largely closed
Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.
His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.
When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.
By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.
On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.
To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.
That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north.
"President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October.
"The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."
2. Building of wall speeding up
A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.
Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (Â£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.
According to government figures, external, about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.
Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.
Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.
Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate.
"Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.
There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.
Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it.
"I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."
3. Detentions and deportations rocketing
Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.
During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.
Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, external, a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.
But the same data, external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.
Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.
But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 202

After a weekend of heavy downpours and severe gales, Storm Boelo is moving away from the UK and the weather is turning calmer.
However, this may not last long as another deep area of low pressure is already approaching from the Atlantic.
As this moves into north-west areas of the UK during Monday and Tuesday it will bring another dose of rain and gales.
Met Office yellow wind warnings have been issued for much of Scotland, northern areas of Northern Ireland, Wales and western England.
However, this latest weather system is unlikely to be as widely disruptive as Storm Boelo - or Storm Austen which came before it - and has not, so far, been named.
The next name on the list for the 2026/2027 season is Chloe.
Rain spreading quickly northwards
Rain to parts of south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland on Monday morning will move rapidly north-eastwards, reaching central, eastern and northern England, as well as most of Scotland by around lunchtime.
It will also be rather misty and murky over some coasts and hills.
As the rain clears, slightly drier conditions will spread across the UK from the south-west.
While many areas will remain cloudy a few bright or sunny spells are possible, especially in Wales and south-west England.
Southerly winds will bring warmer air than of late, especially in the south where temperatures may peak at 18 or 19C.
Winds strengthening
After a breezy start to Monday, winds will strengthen once again during the day, with widespread gusts of 30-40mph and 50mph gusts likely in many coastal areas and 65mph in some locations.
It will turn even windier overnight and Tuesday as the area of low pressure passes close to Northern Ireland and north-west Scotland, the very strongest gusts could reach 70-85mph in the Hebrides.
Yellow wind warnings are in place covering both of these areas starting from Monday evening into late Tuesday evening.
Check here for the latest information on weather warnings and keep up to date with the forecast for your area via the BBC Weather website and app
The Met Office warning suggests that there is a low risk of significant impacts, with the chance of travel disruption, power cuts, damage to buildings and some flying debris. Some trees are likely to get blown over.
Storm Boelo contained a spell of damaging westerly winds which effectively funnelled through the highly populated Central Lowlands, increasing the likelihood of impacts. In contrast the winds in this system will be southwesterly, with areas of high ground providing a greater degree of protection for the biggest towns and cities.
There is a risk of some localised flooding with more heavy rain forecast. Some coastal flooding is also possible where large waves coincide with high tides.
Calmer from midweek
High pressure will build close to the UK from midweek onwards meaning the weather should gradually calm down.
Showers will continue on Wednesday but most places are expected to be dry by the end of the day.
Under light winds on Thursday morning, mist and fog could cause some travel disruption across some parts of the country. This should largely clear to leave a dry day with sunny spells.
A weather front could bring rain back into western parts on Friday but high pressure is then expected to rebuild with most computer weather models suggesting a drier and calmer spell is likely to develop over the weekend and into next week.

bddecd32230e.text: The 2026 midterms have taken a deeply personal turn as campaigns use other people's family tragedies as political ammunition — sometimes over the objections of the families themselves. Why it matters: Some attack ads feature photographs of murdered children and anguished 911 calls, forcing grieving families to relive their worst moments. Georgia governor race: Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson used images of murdered 8-year-old Secoriea Turner and her mother's anguished 911 call to attack Democratic rival Keisha Lance Bottoms, Atlanta's former mayor. Turner's family demanded the ads come down, accusing the campaign of exploiting their grief without permission. Jackson said he would keep airing them . Ohio governor race: Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign is spending $4 million on an ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. In the ad, Donna Arthur calls her daughter a liar and disputes her account of childhood homelessness. Acton says her late stepfather — who was married to her mother until his death — sexually abused her as a child, and she hasn't spoken to her mother in decades. Acton's brother corroborated her account , while court records and contemporary news reports support key details. President Trump urged Ramaswamy to keep running his attack on Acton, despite objections from some fellow Republicans. Between the lines: Ramaswamy's campaign said the ad tested well with persuadable voters , even as critics warned it could backfire. Ohio Senate race: A Republican attack ad against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown featured images of a couple and their 1-year-old son killed in a highway crash to blame Brown's immigration policies. The victims' family demanded its removal , saying nobody sought permission to use their relatives' images or tragedy. North Carolina Senate race: A Republican super PAC featured a grieving father in an attack ad linking the murder of his 23-year-old son to former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper's prison policies. The father said he felt deceived about the ad's purpose. The group disputes his account, while fact-checkers found no connection between the killer and Cooper's prisoner-release agreement. Yes, but: Some survivors willingly share their trauma to challenge politicians' decisions. In Nebraska, Jody Snogren voluntarily appeared in an ad attacking Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts for his 2022 vote to pardon John Arias, who pleaded guilty to raping her. Snogren told The 19th she chose to tell her story to inform voters and had no regrets. Ricketts expressed sympathy for Snogren but defended the pardon , noting Arias had served his full sentence and the pardon came decades after the crime.

d090da3a53f3.text: A tidal wave of litigation is catching up to Meta, leading to $42 billion in recent penalties and settlements , a powerful reminder to AI companies that they could face a court reckoning even when regulation lags. Why it matters : AI companies are racing to build better models and autonomous agents, but they don't enjoy the same legal protections that shielded web platforms for decades. The scale of the penalties Meta is facing offers a preview of potential legal exposure . The big picture : For years, Facebook's parent company navigated a seemingly endless string of scandals — weathering allegations of election interference, privacy lapses and platform harms — and was largely protected from severe litigation penalties due to Section 230. The provision — from a historic 1996 law passed as the internet was just beginning to change modern life — protects tech platforms from being sued over content created by their users. Legal experts say that law doesn't apply to AI. Models create their own content, so companies could face traditional product liability and negligence claims. Catch up quick : The two massive rulings highlight how legal risk for tech giants can extend by a decade, or proceed much faster. Meta was just hit with a $25 billion penalty over the Cambridge Analytica scandal after a jury found the company misled users about Facebook's privacy practices. Many details about that event surfaced nearly 10 years ago. The company said it believes it will win an appeal, and legal experts have said the penalty will likely be reduced. In August, the company agreed to a $17 billion settlement with states related to the impact of Meta products such as Instagram on teen mental health. State of play : A key cog in the Trump administration's regulatory efforts is the threat of litigation. Liability is sure to feature prominently in the risks AI giants such as Anthropic and OpenAI spell out to shareholders as they prepare for massive public listings. Anthropic's IPO is expected before Thanksgiving. The companies face an array of legal threats, including harms caused directly by their models, the potential damage from bad actors who use them and copyright matters that remain far from settled. The potential to be hauled into court isn't limited to AI companies; it could also extend to firms that use AI. Yes, but : Big legal penalties take years to arrive, meaning a product can take off and revolutionize the world long before a court determines whether safeguards are adequate. As recent cases have shown, the AI paper trail is extensive, and records of internal warnings, testing and product decisions will shape the findings by judges and juries. Warnings about catastrophe from AI executives will also be ready at hand, and variations on "I told you so" aren't likely to indemnify CEOs. The bottom line : Meta's recent penalty offers a warning to AI companies: legal exposure can build slowly, then become enormous.

Intense rainfall delayed Iowa’s harvest by nearly three weeks this year, but the combines are finally out in full force. So are top Trump administration officials.
U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin and Vice President J.D. Vance have all traveled to Iowa in the last month, either in their official capacity or to campaign with GOP candidates. President Donald Trump visited Sioux City last Thursday and plans to return to Iowa before Election Day.
Though widespread frustration over affordability could fuel Democratic gains nationwide, Trump’s trade wars, the war in Iran and his support for the oil and gas industry have hit Iowa farmers particularly hard. The state is a leading producer of corn, soybeans and biofuels made from both crops.
With Iowa’s closely watched midterm elections roughly a week away, the Trump administration has rolled out a series of measures aimed at winning over farmers whose livelihoods depend heavily on federal fuel and agricultural policies.
Republicans could lose up to four GOP-held seats in Iowa’s congressional delegation. Democrats hope victories in the state will help them take control of Congress, while Republicans are fighting to preserve their narrow majorities in the House and Senate.
Republican political action committees have recently withdrawn financial support from incumbent Mariannette Miller-Meeks’ campaign in Iowa’s 1st congressional district, signaling little confidence in her ability to defeat Democratic challenger Christina Bohannan, who lost to Miller-Meeks during the 2022 and 2024 election cycles.
In the 3rd congressional district, which includes the more progressive Des Moines metropolitan area as well as reliably conservative Southwest Iowa, incumbent Republican Rep. Zach Nunn must fend off Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott. The Cook Political Report, a non-partisan election analyst, recently shifted predictions for both races from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat.”
The Report calls the U.S. Senate race between current Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek and Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson a toss-up. The race between Republican Joe Mitchell and Democrat Lindsay James in Iowa’s second district is also rated a toss-up, as they vie for the House seat Hinson vacated in her bid for Senate.
The war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz have exposed how much Iowa farmers rely on fossil fuel imports. Spiking diesel prices have left growers paying almost twice as much per gallon this harvest as last year. That amounts to thousands of dollars of additional costs each day, even on smaller acreages.
Meanwhile, Trump’s tariffs have driven up the price of farm machinery and other essential materials, like fertilizer. Retaliatory tariffs from countries like China are devastating U.S. commodity crop exports and depressing market prices.
U.S. farm debt is projected to hit a record $605 billion this year, raising concerns about a repeat of the farm crisis of the 1980s. Back then, soaring debt, plunging land values and federal policies that encouraged consolidation contributed to widespread foreclosures of family farms.
Last week, Trump announced that the U.S. Department of Agriculture would offer American farmers $8 billion in one-time fuel relief payments.
The National Corn Growers Association welcomed the announcement with cautious optimism.
“We appreciate the administration recognizing how the high cost of inputs, especially diesel fuel prices during harvest time, is adding to the economic pain of America’s farmers,” the organization wrote in a statement. Still, they added, “We urge Washington to focus on durable, bipartisan, long-term solutions that will result in lasting improvements to the farm and national economy.”
“Hail Mary” on Fuel Policies
Throughout the summer, Democratic campaign ads in Iowa criticized Reps. Hinson, Miller-Meeks and Nunn for repeatedly voting against war powers resolutions directing the president to end U.S. military action in Iran.
In September, after voting “no” five times, Miller-Meeks and Nunn broke with most of their party and voted in favor of a resolution. Hinson voted against the Senate version for the sixth time, but days later posted on social media that she wanted to see a “successful and immediate end” to the war.
Votes on these resolutions can signal lawmakers’ views and their awareness of how a war affects their constituents, but the resolutions are still subject to a presidential veto, said James McCormick, a professor emeritus of political science at Iowa State University.
Even if the war ends today, Iowa farmers are unlikely to see an immediate drop in prices, McCormick said. Prices on refined oil products like diesel and gasoline could remain high for a year or more after the conflict ends.
Aaron Lehman, president of the Iowa Farmers Union, described last Monday’s fuel relief announcement as a “Hail Mary pass” by Trump to fix a problem his own policies created. “We need genuine efforts to help farmers now while fixing the real causes of our current situation. We need to conclude the war without sacrificing our farmers’ bottom lines,” Lehman said in a statement.
As farmers face mounting financial pressure, many are looking to biofuels for a potential economic lifeline. Ahead of November’s election, Republican candidates and cabinet members have sought to capitalize on that optimism by courting Iowa’s biofuel industry.

Bill McAdams, a 45-year-old travel nurse from Holiday, Florida, was uninsured last year when he experienced a stroke. He hadn’t been able to afford his agency’s health plan, which would have cost $3,600 monthly to cover him and his wife. The hospital that treated him sent him a bill for $93,000.
Janet Marx, 56, of Milford, Connecticut, has doubled up on insurance coverage through her husband’s employer and Medicare because she has lupus and fibromyalgia, disabling chronic conditions. Still the couple sold their home, the house where Marx grew up, to afford the costs of their medical care.
Sheila Robinson, 61, in District Heights, Maryland, has a $10,000 deductible on her Affordable Care Act plan, so she tries to negotiate cheaper self-pay options when she sees a doctor. She puts the $659 monthly premium on her credit card, even though she knows not paying the bill in full means she must pay interest.
“I am just afraid to even go to the doctor,” said Robinson, who has arthritis, a pinched nerve in her neck, and high blood pressure. “Every month, I am in the hole.”
This year, KFF Health News has chronicled how rising healthcare costs are upending the lives of Americans. Reporters have heard from more than 130 people across the U.S. who are trying to afford their premiums, copayments, prescriptions, and medical bills even as housing, energy, and food costs swell. People told us they are forgoing health insurance coverage, rationing their medications, cutting back on doctor visits, and putting off health procedures.
“We’re not talking about the uninsured or those who are low-income who are struggling now,” said Rebecca Kirch, executive vice president at the National Patient Advocate Foundation. “Now it’s become an all-of-us issue.”
While healthcare costs have largely grown faster than the overall economy for decades, they’ve escalated at a dizzying pace recently. In 2023 and 2024, health spending hit its highest growth rates in two decades excluding 2020’s covid-fueled surge.
The prices that hospitals, doctors, and other clinicians charge have increased, along with how much care people are getting. Overall health spending hit nearly $5.3 trillion in 2024, up from $3 trillion a decade earlier, according to federal data.
American health costs, expected to continue growing faster than the overall economy and help fuel it, are projected to hit 20% of the nation’s gross domestic product by 2032, up from just under 19% today.
At the same time, Americans are shouldering higher insurance premium payments and other out-of-pocket costs. Low-income and middle-class people with health conditions are feeling the brunt.
The GOP-led Congress decided against extending covid pandemic-era subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans and cut billions from other federal health programs to offset the costs of tax cuts for wealthy Americans and heightened immigration enforcement, arguing that government insurance programs are rife with fraud and waste.
Despite $500 rebate checks sent by President Donald Trump to fewer than 5% of higher-income ACA marketplace enrollees, his administration has been expanding access to insurance plans with higher deductibles and lower premiums that push more costs to patients if they need care. Employers are passing along rising healthcare costs to employees, and clinicians are charging patients up front.
It’s not all bad news for consumers: Prescription drugs recorded their biggest price drop in decades this year. The Biden and Trump administrations both worked to help lower them amid consumer pressure.
But many say they’re still feeling the pain of rising prices. Ahead of the November congressional midterm elections, healthcare costs continue to top a list of the public’s worries about affordability, according to polling conducted in mid-September by KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. Nine in 10 Democratic respondents and three-quarters of Republican ones said the U.S. healthcare system needs either a complete overhaul or major changes.
She Sold Her Childhood Home To Afford Healthcare
Janet Marx, 56
Milford, Connecticut
Janet Marx is on Medicare and has health insurance through her husband’s employer plan. She also receives Social Security disability income because she has fibromyalgia and the disabling autoimmune condition lupus. But she and her husband still struggle to afford their out-of-pocket medical costs. She’s so frustrated about high healthcare costs that she was a guest speaker at an online event for the National Patient Advocate Foundation. Having to scrounge to cover a recent string of $80 copayments for in-home physical therapy led her to an “aha moment,” she said. She sold her home, the place where she grew up, and the couple moved into an apartment.
“Things are just getting too expensive to afford the house and health problems,” she said.
— Renuka Rayasam and Sam Whitehead
His Premiums Went Up. Now He’s Cutting Back To Make Ends Meet.
Damien Waikoloa, 35
Honolulu, Hawai‘i 
Damien Waikoloa wanted to keep health insurance to manage several chronic conditions, even though premium payments for his ACA plan went up to more than $400 a month, from around $240 a month last year. But keeping his coverage meant the small-business owner in Honolulu had to cut back on other spending. He’s trying to reduce the costs of running his business, including considering lowering his own pay. And he’s cutting back on dining out and traveling to visit friends and family in Seattle and California.
“Things like saving for a down payment for a house or even starting a family have completely gone out the window,” he said.
— Renuka Rayasam

The typical American family spends about $5,600 a year, or 9% of their income, on health insurance premiums, out-of-pocket healthcare costs, and taxes that fund health programs, according to the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker. 8b6d2598a489.text:
Dianne Williams said she lost weight and lowered her blood pressure thanks to quarterly doctor appointments, monthly phone calls with a nurse, and a blood pressure cuff she uses at home that transmits data to her care team.
“It’s good to have somebody talk to you and tell you what your progress is like. And she’s a very nice person,” Williams said of her nurse.
Williams, who lives in rural Georgia, said these services — referred to as remote patient monitoring — encourage her to take her medication and inspired her to revamp her diet and exercise.
But many Medicare patients, especially those in rural areas like Williams, soon may no longer be able to use devices and receive coaching from the comfort of their homes.
That’s because a proposed federal rule would halt Medicare reimbursements for providers who use health technology companies to administer remote monitoring for their patients. Medicare would pay clinicians only when the service is provided by someone at the facility where they work.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ proposed rule is a response to reports on remote monitoring from the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Inspector General, an independent federal oversight agency. The 2024 and 2025 reports raised concerns about fraud, a lack of data collection, and patients’ not receiving treatment from the clinician who prescribed the device.
But Caroline Pearson, executive director of the nonprofit Peterson Center on Healthcare, said “the rule would virtually eliminate the use of remote monitoring services, or dramatically reduce the use,” for many Medicare patients.
“I think the rural communities will be some of the hardest hit,” said Pearson, whose organization focuses on healthcare affordability.
She said remote monitoring programs can be especially helpful in rural areas, where it can be difficult for patients to travel to in-person appointments. Most rural healthcare facilities that offer these programs use third-party vendors since they don’t have the capacity to launch and oversee their own, she said.
CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster said the agency “recognizes the important role that technology-enabled care can play in improving access to care, including in rural communities.” But more safeguards are needed, he said.
The proposed rule says outside vendors may “have little to no established relationship” with patients and their clinicians, which it says can “fragment care.” It also says the clinicians may not be involved enough to warrant being paid by Medicare. Pearson, other health policy experts, and vendors agree with the Trump administration that these programs need further regulation. But public comments show widespread strong disagreement with CMS’ approach.
The proposal “took us by such surprise,” said Andrew Van Ostrand, senior vice president at the Alliance for Connected Care, a group that advocates for wider adoption of health tech, including remote monitoring, on behalf of healthcare organizations and tech companies.
Van Ostrand said many vendors have already made changes inspired by the “very well-reasoned recommendations” from HHS’ Office of Inspector General and were surprised that the proposed Medicare rule didn’t mandate all its suggestions.
The proposed rule would apply only to patients enrolled in traditional Medicare, not those with privately run Medicare Advantage plans, which cover more than half of Medicare participants. But Van Ostrand and Pearson said Medicare Advantage plans, Medicaid programs, and private insurers could end up adopting the same change, further limiting access.
Van Ostrand said the vendor rule and other proposed changes — including a “draconian” cut in reimbursement rates — are in “deep misalignment” with one of President Donald Trump’s signature initiatives: the five-year, $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program, which encourages states to adopt tech solutions to improve rural healthcare.
States have earmarked at least $240 million from their first-year rural health funding for remote monitoring, according to a report by the Alliance for Connected Care, which also wrote to CMS to oppose the rule change.
More than 230 health tech vendors, healthcare systems, and patient and medical advocacy groups had signed the opposition letter as of Sept. 14.
A few organizations largely support the proposed rule, including major health industry players Humana, Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, and Sutter Health, a large health system that offers its own remote monitoring program.
Remote Patient Monitoring 101
Remote monitoring can be used for patients who are in physical therapy, recovering from surgery or hospitalization, or living with a chronic condition such as diabetes or heart disease.
The idea is to help patients manage their health and prevent dangerous complications or pricey emergency room visits. Remote monitoring can also make it easier to obtain care for patients who struggle to travel to in-person appointments — such as those with disabilities, without cars, or from rural areas far from hospitals.
To track her blood pressure, Williams straps a cuff to her arm and presses a button. The device automatically sends her data to CoachCare, a private company whose staff monitor patients.

Commodity crops are continuing to eat up the vast, near-mythical sweep of North American grasslands, with nearly 2 million acres being plowed under every year, mostly for corn, soybeans and wheat, according to new research.
A survey, published this month by researchers at the World Wildlife Fund, analyzes for the first time the breadth of grasslands across three countries, from the Chihuahuan Desert in Mexico, across the Great Plains and other American regions, up to the Prairie Provinces of Canada. Using region-specific datasets, the researchers found a cumulative loss of about 1.8 million acres in 2023—roughly twice the size of Chicago.
Already the United States has lost roughly 70 percent of its grasslands to agriculture and development. These ongoing annual losses nibble away at the iconic landscape, which has seen fewer protections than other ecosystems, including forests. Advocacy groups say grasslands are the most imperiled ecosystems in the world.
“Grasslands get overlooked,” said Suzy Friedman, a senior director who oversees Great Plains policy at WWF. “They are not recognized for the value and benefits that they provide for agriculture, for carbon, for water quality, for wildlife, for recreation and for being a foundational and critical component for countless rural communities and tribal communities.”
The grasslands of the Great Plains contain about 34 percent of the region’s carbon. Because most of that is stored in deep roots, they are less vulnerable to fire than forests, which store most of their carbon above ground. But these soils lose about 70 percent of their carbon when cultivated.
WWF has produced its “Plowprint” analysis since 2014, but this year’s is the first to look at all three countries using data going back to the 1980s. It found that cropland expanded in all of them, but at different rates and for different reasons. In the U.S., corn and soybeans drove the conversion of more than 2 million acres between 2020 and 2024, roughly half of that in the Great Plains. Most of those corn and soybeans are fed to cattle or end up in gas tanks as ethanol or biodiesel. The report notes that the expansion in the U.S. has slowed compared to “earlier periods of agricultural expansion.”
“We’re seeing the most conversion exactly where you’d expect it to be, and that’s in the Great Plains and in the Corn Belt,” said Sarah Olimb, a spatial analyst with WWF. “It’s usually pretty predictable because we have a good idea of where the fertile lands are. Those are the ones that tend to be converted, but we’re also seeing marginal lands that are converted.”
Meanwhile Canada’s grasslands saw the greatest area of conversion: Between 2019 and 2023, 4.7 million acres were plowed under, mostly for wheat in the Prairie Provinces. Mexico saw the most relative growth, losing more than 1 million acres of grassland to crops, a rate of about 7 percent, suggesting rapid expansion of production agriculture there.

The researchers say they plan to make future analyses even more granular, looking into the drivers of grassland loss at the state and provincial levels. They plan to turn the data into interactive maps so people can pick an area and look at trends over time.
The map is part of a broader effort to draw more attention to grasslands conservation. The relative lack of attention, Friedman said, motivated the recent launch of the U.S. Grasslands Campaign, a public awareness effort to spur more policy protections, organized by the America’s Grasslands Coalition, a group of conservation organizations that came together in 2023.
The hope, advocates and researchers say, is for stronger policies to protect grasslands and weaker incentives to plow up more, including the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s crop insurance program.
A key area for conservationists is strengthening tribal leadership and food sovereignty efforts on tribal lands, where much of the country’s remaining bison herd graze. The Indian Buffalo Management Act would provide more funding to tribes and organizations that have buffalo herds and more resources for tribes to establish new herds, which would expand protected grazing areas.
“Tribes play an enormously important role in grassland conservation,” Friedman said. “They’re amazing stewards of bison, which support grassland health.”

A heated debate over how to define what qualifies as an ultra-processed food contributed to the resignation of Trump administration health adviser Calley Means ahead of the midterm elections.
People familiar with his exit say he was frustrated with a lack of progress toward the release of a white paper with a proposed definition. Means blamed ultra-processed foods for the âchronic disease crisisâ in the US.
But the food industry has raised concerns over what impact the forthcoming proposed definition could have on lawsuits across the country, and the White House is still scheduled to meet separately with several groups to discuss the issue in the coming weeks â including the National Restaurant Association on Tuesday, the Center for Food Safety on Thursday, and the Consumer Brands Association and Flavor and Extract Manufacturers Association in the days after the midterms.

The Federal Reserve is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged Wednesday before raising them again in December.
The decision would represent a win for the Trump administration, whose allies have urged the central bank against hiking just days before the midterms.
Though Fed Chair Kevin Warsh continues to provide little indication of which way heâs leaning, other officials have recently signaled a desire to tread carefully as they parse a myriad of conflicting data points â from bottoming-out consumer sentiment to a booming stock market to soaring bond yields.
âThe decision will not be without controversyâ because âthey now run the risk of falling behind,â TD Securities analysts wrote Friday.

The News
SELMA, Texas â James Talarico and Ken Paxton are both attacking one another as outsiders more beholden to California than Texas in the closing days of their competitive Senate race.
Onstage at a Paxton rally at a dance hall in the San Antonio suburbs, retiring Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., whoâd briefly considered a House run in Texas, told the crowd: âIâm from California, known for our technology, but weâre also known for fruits and nuts and flakes. So donât elect Talarico.â
âCalifornia has two senators; it doesnât need a third from here,â added Paxton.
The next day, in a packed nightclub in San Antonio, Talarico accused Paxton, who partially grew up in the Golden State, of being the real Californian: âKen Paxton is not one of us. Heâs not even from Texas. Heâs from California, just like Elon Musk.â
Know More
With the midterms about a week away, economic issues are still front and center for both candidates as war-fueled inflation continues to bite. Talarico and Paxton both acknowledged the impact of high prices on voters at their events over the weekend, though Paxton hasnât publicly put much distance between himself and President Donald Trump.
Paxton said voters throughout the state were âtelling me the same thing: Everything costs more. Gas, groceries, the electric bill, everythingâs up except our paychecks.â He floated tax deductions for medical bills, new home purchases, or healthy living decisions (like prescription GLP-1 drugs) as a way to relieve financial burdens.
Talarico, on the other hand, tried to link cost-of-living issues to alleged corruption by Republicans like Paxton. âThis election is about whether you want a senator whoâs going to put money in your pocket or who puts money in their own,â he said.
Democrats are cautiously optimistic about the race as polling shows Talarico narrowly ahead, though many are still smarting from Beto OâRourkeâs close loss in 2018 to Sen. Ted Cruz. Ronnie Smith, 66, of Schertz, Texas, was among the more than 1,000 people that the Talarico campaign said attended his San Antonio rally with actress Eva Longoria. Smith told Semafor heâd been a lifelong Republican until Trump ran in 2016, and believed things were âlooking more positiveâ for Talarico, though he was still âapprehensiveâ about the outcome.

Both parties remain skeptical that Democrats can win Mississippiâs Senate race. But there are several reasons it could be competitive: Trumpâs visit follows former Vice President Kamala Harrisâ campaign stop for Democrat Scott Colom, and both partiesâ top super PACS are spending in the state.

The News
SIOUX CITY, Iowa â Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek is running ads calling for border security. Heâs touting his votes with Republicans in the statehouse.
Turek is criticizing his party for obstructing farm and data center legislation and says he has âno interestâ in talking about impeachment. He even embraces a term that Democrats rarely use these days.
âPolitically, the term moderate can be pejorative. And I say that Iâm proudly a moderate,â Turek told Semafor on the banks of the Missouri River. âSocially, culturally, you could define me as moderate.â
In one of the countryâs closest Senate races, state Rep. Turek and GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson are competing for a small slice of independent-minded Iowans who will decide their race â and with it, potentially, the Senate majority. Theyâre both blue-chip recruits: Hinson is a former Iowa TV reporter who ousted a Democratic incumbent in 2020; Turek is a gold medal-winning Paralympian who won his first statehouse race by six votes.
And the appeals from each candidate are similar: Iâm the real pragmatist, and my opponent is just pretending to be one. Notably, Hinson launched her campaign with a vow to be Trumpâs âtop allyâ before putting distance between them.
Whatâs more, if Turek and candidates like fellow Great Plains Democrat Adam Hamilton win, it would tilt the center of gravity in the partyâs Senate caucus toward a center thatâs lost ground in recent years. So Republicans are running ads that affirm Turekâs distance from the left, while casting him as unable to hold it back: âI know Josh Turek isnât a socialist, but can we trust him to say no to his party?â asks an Americans for Prosperity ad.
Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, told Semafor that âeven if he is a different kind of Democratâ â emphasizing the âifâ â Turekâs association with his party leadership is still damaging.
âWhen he gets to Washington, DC, which isnât going to happen, heâs going to get a lot of pressure to vote for a lot of these really wild schemes,â Grassley said.
Hinson describes her opponentâs campaign as a âtale of two Tureks. In the primary, he was trashing the president, and now heâs saying that he wants to work with him. I know Iowans are going to see right through that.â
The charge clearly irks Turek who said Hinsonâs âmasquerading. I mean thatâs a problem for me. Iâm genuinely a bipartisan person,â he added. âShe has been partisan. â¦ Just be who you are.â
And on the day of Trumpâs latest Iowa visit, Sioux City newspaper readers were greeted with an ad bragging that Turek âvoted with Republicans 700+ times.â
Turek called it âfearmongeringâ to portray his candidacy as empowering the left, vowing to â100%â be a check on his partyâs liberal impulses.
ââWhat do you think about impeachment?â No interest in that. I believe we should look forward, not backwards,â Turek said.
Turekâs been a lonely Democrat before: He and state Rep. J.D. Scholten, D-Iowa, were the only Democrats representing Western Iowa in the Iowa House for years. Scholten told Semafor that experience positions Turek to convert frustrated Republicans.
âWe donât have the luxury of talking just to Democrats out here in Western Iowa,â Scholten said. âYou have to talk to everybody, and I think that has benefited him in a huge way.â
âHeâs our best candidate since [former Sen. Tom] Harkin,â Scholten added.
Hinsonâs Move to the Middle
Polls show the race as essentially tied, with little real movement for months. Amid the deadlock, Hinson is making her own play for the center.
âThatâs a tradition in Iowa,â Grassley explained. âThey expect us to represent Iowa interests and not just the interests of whoeverâs president of the United States.â
She is a sitting House Republican, with her own voting record in support of the presidentâs agenda, including the tax cut law. Sheâs also campaigning with Trump down the stretch, even as she criticized a polarizing ad by Ohioâs GOP gubernatorial nominee that Trump defended.
After supporting it in several House votes, Hinson now opposes Trumpâs Iran war and is breaking with his Russia dealmaking. Asked if she should have voted against the Iran conflict when she had a chance, she said: âI look forward. Thatâs how I always operate. And when you look at where we are right now, Iâve asked the president to end the war.â
Asked about Turekâs charge that sheâs making a late tack to the center for political expedience, Hinson whacked Turek for missing votes in the statehouse and said âitâs exactly the opposite.â
âHeâs going to be voting with Chuck Schumer 100% of the time,â she predicted. Turek said heâd meet with any leadership candidates before making a decision on who should run the party.
Turek criticized Trumpâs tariffs, the war, expired health care subsidies, and Medicaid cuts as inordinately harming Iowa. He also ticked off the areas on which âI agreeâ with the president.
âLetâs drive private equity out of housing. Letâs drive it out of healthcare. Letâs drive it out of nursing homes. â¦ We should have no tax on tips, overtime, and Social Security. Thereâs a lot that we can agree on,â Turek said.
He said he would have supported the Laken Riley Act, a law tightening restrictions on non-citizens accused of crimes that still painfully splits Democrats. He also objected to the Democratic filibuster of a GOP data center bill and said his party erred in blockading a farm bill.
âThe farm bill isnât exactly as written as exactly what I would want. But I donât think we should let perfection stand in the way of progress,â Turek said. âIf Iâm up there, I will vote for it.â
Room for Disagreement
Iowa is reeling from high gas prices and a moribund agriculture market, causing dissatisfaction with the long-ruling GOP. Three Republican-held House seats are up for grabs, and Democrat Rob Sand is favored to win the governorâs race.
But no matter how much Turek appeals across the aisle, Republicans feel that the party will come home for Hinson as it has in every Senate race since 2010

The News
Donald Trumpâs wartime alliance with Benjamin Netanyahu is exposing a divide within his party that will outlast his presidency â over what âAmerica Firstâ really means for the US-Israel relationship.
Making peace between the GOPâs pro-Israel establishment and its restive right wing will pose an early challenge for Vice President JD Vance, whoâs positioning himself for a posible 2028 run. But any Republican looking for the nomination to succeed Trump will have to sidestep the same sort of internal clashes over Israel that have bedeviled Democrats.
Trumpâs position is clear: The US president, even amid open tensions with the Israeli leader, has aligned tightly with Netanyahu and endorsed his reelection. A White House official, in a statement to Semafor, emphasized Trumpâs âgreat relationshipâ with the prime minister.
Yet that position, unpopular with factions in both parties, is also unpopular with some inside his deeply loyalist White House.
âAt the mid-level and upper levels of the administration, there is not only real frustration, but real anger with Netanyahuâs government,â said one Trump administration official. âThereâs a feeling that they oversold what they could do vis-a-vis Iran, and about how fragile the Iranian regime was. Thereâs a feeling that we had to bear a lot of the brunt for actually defending Israel.â
The next president, regardless of party, will face specific questions about how much to sustain the long tradition of direct US military aid to Israel and deep US integration with its military.
Netanyahu himself, as he prepares for an election that could end his leadership in its current form, acknowledged as much in a Friday interview: âTens of billions of US aid dollars to the defense budget â get used to it â wonât keep coming. Because America has changed. Not because Israel has.â
And as Trump nears his lame-duck era, partisans on both sides of the Israel debate are watching every 2028 hopeful, including Vance. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, a longtime backer of the Israeli government, could try to cut into Vanceâs advantage with likeminded donors if he runs; others in the party are hoping Secretary of State Marco Rubio jumps into a primary for the same reason, though itâs less likely.
Vance, meanwhile, is trying to balance Trumpâs level of support for Israel against a populist right wing thatâs increasingly questioning the current relationship.
In private conversations and public meetings, Vance has sought to assure pro-Israel Republicans that he holds no animus toward the Jewish state, while arguing that the relationship should be more explicitly guided by US interests. Earlier this year, he compared the US relationship with Israel to that of countries like France and the UK.
âWhen weâre partnered, great, letâs work together. And [when] weâre not, letâs just be honest about it,â he said.
Vance declined last week either to endorse or to criticize Netanyahu (Trump appeared unconcerned, telling reporters itâs âup to himâ). As Vance put it to Joe Rogan in July, heâs merely a âguy advocating for a normal relationship with a normal country.â
That posture may not please either side, but it has helped mollify his critics, to an extent.
âI do not think he hates Israel. I donât. I donât think heâs an antisemite, not by any stretch,â said Sid Rosenberg, a conservative radio host who met privately with Vance last month at the White House amid the VPâs charm offensive on the subject. âBut I donât think he has the same passion for Israel moving forward as somebody like Marco or Ted would.â
The Tucker factor
Rosenberg also addressed the elephant in the room for Vance: âHeâs definitely in a tougher spot than Marco Rubio or Ted Cruz because the truth is a lot of Jewish voters donât trust him. Some of that is the way he talks about Israel and Bibi, and some of that is because heâs admittedly friendly with Tucker Carlson.â
The VPâs long friendship with the powerful right-wing broadcaster is, for many on the pro-Israel side, the heart of the issue. Vance has neither criticized his friend nor publicly nudged Carlson to temper whatâs been harsh criticism of Israel â and Trumpâs cultivation of the Netanyahu government.
âI donât think thereâs much debate about the definition of America First. It means putting the interests of American citizens above all others. That would definitely not include sending tens of billions of tax dollars to genocidal ethnostates in the Middle East so they can kill kids,â Carlson said in a text exchange with Semafor. âThatâs not America First. Itâs evil.âÂ
Hawks vs. ârestrainersâ
The real views of Israel among top Republicans arenât as binary as theyâre made out to be. Critics of Israel within the GOP arenât as numerous, or as organized, as their Democratic counterparts.
The real schism exists between traditional pro-Israel hawks, who have allied the US with the Jewish state since the George W. Bush era, and a spectrum of skeptics â led by ârestrainers,â who argue that the US should be more disengaged from Israel but have no ill-will toward the country. (Carlsonâs views on Israel are seen by many on the right as at the more extreme end of the skeptical faction.)
One person close to the White House echoed Vanceâs public position in summing up restrainersâ perspective as not âanti-Israelâ in the same way as a progressive: âItâs just like, I donât spend the vast majority of my day thinking about this country halfway around the world. I think Israel is cool; seems like a fine country. Iâm not sure why we are so devoted to whatâs going on in their country as much as we are.â
At the heart of the debate is whether the US should keep its current spending on Israeli defense â an issue that some in both countries see as an unnecessary irritant to US politics.
Netanyahu said in his Friday interview that heâs preparing to rely less on US aid, and some of Trumpâs senior national security aides are pushing to keep the USâ long-term focus on China.

A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
What is a plenum?
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.
What is on the agenda this year?
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy â branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" â to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

A project to transform a recreation ground into a wildflower meadow has taken another step forward.
Members of the Nature Volunteer Network and staff from the Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk have planted hundreds of native wildflower plugs in Fairstead Recreation Ground in King's Lynn.
The council said it wanted to establish a diverse mix of wildflower species to enhance the meadow and support local wildlife.
"Every plug planted brings us one step closer to establishing a thriving meadow," said Michael de Whalley, the cabinet member for climate change and biodiversity at the authority.
"[It will] benefit bees, butterflies, birds, and countless other species."
Valuable habitat
The authority said the wildflower meadow project, which followed the introduction of green hay in the area earlier this year, was one of its first practical initiatives to protect and restore habitats for insects and other wildlife across the borough.
Chris Walker, the biodiversity officer at the borough council, said: "We will be able to take what we learn from this project to recreate wildflower meadows in other areas of the borough, fitting in with our long-term investment in nature."
Wildflower meadows are among the UK's most valuable habitats, external, supporting a wide range of insects and wildlife while helping to connect fragmented natural spaces.
The council said once fully established, the Fairstead Recreation Ground meadow would provide food, shelter and breeding opportunities for numerous species.
It added it would continue to monitor the site's progress as the meadow develops, with the aim of creating a self-sustaining habitat to support biodiversity and potentially provide seed and plant material for future meadow creation projects elsewhere in the borough.

The Ballon d'Or winner will be announced in London on 26 October - but who is going to win it?
Bookmakers have Spain winger Lamine Yamal and England captain Harry Kane very close together as clear favourites.
Lamine Yamal won La Liga with Barcelona and the World Cup with Spain, while Kane scored 73 goals for German champions Bayern Munich and England.
Eight-time winner Lionel Messi, of Argentina and Inter Miami, and Real Madrid's France forward Kylian Mbappe are the other probable candidates.
Or how about one of Paris St-Germain's back-to-back European champions?
BBC Sport asked several of its football experts who they think should take home the award.
Lamine Yamal
European football expert Guillem Balague: Can you imagine this Ballon d'Or not won by a PSG player or a Spanish player? Impossible. So gone is Kylian Mbappe.
The PSG players, there are so many of them that deserve it - Fabian Ruiz, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Ousmane Dembele, Vitinha. So the vote is going to be split.
There is only one Spaniard who deserves it, and that's Lamine Yamal, who has given us individual performances, collective trophies, and has that aura. He's going to win it.
Khvicha Kvaratskhelia
European football expert Julien Laurens: I think he was the best player in Europe last season, especially in the Champions League where he was outstanding. He helped lead the team to another title, a back-to-back one.
He got the penalty in the final, scored in both semi-finals, in the quarter-final, and in the last 16. He was amazing in those huge, huge games where you want your best players to step up. He deserves to win the Ballon d'Or for being the best player in the world all the way up to the World Cup.
He won't win it, unfortunately, because Lamine Yamal, for the player he is and how entertaining and spectacular he is, didn't really shine at the World Cup, even if Spain won it. He didn't really do that well in the Champions League for Barcelona, getting knocked out early. However, his style of football means he'll probably win it - but it should be Kvaratskhelia.
Ex-Liverpool and Blackburn full-back Stephen Warnock: I think it will be Lamine Yamal for helping Spain to win the World Cup. If you were asking who else is in the hunt, I would say Michael Olise, but my pick personally would be Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, he is unbelievable. I love watching him play. He had such an impact for Paris St-Germain and last season he was incredible. I just don't think he will get the votes with Georgia not being in the World Cup.
BBC Radio 5 Live Euro Leagues guest and Athletic reporter Rory Smith: It will probably go to Lamine Yamal because it generally goes to someone who has won the biggest trophy, and this is the World Cup. It shouldn't be him because he wasn't necessarily Spain's most important player but his fame and talent means it will be him.
Personally I would give it to Kvaratskhelia. He has been the most exciting player in European club football for a while now, a valuable part of the PSG team who retained the Champions League, and crucially I think you shouldn't suffer because you come from a country who isn't in the running to win the World Cup.
Harry Kane
Former England striker Alan Shearer: The winner of the Ballon d'Or should be Harry Kane. His numbers for the last 12 to 18 months have been absolutely sensational for Bayern and for England. For that reason, he should get it.
Ex-England midfielder Danny Murphy: My choice for the Ballon d'Or is Harry Kane. I think his goalscoring has been relentless, brilliant. He's had one of the best seasons of his career and it'll be a great reward for him if he gets the trophy. He's been brilliant at Bayern Munich since he's been there, adapted really well and he's been the best centre-forward in the world for the last 12 months.
Former Tottenham and Crystal Palace forward Andros Townsend: Harry Kane should win the Ballon d'Or. He scored 73 goals in 65 games, 36 of those in the Bundesliga. He led Bayern Munich to the league and cup double. He scored 14 goals in the Champions League, helping Bayern Munich to the semi-finals and scored six goals in the World Cup, leading England to the semi-finals. He has had an outstanding year.
Former England striker Ellen White: It's a tough one but I'll go with my heart - I'd love to see Harry Kane win it. I know he didn't win the World Cup but his numbers are absolutely extraordinary, with what he has achieved with Bayern Munich and England. Lamine Yamal had a few injuries but I know he won the World Cup and I'm sure he will win the Ballon d'Or one day. Michael Olise has also been phenomenal.
Norwegian football journalist Lars Sivertsen on Champions League Match of the Day: I would like to see Harry Kane win it, he deserves it. He is a real leader at Bayern Munich. He never makes trouble and is a role model. But I do wonder if him being a low-key character hurts him. The Ballon d'Or is a popularity contest. I love that he doesn't do all that but maybe he should.

Eric Bauza, the voice artist behind Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died aged 46.
A statement from the Emmy award-winning star's family posted on Instagram, external said he had died "suddenly".
Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme, and appeared in the recent release Forgotten Island.
Variety reports that the cause of death was hypertensive cardiovascular disease and that Bauza died at home on Sunday.
In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza, who was born in Ontario and was of Filipino descent, said he grew up a huge fan of the Looney Tunes characters and used to copy the voices as a child.
"Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures," he said, external. "It doesn't matter what part of the planet you're from. You get the comedy."
He voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd and Foghorn Leghorn in 2021's Space Jam: A New Legacy before reprising those roles and that of Road Runner in Coyote vs. Acme.
He also played the part of Toad General in 2023's The Super Mario Bros. Movie and its sequel The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, the fifth highest-grossing film internationally this year.
Between 2022 and 2025, he won three Emmy awards for outstanding voice performance in a number of TV series.
In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter, external, Channing Dungey, the chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks, said: "Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world.
"He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life."

A nature reserve has said the wildlife "will never really be the same again" after a huge wildfire almost three months ago.
The blaze, which broke out on 29 July, started on the edge of RSPB Minsmere before it spread to neighbouring Dunwich Heath on the Suffolk coast.
Firefighters have been unable to determine the cause.
Ian Barthorpe, visitor experience officer at Minsmere, said the team was concerned about the long-term implications the fire.
"It's going to be a long process of recovery of the habitat and some species like the deer and the birds have relocated to other parts of the reserve," he explained.
"But unfortunately we're really concerned about the impacts it will have on some of the invertebrates, the plants and the reptiles.
"It'll be 20 years or more before those parts of the reserve start to look like they used to."
Some trails and heathland areas of the site were hit by the fire, but fortunately wind conditions as well as the vegetation and marshland had stopped it spreading further into the reserve.
Parts of the heathland were still recording temperatures of more than 53C (127F) underground earlier this month.
Barthorpe said he had been shocked at the "apocalyptic scenes" following the fire which he said had been "quite sobering".
"It's changed the landscape so much," he continued.
"We were lucky in many ways - we didn't lose buildings, we didn't lose life or human life, but from a wildlife point of view, it will never really quite be the same again."
The main nature reserve, visitor centre and trails around its wetland areas were not affected in the fire and are all open, although the National Trust has closed Dunwich Heath and the adjoining beach to visitors.
The reserve is best known for its avocets, bitterns and other water birds, and has been a base for the BBC Springwatch programme.
Barthorpe said there was still "amazing wildlife" and "stunning scenery" for visitors to enjoy and see.
"Let's celebrate what we've got more than what we've lost and ensure that we've still got it for the future," he added.

This year's spike in House Ethics Committee investigations related to sexual misconduct prompted congressional leaders to set up a working group led by Cammack and Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, D-N.M. What they have found is disturbing, Cammack said. Victims are unclear about where they can go for help. They do not trust there will be repercussions for the perpetrator. And the current requirements for reporting harassment can work against them, such as a 180-day "shot clock" for filing a claim after an alleged violation. "It's a disaster," Cammack said. "The entire system on Capitol Hill is really designed to create a chilling effect for victims." The task force is expected to release recommended changes after the Nov. 3 elections with a goal of taking action before the end of the year.
