Three lawmakers resigned this year rather than face the prospect of an expulsion vote. Two of those cases involved alleged sexual misconduct. Another member was censured for his interactions with two female aides on his staff. Other investigations are ongoing. Those stories emerged at a time when Congress was confronted by public outrage over the government's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case. In the previous months, members of the Democratic Women's Caucus had multiple meetings with survivors who were pushing for the release of Epstein-related files at the Department of Justice. In April, the Ethics Committee began an investigation into whether then-Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., engaged in sexual misconduct toward an employee working under his supervision. Swalwell would soon resign as colleagues called for his expulsion. Similarly, Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned as the committee investigated whether he had engaged in sexual misconduct toward an employee in his office. Gonzales had acknowledged an affair with a staff member who later died by suicide. Most recently, the committee recommended the censure of Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., following an investigation that concluded he engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct toward two young female staffers in his office. The House went along with the recommendation by a vote of 413-2. Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., is also the subject of a committee investigation that he may have engaged in sexual misconduct with a House staffer. Gomez said he would cooperate with the investigation but also stressed that his actions were consensual in nature and did not violate the law or House Ethics rules. He also apologized to his family and constituents. The committee is also investigating whether Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., engaged in sexual misconduct or dating violence, among other allegations. Mills has denied the allegations and recently lost a Republican primary. Lawmakers felt called to action This photo combination shows Rep. Kat Cammack, R.-Fla., (left) in 2021, and Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez, D-N.M., in 2024. Photos by Marta Lavandier and Jose Luis Magana/AP Cammack said that as stories began to surface about some of the cases before the committee, she and colleagues began talking about what they could do to "clean up the House." She approached Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., about getting on board. Johnson's response, she said, was: "Well, good timing, because I was going to come to you and ask you to take this effort up." Leger Fernandez was also talking with Democratic leadership about reforms when Cammack reached out to her about working together. "What was neat is on both sides of the aisle, the Democratic Women's Caucus and the Republican Women's Caucus were both saying there needs to be structural changes. We need to work together," Leger Fernandez said. The working group started with listening sessions that included lawmakers and staff. They also reached out to people in the military, corporate America and victims advocacy groups for advice on best practices. Cammack and Leger Fernandez held a packed-room meeting with staff in July. Several ideas for reform are on the table Congress has tried to address the issue of sexual harassment before. It passed legislation in 2018 that among other things required lawmakers to reimburse the Treasury Department for awards and settlements related to sexual harassment cases. bfb15676b52a.text: By — Jonathan Landrum Jr., Associated Press Jonathan Landrum Jr., Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/walter-koenig-ensign-chekov-on-the-original-star-trek-series-dies-at-90 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Walter Koenig, Ensign Chekov on the original 'Star Trek' series, dies at 90 Arts Oct 26, 2026 4:10 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the " Star Trek " television series and several movies, has died. He was 90. Koenig died Monday at his home in the North Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles, talent agent Zachery McGinnis said in a statement. In "Star Trek," Ensign Chekov was the sole Communist-bloc member of the spaceship Enterprise bridge staff. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together. Speaking Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied stereotypical Russian personality traits, including fierce pride, love of poetry and blind loyalty. "Star Trek" ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969 and has had an almost unprecedented afterlife as fans, or Trekkies, kept interest in the show alive. Members of the "Star Trek" crew, from left -- James Doohan, DeForest Kelley, Walter Koenig, William Shatner, George Takei, Leonard Nimoy, and Nichelle Nichols -- toast the newest "Star Trek" film at Paramount Studios on Dec. 28, 1988. Photo by Bob Galbraith/AP Koenig was born Sept. 14, 1936, in Chicago, the son of a businessman. He graduated from the University of California, Los Angeles in 1958, then studied acting at New York's The Neighborhood Playhouse for two years. He began getting television roles in the early 1960s, appearing on "Mr. Novak" and "Ben Casey." "My heart is heavy," Koenig's castmate, George Takei, said in a post on the social platform X. "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend." Koenig was the best man at Takei's 2008 wedding to Brad Altman, his partner of more than two decades. "Walter's legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it," McGinnis said. "Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before." McGinnis said Koenig died surrounded by his daughter and niece. Koenig played Chekov in seven "Star Trek" movies starting in 1979, as well as innumerable other spinoffs, including writing a "Star Trek" book, "Chekov's Enterprise," in 1980. The TV show has also inspired two spinoff TV series with new casts, and conventions that draw thousands of fans. After "Star Trek" ended, Koenig continued acting and wrote scripts for "Family," "The Incredible Hulk" and other shows. He also taught part time at UCLA and other schools. Koenig also worked in the burgeoning field of computer games, including some with a "Star Trek" theme. In 1995, he took a role in the CD-ROM game "Maximum Surge." "I'm at a point where I could opt in my life for complacency and a bit of predictability, or I could have one last holler — one last try for adventure," Koenig told The Associated Press in 1995. "I'm of the opinion that adventure is still a very enticing and exciting option." He returned to the science fiction genre with occasional appearances in the syndicated 1990s TV series "Babylon 5." Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, in a statement titled "A Public Apology," said Sunday that he had received many questions and comments — some of them distraught — about the meeting on Thursday which he and 11 other bishops attended. Please check your inbox to confirm. He said the meeting was speedily publicized by the White House with photos and a video, without consent of the participants, and less than two weeks away from the midterm elections. "I feel a heavy sadness, not only over the pain I caused, but also for the fact that something so sacred to a group of religious leaders, prayer to our Heavenly Father, would be manipulated in that way," Grob said. The bishop of Des Moines, Iowa, William Joensen, also issued a statement making clear he felt the White House had taken advantage of the bishops. "I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purpose," he wrote. "I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward, even as I remain resolute in my openness to engaging and praying for political leaders at all levels." Asked whether the White House had or hadn't received the bishop's consent for releasing the photos and video, the press office declined to answer that question. Instead, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers replied, "There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it." The White House invitation to the bishops — extended in September — offered discussion about such issues as immigration enforcement, religious worker visas, abortion and use of federal tax credits to support private education, according to Joensen and Grob. "The meeting was in no way an endorsement of the president, his policies, or his party," wrote Grob. "We were told the meeting was to be a private discussion, that several Catholic members of the cabinet might make an appearance, and that there could be an opportunity to pray privately with the president." "It did not take long thereafter for the White House to post a video and photos of the prayer," Grob said. "I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he added. "I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family had been harmed by the president's policies." "I did not go without reservations. I wish I had heeded them," Grob concluded. "I apologize for any damage my actions have done." Collectively, members of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops have diverse views on Trump and his administration's policies. Minnesota-based Bishop Robert Barron, for example, agreed to serve on Trump's Religious Liberty Commission, which was filled almost entirely with conservative Christians. Some other bishops vehemently denounced aspects of Trump's tough stance on immigration enforcement, saying it runs counter to Catholic teaching. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.
The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.
Anthropic also detailed some of the the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.
Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.
1. Armageddon is an occupational hazard
Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.
Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.
"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.
It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.
But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".
One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.
2. The company is haemorrhaging cash
Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.
The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.
Anthropic lost $80.7bn (Â£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.
The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn billion for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.
Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.
Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.
"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.
3. But luckily it has plenty of cash on hand
Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.
At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.
Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.
Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.
The leasing of data centres alone is costing the company $321.4bn so far this year.
Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.
Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.
4. Anthropic relies on a few big customers
Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.
A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10mn in the past year.
An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.
Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".
The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.
Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.
Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.
Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".
The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.
5. AI promises 'extraordinary' benefits to the world
For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.
"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.
That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."
"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission. "
Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.
Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy.

Beyond national, state and local leaders, millions of Americans in 39 states will vote on issues including election laws, transgender rights, taxes and abortion. Out of 145 total initiatives around the nation, California and Colorado have the largest number of ballot measures at play this fall with 14 each. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Sometimes, initiatives are put on the ballot to incentivize voter turnout, Rick Hasen, election law expert and political science professor at University of California, Los Angeles said in an email. Historically, midterm elections have lower voter turnout than presidential ones. WATCH: A look at the major state ballot measures voters will decide in the midterms Some measures create new constitutional amendments or laws while others repeal existing policies. Every state has different laws governing how measures make it on the ballot. In states like California, citizens can bypass state legislatures and include their proposed initiatives on the ballot. Other states require legislators to vote to include a measure. The threshold for passing a ballot measure also varies. In Florida, for example, constitutional amendments require 60% of the vote to pass. In Nevada, citizen-initiated constitutional amendments must be passed by voters twice, in successive elections, before they're implemented. In November, citizens in five states will vote on their ballot measure processes. With about a week before the elections, here's a look at ballot measures across four key topics. Measures on noncitizen voting and voter IDs It's already illegal for noncitizens to vote in federal elections, and no state allows them to vote in statewide elections. However, six states — Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia — are voting to amend their state constitutions or laws to explicitly include language saying only U.S. citizens can vote in state elections. While some jurisdictions allow noncitizens to vote in local elections, such as school board elections, none are in states with noncitizen voting ballot measures. "One reason for ballot measures in states might be to prevent this choice," Hasen said. President Donald Trump has long made false claims of widespread voter fraud by noncitizens and his Justice Department is leading efforts to catch and prosecute people they say have illegally cast ballots. But so far, there's been no evidence to support Trump's statements. WATCH: Examining the DOJ's effort to prosecute non-citizens accused of voting Noncitizen voting is extremely rare, and noncitizens who register as voters or vote in federal elections face significant penalties, including steep fines, time in federal prison and deportation. Voters in six states — Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio — will also have a say on another election security measure. They'll vote to amend their state constitutions to require voter identification when people vote in person or by mail. The amendments vary by state but would generally require voters to present a government-issued ID or Social Security numbers when they cast their votes. Trump previously led an unsuccessful charge to pass a federal voting bill that would in part require all voters across the country to present a photo ID when voting regardless of the method. WATCH: How Trump's SAVE America Act would reshape voting and why critics are concerned Trans athletes in sports, gender-affirming surgery for minors Voters in five states — Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska and Washington — will decide on issues related to the rights of transgender people in November. Over the past several years, states across the country have passed laws banning trans women and girls from playing on sports teams that match their gender identity. In June, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld those laws. WATCH: Who is affected by the Supreme Court's ruling on trans athletes in women's sports Several of the measures seeking to limit the rights of trans athletes are in Democratic-led states. The ballot initiatives are petitioned by citizens who know their state legislatures aren't going to pass similar laws. "Instead, supporters of these measures have gone to the people, gotten the signatures, and gotten on the ballot," Reid Wilson, editor and founder of Pluribus News, a site that covers politics and policy at the state level, previously told PBS News. "We see this in progressive states where conservatives use the ballot measure to get something on the ballot that the legislature won't pass." Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. Most laws dictating gender identity in school sports ban trans girls from participating in girls' sports, according to the Trans Journalists Association. Ballot measures in Arizona and Colorado would also ban trans boys from competing on boys' teams. Arizona's ballot measure would also ban trans kids from using restrooms or locker rooms that don't match the sex recorded on their birth certificates. Nebraska already has a law banning trans girls from girls' sports. But in November, its voters will decide whether to enshrine the ban in the state's constitution. US President Donald Trump is facing a backlash after invoking 9/11 as part of a verbal assault on Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Michigan.
Speaking at a rally in the state on Sunday, Trump accused El-Sayed of being "a jihadist". He introduced as a guest speaker the father of a passenger who fought back against the 9/11 hijackers.
Trump also suggested that El-Sayed would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate".
Critics condemned Trump's attack as Islamophobic. El-Sayed himself responded to Trump's decision to refer to him by his middle name, Mohamed, saying during a rally of his own: "I'll be Senator Mohamed to you, bro."
He also said: "They think that by pointing at my name and my faith, that somehow you're going to ignore the fact that you can't afford your gas or your groceries, can't see a doctor."
Appearing alongside him, Senator Bernie Sanders said: "The reason they are using Islamophobia against Abdul is because they have nothing to say about the real issues."
El-Sayed is taking on Republican candidate Mike Rogers on 3 November. The race is expected to be one of the closest in the midterm elections, and is proving to be particularly bitter.
The seat is considered to be one of just a handful that could decide the balance of power in Congress. It is currently held by the Democrats.
El-Sayed, a former public health official who was born in the US to Egyptian parents, will be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate if he wins the seat.
He has previously dismissed the various attacks made against him by both Trump and Rogers and denied any connection to extremist groups.
During his remarks on Sunday, Trump said: "If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas."
Trump made a variety of allegations against El-Sayed and his family members, including that he was a member of the Muslim Brotherhood.
He introduced as a guest speaker the father of Todd Beamer, a man from Michigan who was part of a group of passengers who fought back against the hijackers of United Airlines Flight 93, before the plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.
"Michigan needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol," Trump said.
Claims centre on proscribed Muslim Brotherhood
El-Sayed's opponents have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist organisation that was founded in Egypt. Trump designated certain chapters of it as Foreign Terrorist Organisations earlier this year.
Some of the scrutiny of the affiliations of El-Sayed and his family members relates to their writings from more than a decade ago.
A social media post, external in 2012 by El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, appeared to refer to the movement, saying "my family has long been MB". El-Sayed's team have previously distanced him from other comments by Abdelhadi.
Critics have also pointed to an opinion piece El-Sayed wrote in Huffington Post in 2011, external about pro-democracy protesters in Egypt. In it, he acknowledged concerns that "supporting democracy in Egypt might allow the country to fall to the hands of the Muslim Brotherhood".
A year later he also allegedly signed an open letter by Egyptian Americans. In it, the group urged Mohamed Morsi, Egypt's first democratically elected president and a leader of the Muslim Brotherhood, to "purge the media and police" following the toppling of the authoritarian regime in the Arab Spring. This letter has not been discussed by El-Sayed.
El-Sayed has previously denied any connection to the Muslim Brotherhood and has stressed his loyalty to the United States. Asked recently at a town hall event whether he would disavow the organisation, he responded: "Absolutely."
Also in 2012, El-Sayed's current opponent Rogers, who was then a US representative and chairing the House Intelligence Committee, appeared to call for cautious engagement with the Muslim Brotherhood, telling Reuters, external: "Do I think there are moderate Muslim Brotherhood individuals we are going to have to reach out to and talk to? Yes but we are going to have to watch it carefully."
'Crossing a red line'
Among the others who condemned Trump's attacks were one of his key supporters ahead of the 2024 presidential election.
"The president's statements are out of line," Bishara Bahbah told the Associated Press. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist."
Bahbah was the founder of Arab Americans for Trump, a group believed to have been important in helping the president connect with a wider range of voters two years ago. The group later changed its name, removing the reference to Trump.
Trump clinched the White House in 2024 after victories in Michigan, which has a prominent population of Arab Americans, and a number of other swing states.
Asked about accusations of Islamophobia, White House spokesman Davis Ingle said: "Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed wants to massively raise taxes, advocates for defunding the police, and wants to destroy the Michigan auto industry by banning gasoline powered vehicles.
"President Trump will continue to call out complete and total extremists like El-Sayed without apology."
Additional reporting by Jake Horton

afabe52abb42.text: By — Krysta Fauria, Associated Press Krysta Fauria, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/to-make-ai-morally-good-tech-companies-are-turning-to-religion-but-some-experts-say-it-isnt-that-simple Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter To make AI morally good, tech companies are turning to religion. But some experts say it isn't that simple Nation Oct 26, 2026 3:50 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — As tech companies race to build the most powerful artificial intelligence, some are also asking how to teach a chatbot right from wrong. Their answer? Religion. "These are not questions a lab can answer," Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah said earlier this year at the Vatican's presentation of Pope Leo XIV's encyclical on AI. "They are questions traditions like yours have carried for millennia." Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Amid this much-discussed turn to faith, there has been little public scrutiny surrounding what exactly these technology companies think religion is — and, perhaps more important, what they hope to get out of it. As executives sound the alarm about AI's destructive potential and debate the need to develop morally good models, they are increasingly seeking input from philosophers and faith leaders. The executives' philosophy goes something like this: that religion can help inform AI to be morally good in an environment where fears about it — founded and unfounded — are hopscotching across the culture. Because these companies are not bound to a particular religion, the goal is often quite broad — an aggregate of moral ideas that can inform their models. "What I think ChatGPT should do is reflect that weighted average, or whatever, of humanity's moral view," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said last year. But experts and adherents alike warn that this idea fails to reckon with how different traditions and worldviews can often contradict one another. In short, they say, it's not exactly how religion works. Religion is more than a set of rules to follow For decades, scholars have pushed back against a widespread view of religion as a set of rules or principles that can be divorced from the "messy, practical, ad hoc" ways adherents live, argues Webb Keane, an anthropologist at the University of Michigan. The idea that religion can be separated from things like culture and politics remains entrenched, even though it suffuses both in many ways. Some worry that AI companies, as they ask various faith leaders to answer ethical questions, will further perpetuate a theory of religion that fails to recognize the importance of doctrine, ritual and relationships. Here's the issue, Keane argues: If you assume that religion overall can offer a distinct set of extractable moral principles, using it to train AI risks prioritizing certain traditions and distorting others — particularly when it comes to faiths that do not see themselves primarily as a system of ethics. "There's a very conventional way of thinking of religion as a rule book," he said. "It is certainly very tied to scriptural religion, and the scriptural religions at the end of the day really turn out to be the Abrahamic religions." Believers say tech companies are making an effort Watch the segment in the player above. That's not to say these meetings have lacked diverse representation. Nor does it suggest that their engagement with religion hasn't been thoughtful from the perspective of those in attendance, like Meghan Sullivan, a philosopher of religion who leads an initiative on ethics and AI at the University of Notre Dame. Though it doesn't enumerate the traditions it has consulted, Anthropic said in a May blog post that they'd met with "scholars, clergy, philosophers and ethicists from more than 15 religious and cross-cultural groups" — a pool they hope to broaden in the future. Earlier this year, Sullivan went to Anthropic for one of their meetings, which included Christians from different denominations. In contrast to conversations she'd had with other tech companies, she was impressed by the rigorous engagement with religion at Anthropic, which is widely seen as the AI company taking ethics and safety most seriously. "The culture inside the company is similar to that on a good college campus in the sense that you've got a collection of very intellectually curious people," she said. "These meetings are pretty nerdy — I don't know if that's the best way to put it — in a good way." Their meeting was split into two parts. First, the company explained their models "in layman's terms" to those in attendance. Next, the faith leaders responded with feedback and discussions, Sullivan said. "Every kind of moral question that this technology raises — everything from, 'Do humans have souls?' to 'Should third graders be able to access a chatbot for literacy education?'" Representatives from Meta, Google and Amazon have also met with the Vatican, while Microsoft has been vigorous about its religious outreach. Religion is ancient. The study of it is not Religion is generally considered both ancient and universal. And while experts like the late influential scholar of Jonathan Z. Smith concede that is true in some ways, they say it's also not the full picture. "Man has had his entire history in which to imagine deities and modes of interaction with them. But man, more precisely Western man, has had only the last few centuries in which to imagine religion," Smith wrote in 1982. Many scholars of religion today share Smith's view of their field. They call into question the idea that religions are a set of distinct, comparable systems, saying it's a modern notion that can be traced to as late as the 19th century. Buddhism and Hinduism, for example, were not recognized as clearly bounded traditions

Press freedom groups are suing the Trump administration over its efforts to block mainstream US news outlets from covering the White House, according to court filings.
The six plaintiffs, which include scholars, advocates and journalists, argue media bans issued by the White House violate the First Amendment of the US Constitution - a critical statute that provides broad protections for the press and freedom of speech.
Their suit comes after CNN, Politico, and MSNOW brought a separate legal challenge over the White House's attempts to revoke or restrict their press access.
The Knight First Amendment Institute and Yale Law School's Media and Information Access Clinic filed the legal case on the plaintiffs' behalf.
The six plaintiffs have asked a New York federal court to declare the White House's selective media bans violate the First Amendment, and to block the administration from continuing to enforce it.
In court filings, the plaintiffs allege they are no longer able to do their work without access to information delivered by the White House press.
The White House policy, they claim, "deprives the public" of reporting, and forces journalists who cover Donald Trump "to account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked".
Such a ban has a "distorting effect" on coverage from the White House, the court filing argues.
The BBC has asked the White House for comment.
The lawsuit did not ask a judge to award financial damages, only to require the defendants to cover their legal fees if they win.
Since Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, the White House has engaged in a contentious standoff with many longstanding US media outlets, which the president has frequently accused of publishing "fake news".
Last month, it banned reporters from CNN, Politico, and MSNOW from the White House, leading several other media organisations to temporarily suspend their pooled coverage of the president in protest.
The affected news outlets sued, arguing the White House was illegally discriminating against them because of the content of their coverage.
A federal judge later ordered the White House to restore the credentials of the impacted journalists while their lawsuit plays out.
The reporters later said they were allowed back into the White House complex.
The White House has, however, continued to selectively bar journalists, which news organisations in the US argue violates their press freedom protections.
CNN, for instance, has threatened to take further legal action in court as its reporters continue to be denied access aboard Air Force One to cover the president.
And last week, the White House banned a correspondent from The Independent from covering the president's trip to the state of Iowa, after Trump berated the reporter from the UK news outlet during a press conference.
In his second term, Trump has also moved to bring conservative bloggers, influencers and other "new media" figures into the press room, arguing it is necessary to provide diverse perspectives in White House coverage.
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool - the small group of journalists that has access to the president on any given day - which for more than a century had been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.
The same month, the White House moved to bar Associated Press journalists from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because the outlet used the term "Gulf of Mexico" rather than "Gulf of America".
AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.
Trump last week confirmed he is considering moving the entire press corps from the White House grounds following reports he was contemplating the reconstruction of a swimming pool that sits underneath the James S Brady briefing room.
"I am thinking about moving the press, and putting them in a different location," he wrote on Truth Social. "I will use that location for very badly needed space."

8132e57e8be7.text: By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/6-citizens-sue-trump-over-media-ban-saying-it-deprives-them-of-news-as-audience-stakeholders Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 6 citizens sue Trump over media ban, saying it deprives them of news as audience stakeholders Politics Oct 26, 2026 3:36 PM EDT In the increasingly bitter legal standoff between President Donald Trump and media outlets whose reporting he dislikes, a new and crucial third party has emerged: citizens who watch and read the news and need it to do their jobs. A lawsuit filed Monday on behalf of six such citizens — essentially representing the wider public audience — argues that it's not only the rights of news organizations that are violated when Trump bans them from White House premises. Even more fundamentally, the lawsuit argues, such bans violate the public's right to independent reporting about its president and government. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The ultimate injury here … is to the democratic public," says the suit, filed in federal district court in New York against Trump and three key aides, including the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles. "The First Amendment protects the public's right to know what its government is doing," said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute, which filed the lawsuit on behalf of the plaintiffs, along with the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School. "The White House cannot decide what information Americans receive by punishing critical reporting," Fallow said in a statement. "When the White House expels reporters because of their coverage and threatens others with expulsion, it isn't just the press that suffers — the public loses access to independent reporting and gets something closer to government propaganda." The Trump administration, asked for comment on the lawsuit, responded in a statement that it attributed to an unidentified White House official: "No person may demand access to the Oval Office." It said media that peddle "misinformation and defamation are completely capable of reporting their manufactured stories from directly outside." The plaintiffs all rely on White House news for their work The six plaintiffs are all people who say they rely on independent and diverse White House reporting for their teaching, journalism or advocacy. They include a noted human rights advocate, a political journalist, a Yale history professor, a high school civics teacher, a legal journalist, and a student journalist at the University of Pennsylvania. The complaint filed Monday recounts how various news organizations that have been targeted by Trump are already battling the administration in the courts. These cases include the current lawsuit by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, whose journalists were banished from the White House in September. A federal judge recently extended an order preventing the White House from enforcing the ban while the case makes its way through the legal system. Still affected, though, is CNN's pool coverage of Trump. The White House has been denying the network its usual slots in the video pool covering the president's activities and travel, and CNN has threatened further action. Also continuing is the legal case involving The Associated Press, whose reporters were barred last year from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some events in retaliation for the outlet's decision not to follow Trump's lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, to the Gulf of America. The New York Times is also involved in litigation, over a Pentagon policy requiring escorts for journalists on its grounds. And ABC is fighting back against the Trump administration in a dispute over renewal of its broadcast licenses. This lawsuit seeks more wide-ranging relief The new lawsuit filed Monday, though, is different from previous legal action against the president — first, in that the plaintiffs are ordinary citizens, shifting the focus from news gatherers to news consumers, and thus implying a much larger pool of stakeholders. In addition, it seeks more wide-ranging relief. The suit, which names Trump as defendant along with Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, and Secret Service Director Sean M. Curran, calls not merely for reinstatement of access that has already been impacted, but for a broad injunction that would protect from retaliation every news outlet that covers the White House — now, and in the future. "Defendants' policy of restricting the access of disfavored news organizations deprives the public of the reporting of those organizations," the complaint says. It also "inevitably deprives them of the independent reporting of other news organizations as well, since every journalist who reports from the White House must now account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked." "Plaintiffs ... seek a declaration that the policy is unconstitutional because it imposes restrictions on a limited public forum that are viewpoint-based and unreasonable," the complaint adds. "They also seek an injunction barring defendants from enforcing the policy." Plaintiffs include a human rights advocate, a teacher and a student journalist The plaintiffs are: Kenneth Roth, former longtime executive director of Human Rights Watch and a lecturer at Yale's law school and school of global affairs. Roth "relies on newsgathering and reporting from members of the White House press corps to inform his public writing and commentary," the suit says. Daniel Fro

DoorDash is in exclusive talks to acquire Instacart, according to people familiar with the matter.
A deal is far from certain and the talks could fall apart, the people cautioned. It could not be determined what price was under discussion or how a deal would be structured.
Instacart declined to comment. DoorDash did not immediately return a request for comment. Instacartâs sale process was first reported by the Information. The Information also reported that Uber was interested in a deal for Instacart, but Bloomberg later reported that that interest had cooled.
Know More
A combination would create a home-delivery giant, fusing Instacartâs grocery-store centric platform with DoorDashâs restaurant-focused one. DoorDash previously bid for Instacart in 2021, but at a significantly higher valuation. Those talks collapsed over price and worries about antitrust pushback, neither of which hold true today. Instacart has a valuation of roughly $12 billion, but at a conservative premium would likely fetch around $15 billion. DoorDash has a market capitalization of roughly $75 billion.
The grocery and home delivery space faces stiff competition chiefly from Amazon and Walmart, which has pressured conventional grocers for years.
The companies would likely not face antitrust issues as well: the Trump administration has taken a light-touch approach to other mergers, including a mammoth combination between Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount. But dealmakers expect that window to close, or at least shift, if Democrats succeed at the ballot box next month: senior Democrats have already said they will look to probe antitrust approvals and closed deals.

The US justice department illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director James Comey, a federal judge has ruled.
Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father, a critic of US President Donald Trump, and because of her perceived political affiliations.
Judge Jesse Furman ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.
A spokesperson for the justice department said in a statement that it disagreed with the decision and "will appeal in due course".
In his ruling, Judge Furman said Comey's dismissal violated the US Constitution as well as his right to a fair legal process.
He said the US attorney general can fire federal prosecutors but only "in a particular manner and only for certain reasons".
Furman noted that in Comey's role, "she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases and consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike".
Comey has worked on cases against the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and hip-hop mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs, who was convicted on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends last year.
Furman ordered that Comey to be given back pay from July until December 2025, when she accepted a new job.
In a statement, Comey's lawyers said: "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law".
Comey had previously said the only reason she was told about her firing was that it "came from Washington".
A complaint filed by her lawyers in September 2025 stated that they believed Comey had been fired "solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both".
The justice department said in court filings that the decision was made by former Attorney General Pam Bondi.
The Trump administration has twice brought charges against James Comey, including for allegedly lying to Congress, but that case was dismissed by a judge who said the prosecutor who brought the case was unlawfully appointed.
Earlier this year, the justice department charged Comey with knowingly and wilfully making a threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm, on the president. He has denied any wrongdoing.
The case stems from a 2025 Instagram post shared by Comey, which contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47". "Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump.

Americans have gone all in on "maxxing", making it the 2026 Word of the Year for Dictionary.com.
Short for maximising, the term "can be used on its own or added to the end of any word to convey you're doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible", Dictionary.com said in a statement.
It's a major departure from two years ago, when the site, after analysing US social media trends, news stories, and search data, chose demure as word of the year. Last year's was "67".
"Maxxing is the linguistic manifestation of a culture increasingly preoccupied with getting the most out of everything," said Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group.
Digital media used "maxxing" nearly 19 times more in August 2026 compared to the 2025 monthly average, Dictionary.com found. The site also considered affordability, data centre, odyssey, and the shortened form of uncle, "unc", as potential words of the year.
On social media, many people in Generation Z and younger - those under 30 - post extensively about their maxxing efforts to achieve all sorts of perfection.
Influencers focused on fitness and wellness post about "proteinmaxxing" and "fibermaxxing". Those giving their full attention to improving sleep habits say they are "sleepmaxxing".
The influencer Clavicular has gained thousands of followers as he chronicles his extreme "looksmaxxing" - working to meet a set of prescribed criteria for attractiveness, with particular importance given to jawlines, eyes and physique.
"Whatever we're doing, we want to push it further," Johnson said. "But its expanding uses also reveal how people are responding to that impulse. Some embrace it. Some exaggerate it for laughs. Others subvert it entirely to describe stepping back from the relentless pursuit of more."
People were playing with the term - and idea - for decades before Clavicular started posting videos.
In the opening song for the 1990's television show The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, for example, Will Smith raps: "Chillin' out, maxin', relaxin' all cool."

c0c86131b518.text: By — Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/lula-bucks-regional-shift-to-the-right-and-denies-trump-a-powerful-ally-in-brazil Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Lula bucks regional shift to the right and denies Trump a powerful ally in Brazil World Oct 26, 2026 2:48 PM EDT BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Brazilian voters have denied Latin America's resurgent right its ultimate prize, snapping a streak of seven straight conservative presidential victories in 18 months. The stunning triumph of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva over Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, with 51.8% of the vote to 48.2%, limits U.S. President Donald Trump's drive to tighten his grip on the Western Hemisphere and cements Latin America's most populous country and largest economy as a counterweight to Washington. A Bolsonaro victory would have left Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum as the only progressive president among the region's powerhouses. More broadly, Brazil's vote — held the same day Serbia's opposition scored a stunning win — opened a stretch of high-stakes elections that could reshape global politics, with Israel on Tuesday holding its first national election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack and the U.S. midterms on Nov. 3. For the Trump administration, which has wielded punishing tariffs, severe sanctions and military force to reassert its dominance in the region, Lula's victory complicates its campaign to enlist Brazil in its military coalition against cartels and to gain preferential access to the country's critical minerals, analysts say. By Monday morning, with his ally Flávio Bolsonaro refusing to concede and calling for the result to be annulled, Trump had yet to publicly acknowledge Lula's reelection, even as congratulations poured in from Brazil's allies and rivals around the world. Yet both sides see reasons to cooperate. Washington wants access to Brazil's vast trove of rare earths to reduce its defense industry's reliance on China. Lula wants foreign investment and tariff relief for Brazilian exporters. "Lula is pragmatic enough to work out some kind of modus operandi with the Trump administration," said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, adding that the Bolsonaros' allies in Washington would likely lose sway after the family's second electoral defeat. Flávio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, lost to Lula in 2022. "I'm not sure anyone in the Trump administration, beyond a few individuals, will want to keep making the Bolsonaros the central issue in the U.S.-Brazil relationship," he said. Trump's missing piece Across much of Latin America, voters fed up with rising crime have rewarded presidential candidates promising to restore order. From Peru's Keiko Fujimori to Colombia's Abelardo de la Espriella and Chile's José Antonio Kast, newly elected conservatives have courted Trump while taking their cues from El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, whose sweeping gang crackdown has sharply reduced homicides at the cost of mass arrests and suspended civil liberties. Trump has reinforced that shift with electoral endorsements, financial bailouts and pledges of military aid. "The U.S. is certainly putting its finger on the scale to try to help the more hard-line right-wing elements in the region," said Kenneth Roberts, a professor of government at Cornell University. Brazil would have been Washington's most consequential addition. Bolsonaro had promised to join the U.S.-led security coalition "with great enthusiasm and great honor," making his alliance with Trump part of his pitch to voters. Lula, by contrast, has championed Brazil's long tradition of nonalignment, cultivating ties with competing powers. His government deepened trade ties with China and sought greater global influence through BRICS, a group of emerging economies. Trump's heavy-handed support for the Bolsonaros played into that message. The double-digit tariffs he imposed on a range of Brazilian goods to punish Brazil for prosecuting former President Jair Bolsonaro over a coup plot to oust Lula stirred a nationalist backlash that the leftist leader channeled into the rallying cry "Brazil belongs to Brazilians." "To the extent that the regional superpower becomes a threat to Brazil's democratic institutions, defending Brazilian national sovereignty also becomes a form of defending Brazilian democracy," Roberts said. In his victory speech late Sunday, Lula described the outcome as "a demonstration that this country does not accept being anyone's backyard." Lula's red lines Brazil resisted joining the Shield of the Americas, a U.S.-led military coalition targeting cartels. When Washington in May designated Brazil's two largest criminal factions, the First Capital Command and the Red Command, as terrorist organizations, Lula warned the labels could become a pretext for American intervention. Countries along the main northbound cocaine and migrant routes, many of them heavily dependent on the U.S. market, have been more accommodating. In Ecuador, U.S. troops have joined local police in raids targeting suspected drug networks across the coastal lowlands. Honduras, Guatemala and Colombia have also agreed to joint military operations, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says, though Guatemala's government has denied it. It's a large country with a very independent history and a military that would not look kindly upon foreign troops in its own territory," said Brian Winter, a veteran Latin America analyst and editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly, a policy journal. "The Trump administration will have to walk a certain line here." On critical minerals, Lula wants Brazil to control its resources and preserve its freedom to sell beyond the U.S. Brazil holds t

Lieb, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/massachusetts-and-idaho-put-guns-on-the-ballot-one-to-restrict-them-the-other-to-honor-them Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Massachusetts and Idaho put guns on the ballot. One to restrict them, the other to honor them Nation Oct 26, 2026 2:27 PM EDT Parked in his truck along a rural Idaho highway on his way to an elk hunt, Neill Goodfellow pondered a question that will appear on his November ballot: which of six historic firearms to choose as the official state gun? Goodfellow is going to vote for the M1 Garand, a semiautomatic rifle widely carried by U.S. troops in World War II. In Massachusetts, voters are deciding a vastly different ballot question — whether to uphold a 2024 law requiring all firearms to be serialized and registered with the state and broadening a ban on "assault-style" guns. Massachusetts and Idaho are about 2,000 miles (3,200 kilometers) apart — literally and figuratively — in America's gun debate. The November election won't settle the tension between firearm freedoms and restrictions, but the ballot questions will provide a gauge of public opinion. Should voters approve it, Massachusetts Question 9 will continue an array of gun restrictions passed overwhelmingly by the Democratic-led Legislature in a state with one of the nation's lowest gun ownership rates. The question is going to voters because opponents gathered petition signatures forcing a referendum. In Boise, the Republican-led Legislature placed a nonbinding question on the ballot seeking voters' advice on designating "the state gun of Idaho." About 3 in 5 Idaho adults live in households with guns, which ranks among the highest rates nationally, according to an estimate from the RAND Gun Policy in America initiative. Some Republican lawmakers hope the ballot question will encourage more people to vote. Massachusetts gun owners face a registry deadline Residents in Massachusetts face a Wednesday deadline to register their firearms with the state. The referendum on whether to repeal that requirement happens six days later. That sequence has frustrated some gun owners. "It's a total violation of people's rights to require this before they have their chance to vote on it," said Toby Leary, chair of The Civil Rights Coalition, a group formed to lead the effort to repeal the gun law. Normally, when a referendum petition is submitted, a law is placed on hold until an election can occur. But Democratic Gov. Maura Healey signed an emergency provision making the gun law take effect immediately in 2024 — two years ahead of the referendum. Advocates tout the measure as the most comprehensive update in a decade to the state's firearms laws. In addition to establishing a state firearm registry, it bars "ghost guns" that lack serial numbers and devices that convert guns to fire rapidly, and expands a ban on assault-style weapons. It also broadens a "red flag" law to add healthcare providers and school administrators to the list of those who can ask courts to temporarily remove guns from people who pose a risk to themselves or others. "This legislation both preserves a legal pathway to gun ownership while also putting guardrails in place that keep people safe," said Ruth Zakarin, who chairs the campaign committee backing the gun law and is CEO of the Massachusetts Coalition to Prevent Gun Violence. Few states have wide-ranging gun registries A 40-year-old federal law prohibits the U.S. government from establishing a national registry of firearms or their owners. But some states have adopted their own requirements. Massachusetts was the third jurisdiction, behind Hawaii and the District of Columbia, to enact a comprehensive gun registry. Six additional states require registration of some firearms, such as handguns or those defined as assault weapons, according to the Giffords Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence. WATCH: Two doctors offer new ideas to prevent gun violence in America "These laws help law enforcement solve crimes, track down stolen and trafficked guns," said Lindsay Nichols, the center's policy director. "They also discourage illegal gun sales, and they help protect law enforcement by providing them information about what guns might be present when they are responding to an incident." But creating a government database of gun owners also could put people at risk, if the information is hacked and leaked, Leary said. Thieves possessing the addresses of gun owners could monitor their homes, waiting for them to leave for work or vacation to rob them of their firearms, he said. "The criminal element will know exactly who has what, where they live," he said. "It's a wish list for nefarious actors for where they can go get guns." About a dozen states have official firearms Utah and Arizona were the first states, in 2011, to adopt official state firearms. Utah lawmakers chose the Browning M1911 pistol, which was designed by a Utah native. Arizona lawmakers picked the Colt single-action Army revolver, described by the National Rifle Association as "an iconic firearm of the American West." Of the six options presented to Idaho voters, "none of them really have a significant place in the history of Idaho," said Goodfellow, a board member of the Idaho State Rifle & Pistol Association. "My suspicion is a lot of folks are not going to have a clue" which one to choose, he said. Yet for some people, the gun vote is a fun topic to debate. Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is wading into the political battle which is intensifying over the Rosebank oil field.
He is making a direct appeal to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to approve the plans to allow production to begin in the North Atlantic.
Environmentalists have long campaigned against the proposals for drilling in the UK's largest untapped oil field, 80 miles north-west of Shetland.
That the debate is now taking place within the Labour Party is a sign of the UK's recent journey on the politics of energy.
When Labour came to power in 2024, it was with a manifesto pledge not to allow any new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea.
A legal challenge thrust the future of the Jackdaw and Rosebank developments into the hands of the then-Energy Secretary, Ed Miliband.
At that point, senior offshore industry figures didn't hold out much hope of getting the go-ahead, given Miliband's deep commitment to renewable energy and his close political ties to Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
All that was before the outbreak of the war between the US, Israel and Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz and made an ongoing cost of living crisis even worse.
A new government under Andy Burnham entered 10 Downing Street with greater political freedom on the issue - and a new energy secretary to make the decisions.
Strictly speaking, Jackdaw and Rosebank aren't applications for new drilling licences, just the adjudication of existing ones.
But in political terms, the change of tone within Labour has been clear.
What had been an article of faith on energy has become something much more flexible.
It's a shift that's also plain to see within the SNP, with the Scottish government that once favoured a presumption against new oil and gas drilling now issuing a careful welcome to the Jackdaw announcement.
Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh announced that production could begin on the Jackdaw gas field.
She said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, the project would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add Â£2.9bn to the economy.
Environmentalists said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
The UK government has always insisted that these decisions are part of a quasi-judicial process, judged on strict environmental criteria, not politics.
But as attention turns to Rosebank, the politics are seeping in.
Within hours of Jackdaw being granted approval, a briefing campaign began suggesting that Fahnbulleh was "minded" to reject Rosebank.
Now, in the week of the Budget, reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.
The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank
Neither cabinet minister has given their view publicly, of course.
Fahnbulleh has insisted that the decision is "a regulatory process not a policy process," adding: "It sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because in the end only I can make it."
Even though she isn't looking for advice, the Scottish Labour leader is willing to offer it.
Marra is in Westminster meeting both Healey and Fahnbulleh in the run-up to the Budget on Wednesday.
Marra believes that on jobs and investment, the case for Rosebank is clear.
"I supported Jackdaw and Rosebank because I think they're really crucial for the Scottish economy, for employment, and for the public finances as well," he told me.
"We need to make sure that we're a country that people feel they can invest in.
"You've seen what's happened with Jackdaw in recent days - a real boost to the morale and the investment climate in the north east of Scotland."
He's also arguing for increased levies on banks in the Budget, to contribute towards the cost of help on the cost of living.
That second request looks set to be granted - which is likely why Marra feels able to make it publicly.
On Rosebank, we still can't say for sure how things will go.
But the fact this debate is even being had is itself a symbol of our new energy reality.

Guests attending a wedding on an island in Lower Lough Erne in County Fermanagh ended up stranded after a ferry took on water during Storm Boelo.
At the weekend, the storm brought winds of almost 80mph (129km/h) in some parts of Northern Ireland and caused the cancellation of flights and ferries.
About 12,500 households were left without electricity as a result of the storm, although all have since had power restored, according to Northern Ireland Electricity Networks.
Further strong winds - of up to 65mph (105km/h) - are expected on Monday night, with the Met Office issuing a yellow weather warning for coastal areas in counties Antrim and Down from 18:00 GMT until 03:00 on Tuesday.
Wedding guest ShÃ©a Clarke, who was on Lusty Beg Island, said: "You could see the waves were rough and the wind was going."
A yellow warning for wind along the north coast of counties Antrim and Londonderry takes effect from 03:00 GMT on Tuesday until 21:00 , with gusts of up to 60mph (97km/h) expected.
"Obviously it's too dangerous to cross and the boat can't cross so safety comes first," he added.
Despite the weather, the mood among the wedding guests on the island was good, he said.
"Some people have slept in cars, some people have slept on sofas there's been eight people in one room sleeping on the floor," said Clarke.
"But the spirit has been good the craic is 90... "as long as we don't run out of Guinness or chips."
A boat has since been taking guests off the island.
Olivia Millar, an airline cabin crew worker based in London, was also a guest at the wedding and had planned to be in South Africa on Monday night.
"It hasn't felt like real life but everyone's been amazing and we've just made the most of it," she said.
Michael Cadden, managing director at the Lusty Beg Island Resort and Spa, which hosted the wedding, said the ferocity of the storm was "unlike anything we've experienced on the island before".
"This was a crisis but we've now arranged to transport and are getting all our staff and customers safely home," he said.
Kacper Dymarczyk, a bartender, was locked down with the guests and worked through the storm.
He said there was "no concern" of running out of food or drink as the hotel was "well stocked at all times".
Flights were cancelled at airports across the island of Ireland at the weekend including about 40 at Belfast International Airport and about 30 at Dublin Airport.
On Sunday, the Department for Infrastructure (DfI) said about 470 storm-related incidents had been reported, including fallen trees and flooding.
A spokesperson for Northern Ireland's public transport provider Translink said that some bus services were diverted over the weekend due to fallen debris and rail restrictions were put in place in affected areas.
The Foyle Bridge in Londonderry was closed on Saturday due to high winds but reopened again on Sunday evening.
SDLP assembly member Mark H Durkan said he understood the need to close the bridge during the storm but added that its prolonged closure caused major traffic congestion in the city.
Speaking to BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today, Durkan said redirecting vehicles to the lower deck of the Craigavon Bridge caused a traffic build-up and showed that the city was in desperate need of a third bridge.
"The infrastructural capacity of Derry needs increased," said Durkan.
"I don't think two vehicular bridges for a city of this side and a population of this city is enough."

63d80ce85941.text: By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/thune-campaigns-for-republicans-in-marquee-senate-races-in-scramble-to-save-majority Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Thune campaigns for Republicans in marquee Senate races in scramble to save majority Politics Oct 26, 2026 2:06 PM EDT SIOUX CITY, Iowa (AP) — Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he wouldn't be offended if some Republicans didn't want to campaign with him. He knows that he's taken intense criticism from the party's base — and from President Donald Trump — for his chamber's inability to pass voter legislation this year. But Republican candidates in marquee Senate races have welcomed Thune's help as he's traveled around the country in the weeks before the midterm elections, scrambling to save his majority. That includes Rep. Ashley Hinson in this deep red corner of Iowa, a state that Republicans couldn't have envisioned as a tossup race a year ago. Hinson is locked in a tight contest against Democrat Josh Turek to replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Hinson said she was grateful for Thune's visit as the two spent Friday campaigning together in the northwest part of the state — a luncheon at the Sioux City chamber of commerce, a tour of the Iowa Air National Guard's refueling wing, a roundtable with local business owners and meet-and-greets at a packed high school football game that night. "I'm absolutely convinced that she flat has to win, and if she doesn't, we're not going to be in the majority," Thune said in a joint interview with Hinson between stops, during a brief moment of rest in the back of her campaign bus. He acknowledged the environment for Republicans is tough, but "we have to be able to deliver a message that you have a clear choice in front of you about two very different paths." The stakes for Thune and his party are enormous in Iowa and in several other traditionally Republican states as voters voice frustration with Trump, his war in Iran and high gasoline and grocery prices. Despite a map favoring Republicans, Democrats are hopeful that they can win the Senate. And like several other Democrats running in red states, Turek, a state legislator, is telling Iowa voters that he would be a bipartisan voice in Washington. Hinson acknowledges that voters have concerns. But "there is a lot at stake in this election," she says, "and Iowans are pretty savvy people to understand that this is a six-year term." Thune told voters who showed up to the business roundtable to "do everything you can to help her get there." "We've got to turn out the vote," he said. Thune makes closing argument to save his majority Beyond Iowa, Thune has campaigned with Republican Senate candidates in Nebraska, Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Mississippi, Kentucky, Florida and Minnesota. He's headed to Ohio in the coming days to help Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who is facing a tough challenge from Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown. It wasn't always a given that Thune, elected by his conference to replace Kentucky Sen. Mitch McConnell two years ago, would have so much face time with voters and candidates. Some on the right blame Thune for the failed effort to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship for voters and mandate voter ID across the country. Thune supports the bill, but it has no chance in the 100-member Senate with the filibuster intact, because Republicans need Democratic support for any piece of legislation to win the necessary 60 votes. Trump has pressed Thune to change the rules of the Senate and ditch the filibuster, but Thune has staunchly refused, citing the need to stop Democratic legislation if and when Republicans lose power again. Tensions between the two men peaked this summer, when Trump appeared to question Thune's leadership. Asked in the Oval Office if the South Dakota Republican was the man for the job, Trump replied that "we're going to find out, and I'll let you know." WATCH: Trump says he ordered suit to block Alaska Senate results if GOP loses Still, Trump has said more than once that he likes Thune personally, and Thune's office released photos earlier this month of the majority leader and his grandchildren at the White House, on a personal tour led by a smiling Trump. Thune is also well-liked among his colleagues and enjoys strong support from within his GOP conference — and from possible future members like Hinson. Thune joked at one of the Iowa events that "I tell all of our candidates, I'll come out for you or against you, whichever helps you the most." Thune navigates Trump, just like GOP candidates Voters in Iowa weren't asking Thune and Hinson about the SAVE America Act. Instead they were mostly focused on issues like childcare and how the economy and farm input costs are affecting their businesses. Like Thune, Hinson has been navigating Trump throughout her campaign — appearing with him at a rally in Sioux City the night before but also speaking out against decisions she disagrees with, like increasing beef imports and a deal with Russia to import diesel fuel. When the president is right about something, "I'm going to be with him, and if he's wrong about something, I'm going to be in his ear telling him," Hinson said. Both are also having to answer for Trump's war in Iran, as they have joined most Republicans in voting against repeated Democratic attempts to stop it. Rising gas prices since the war's inception along with Trump's trade war have hit farmers in the state particularly hard. Despite those votes, Hinson has said on the campaign trail that she wants to see the war come to a "successful and immediate end." Thune told attendees at the chamber of commerce lunch that the war is "not going to be a long-term thing."
