“The bright sun was extinguish’d … and the icy earth swung blind and blackening in the moonless air.” These words from Lord Byron’s 1816 poem Darkness evoke a hellish apocalypse. But Byron may have been inspired by the fallout of a real cataclysm — one that happened half a world away.
Mount Tambora, in present-day Indonesia, blew its top in 1815. More than 71,000 people in the vicinity died. And climate-cooling aerosols from the eruption ushered in extreme weather the following years in far-flung places. Cold weather in the summer of 1816, sometimes with frosts and snow, destroyed corn in New England, rice and buckwheat in China and wheat, oats and potatoes in Ireland. In some places, the rising cost of bread sparked protests and riots. The circumstances may have helped spread typhus. Some called 1816 “the year without a summer,” others “the year of the beggars.”
Like Tambora, volcanoes, and the cooling they cause, may be an underappreciated geologic force at times moving behind the scenes of human history.
“These climatic impacts of the Tambora eruption were recorded without any knowledge that this had anything to do with an eruption,” says Clive Oppenheimer, a volcanologist at the University of Cambridge.
While Tambora is the most well-studied eruption in history, others have also rattled the planet. Oppenheimer and his colleagues analyzed 38 large eruptions in the 2026 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences. Their work pulled together studies linking the geologic events and their effects on climate with their potential societal fallout in food systems, the economy, unrest, culture and religion. The locations and exact timing of the eruptions that spurred some notable cold spurts aren’t known. But understanding how the events impacted the climate, environment and society can offer clues to the past, including how people coped with climate stress.
“Volcanic eruptions, they are kind of this like hammer blow to the climate system,” says Heli Huhtamaa, a climate and environmental historian at the University of Bern in Switzerland. Volcanoes may offer lessons about resilience for modern societies in a warming world, she says.
Volcanic gases create a chilling effect
Volcanoes spew sulfur-containing gases. Over weeks, those gases react in the atmosphere to form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. Paintings from years after eruptions show bloodred sunsets or landscapes shrouded by hazy skies.
Because no two eruptions are exactly alike, it takes work to grasp each one’s impacts on weather and climate. “If we understand the climate response of one [eruption], that does not mean that we understand the climate response of another,” says Ulf Büntgen, a paleoclimatologist at the University of Cambridge.
Up in the air
A volcano’s explosivity impacts how high it shoots its gases and where they travel. Over time, those gases form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. In this computer model of a 1991 eruption, colors represent how high particles are in the atmosphere. Red is high and blue is closer to Earth’s surface.
Researchers find the traces of past eruptions in ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. Scientists try to nail down the date on a sulfur-loaded ice core layer and compare it with tree ring data, a logbook of sorts for summer growing conditions since temperatures impact how trees lay down their wood each year. Scientists can pull together tree ring records from far-flung places and use statistics to work out annual temperatures in a hemisphere.
Cold spells sometimes jump out from tree ring records. For years when cool summers impeded the final stages of wood formation, a chemical method used to estimate temperatures turns wood layers blue. Büntgen and colleagues saw two blue rings around 1345. “And that is very rare. We never saw that two years in a row,” he says. The rings coincided with the timing of the Black Death’s spread in Europe, the team reported in 2025 in Communications Earth & Environment. The researchers traced the connections between chilly summers, poor grain harvests in the Mediterranean and shipping records showing how Italian city states imported flea-ridden grain from the Caucasus.
Oppenheimer, Büntgen and their colleagues broadened the detective work for their 2026 review. The team studied Northern Hemisphere temperature responses to the 38 largest eruptions between A.D. 1 and 1900. On average, each volcano caused about 0.5 degrees Celsius of cooling in the year after the eruption. Recovery to normal temperatures was slower for eruptions that occurred in times that were already colder on average, Büntgen says. In some periods, large or successive eruptions may lead to an elevated amounts of particles in the atmosphere for a long time. The team’s calculations show that high aerosol levels concur with some of the past two millennia’s coldest spells, such as the one preceding the Black Death.
Human agency factors into eruptions’ outcomes
Those cold snaps often had dire consequences. Out of 17 large-scale famines in Europe from 1300 to 1800, 11 followed major eruptions. In addition to faltering crops and famines, the most frequently societal responses described in studies collected by the review authors were disease outbreaks, political turmoil and migration.
The societal circumstances surrounding eruptions are as important as the amount of cooling, Huhtamaa says. She and her colleagues studied crop failures and farmstead desertion in three different volcanic eruptions that impacted Ostrobothnia, in what is now Finland. During the 17th century, Ostrobothnia experienced cooling from three sets of eruptions at different time periods.
Although the latest eruption event, in 1695, was the coldest of all, peasants fared better than they had after eruptions earlier in the century, Huhtamaa and colleagues reporte

1f6edcea35a8.text: By — Julia Frankel, Associated Press Julia Frankel, Associated Press By — Joseph Krauss, Associated Press Joseph Krauss, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/whatever-the-outcome-of-israels-election-netanyahus-policies-toward-palestinians-will-likely-endure Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Whatever the outcome of Israel's election, Netanyahu's policies toward Palestinians will likely endure World Oct 26, 2026 1:34 PM EDT JALUD, West Bank (AP) — Even if Tuesday's pivotal elections in Israel mark the end of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's decades-long political career, his legacy in the Israeli-occupied West Bank — of massive settlement expansion, the displacement of tens of thousands of Palestinians and the empowerment of armed settler extremists — will likely endure. Israelis are deeply divided over Netanyahu's leadership and moral character, but they largely support settlement expansion and are opposed to a Palestinian state. So while Netanyahu's opponents have vowed to crack down on settler violence and remove the most contentious outposts, they are mostly against a two-state solution, seen internationally as the only realistic way to resolve the conflict. "There shouldn't be any illusions," said Mairav Zonszein, senior Israel analyst at the International Crisis Group. "At best, (a new government) would be able to slow down the extremely crazy acceleration that we've seen in the last four years of every aspect of Israel's aggression in the occupied territories and inside Israel itself." The military stands down in the face of settler violence One legacy of Netanyahu's nearly unbroken 17-year rule — the longest of any Israeli leader — is that large groups of armed settlers now routinely defy the Israeli military as they rampage through Palestinian communities, drive people from their homes and seize ever larger swaths of their land. Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack out of Gaza turbocharged the process. Netanyahu's opponents could bring in more troops and authorize stricter measures, but the genie may already be out of the bottle. Netanyahu's government has distributed thousands of firearms to the settlers, who have allies in the military and security forces. Some extremist settlers have become like sheriffs — making arrests, killing Palestinians they say posed a threat, summoning security forces and driving Palestinian families from their homes. The Palestinian Tubasi family was forced out in July after settlers besieged their hilltop home in the West Bank village of Jalud for 19 days. The settlers cut off their water access and their electricity, and threatened to "barbecue" them if they didn't leave, said Mahmoud Tubasi, 60, the patriarch. An Israeli court ordered the military to bring the family back, but that hasn't happened. Troops aborted their latest mission soon after it began, when a mob of over 150 armed settlers quickly assembled, scaled the walls of the home and set a car on fire. Troops threw Tubasi and his family into an armored jeep and drove them away as settlers torched the place. They now live in relatives' houses in the valley below their gutted and blackened home, around which settlers still roam. Israel's military did not respond to a request for comment. "If they wanted to evacuate them, of course, 100%, they can do that," Tubasi said. "This is an army that fights in Lebanon, Gaza and in Iran — they can't control 150 or 200 settlers?" The process is repeated across the West Bank Under Netanyahu, settlers have established over 250 rustic camps across the territory, focusing particularly on areas where Palestinian herding communities have dwelled for decades. The outposts allow the settlers to effectively run Palestinians off vast rural areas by attacking shepherds, taking over water resources and grazing their own herds, all under the eye of Israeli troops. Dror Etkes, a researcher with an Israeli anti-settlement group, says the outposts have allowed the settlers to seize effective control of around a fifth of the West Bank. Israel captured the territory, along with Gaza and east Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war. The Palestinians want all three territories for their future state. READ MORE: Netanyahu denies allegations he's escalating tensions with Iran before Israel's election Since 2023, the strategy has forced at least 127 Palestinian herding communities off their land, according to data gathered by Etkes' organization, known as Kerem Navot, and B'Tselem, another Israeli anti-settlement group. The departures have cleared nearly the entire eastern flank of the West Bank, along the border with Jordan, of Palestinians. The settlers' explicit goal is to prevent the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. Netanyahu's opponents say they will go after the most violent settlers and dismantle outposts — which are illegal under Israeli law. But they will not evacuate the over 100 new settlements Netanyahu's government legalized, including 44 that were formerly outposts. Nor will they remove settlements dating back decades, many of which now resemble fully developed suburbs. Most of the international community views all Israeli settlements as illegal and an obstacle to a two-state solution. Israel views the West Bank as the biblical and historical heartland of the Jewish people and says its future status should be decided by negotiations — which have not been held in over a decade. Even if some outposts are removed, many Palestinians seeking to return would find their homes burned and looted, and would continue to face threats from nearby settlers. "The story is over. There will be no massive dismantlement of settlement," said Etkes. "It's now a full and prouder-than-ever apartheid regime." Amnesty International and other major rights groups accused Israel of the international crime of apartheid even before the Oct. 7 attack and its aftermath. Israel denies the allegation. Netanyahu's opp

035698e30f0b.text: By — Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/netanyahu-denies-allegations-hes-escalating-tensions-with-iran-before-israels-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Netanyahu denies allegations he's escalating tensions with Iran before Israel's election World Oct 26, 2026 1:22 PM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Israelis entered the final 24 hours of an intense election season on Monday, as reports circulated that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have clashed with the Israeli military over initiating a possible escalation with Iran immediately before the vote. Tensions flared over reports that Netanyahu and his military chief of staff disagreed over an instruction by the prime minister to carry out an "action" that the army worried could reignite the conflict with Iran. Netanyahu's office denied the report, first published by Israel's Channel 12, as "fake news." Defense Minister Israel Katz also quickly denied the report. "I state unequivocally that there has been no intention by Israel of initiating an attack on Iran before the elections in Israel," Katz wrote on X on Monday, calling reports of rifts between political and military leaders "completely baseless and false." However, he said that Israel would respond forcefully if Iran attacks first. Israel's opposition candidates accused Netanyahu of endangering regional stability for his political preservation. Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, warned Netanyahu not to "dare to place your own political interests above the security of the state." He posted on X, "Netanyahu, my eyes are on you." Avigdor Lieberman, head of the hawkish Yisrael Beytenu party which is part of the opposition bloc, sent a letter to Israel's attorney general demanding a criminal investigation into possible treason by Netanyahu's "attempts to drag Israel into a war on the eve of elections, including a willingness to sacrifice (Israeli) soldiers out of fear of losing the election." The election on Tuesday is the first since the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which sparked the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza and conflicts across the Middle East. READ MORE: Signs of fraying loyalty emerge in Netanyahu stronghold before Israeli election Israelis are deeply divided heading into what is expected to be a close race, and the veteran Israeli leader's legacy is on the line. Netanyahu's opponents say he should be held accountable for the failures surrounding the Oct. 7 attack. His supporters say that he has led the country back from its toughest moment. The vote also marks another important test for the populist right. Brazil's voters dealt a stunning setback to the movement on Sunday, lifting President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to a surprising victory over Flávio Bolsonaro. The Republican Party of U.S. President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Netanyahu, faces a new test next week in the U.S. midterm election. Although Israelis are breathlessly approaching the election as one of the most crucial in years, people across the Middle East aren't expecting dramatic changes regardless of the victor. Both Netanyahu and his main rivals have similar approaches to Israel's regional security in both Gaza and Iran. In southern Gaza, Jamal Abu Deeb, who was displaced from Khan Younis, said that no matter who is elected, it won't be good news for the Palestinians. "It is all war and destruction," he said, adding that there are still strikes every day that kill people and children across Gaza. "Do you think whoever gets elected will give us a better life? Quite the opposite." Ibrahim Qeshta, who was displaced from Rafah, said that "they all have the same playbook, they have no mercy — death and destruction for everyone." "Eisenkot is like Netanyahu, he will be the same," Qeshta said. "Our people die every day, for nothing." Iran also watched the last-minute electioneering warily. "It makes no difference to us who ultimately takes the helm of a regime whose track record shows that it has brought nothing to our region but violence and bloodshed," Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said in his weekly media briefing on Monday. Wafaa Shurafa contributed to this report from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. d93534832e7d.text: A pair of Trump-friendly right-wing populists took a one-two punch Sunday: Brazil rejected a Bolsonaro comeback, and Serbia toppled a strongman's ruling party. The big picture: Brazil denied Trump a close ally at the helm of Latin America's largest economy, snapping a streak of seven straight conservative wins in the region. In Europe, Serbia and Hungary toppled leaders with close Trump ties who had dominated their countries for years. Now, another massively pivotal election looms Tuesday, when Trump ally , Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, will face a battle for political survival . On the eve of the election, Netanyahi touted Trump's endorsement and his "friendship" with the American president. But as the global right has made gains, opposition forces proved this weekend that they still have fuel. Driving the news: In Brazil, leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva staved off a challenge from Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro . The younger Bolsonaro, widely seen as the heir to his father's populist movement, refused to concede and called for the results to be annulled, according to translations . The elder Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence after being convicted of plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 loss . Trump has called the prosecution a "WITCH HUNT." The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the race. Between the lines: Brazil's election emerged as a test of Trump's political influence in Latin America, where right-wing and Trump-backed candidates have celebrated an uninterrupted series of wins . Those victories include Trump-endorsed Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia , Nasry "Tito" Asfura in Honduras and José Antonio Kast in Chile . Trump did not formally endorse Flávio Bolsonaro, but he met with him earlier this year and imposed ignificant tariffs on Brazil as he protested the charges against Bolsonaro's father. Lula is a vocal Trump critic. In March, Flávio Bolsonaro told an audience at the Conservative Political Action Conference that America faced a "fork in the road" in the election: "Either you have the most powerful ally in the hemisphere, or an antagonist." Zoom out: Meanwhile, across the Atlantic, a student-led opposition movement toppled the right-wing party of long-serving strongman Aleksandar Vučić, who was seeking to become prime minister. Unlike the Bolsonaros, Vučić conceded defeat Sunday. The Balkan leader had courted Trump's inner circle, including Donald Trump Jr., and described the president as a "kindred spirit." It reflects the shifting tides that also allowed next-door Hungary to oust Trump-allied Viktor Orbán , once one of the Western world's most entrenched populist leaders, in April after 16 years in power. Yes, but: Europe's political upheaval is cutting both ways: While the populist right has fallen in Serbia and Hungary, it's gaining ground in two of the continent's largest economies. In France, far-right presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen launched her 2027 campaign this weekend, seizing on nationwide unrest to pitch her tough-on-crime, anti-migrant agenda. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany won a record 44% in a state election last month and continues to lead in national polls. What we're watching: Trump's historic move of endorsing Netanyahu in Tuesday's Israeli elections will once again test his influence abroad. Tuesday's election in Israel is set to be tight for Netanyahu, who has sought to elevate Trump's endorsement as he jockeys with former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot . The 77-year-old Netanyahu has been prime minister for some 19 years in nonconsecutive terms. Analysts see the election as a referendum on the security failure of Oct. 7, 2023, that killed around 1,200 people. Whoever governs Israel could shape Trump's next moves in the Middle East — including whether to escalate the war in Iran. Go deeper: Lula v. Bolsonaro: Brazil election unfolds in Trump's shadow

Sisak, Associated Press By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press By — Alanna Durkin, Associated Press Alanna Durkin, Associated Press By — Larry Neumeister, Associated Press Larry Neumeister, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-doj-illegally-fired-ex-fbi-directors-daughter-maurene-comey-as-a-federal-prosecutor-judge-rules Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump DOJ illegally fired ex-FBI director's daughter, Maurene Comey, as a federal prosecutor, judge rules Politics Oct 26, 2026 1:11 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The Trump administration last year illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, from her job as a federal prosecutor in New York, a federal judge ruled Monday. Maurene Comey, who was an assistant U.S. attorney for a decade, was illegally fired in July 2025 despite her work on some of the nation's highest-profile cases and consistently receiving "the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike," Judge Jesse M. Furman found. READ MORE: Fired federal prosecutor Maurene Comey sues Trump administration over abrupt dismissal After her firing, Comey sued the Justice Department and others, saying her termination violated the constitutional separation of powers, the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. She asserted that she was fired because she was the daughter of James Comey, whom President Donald Trump has long viewed as an enemy, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, the judge noted. Furman rejected the government's claim that Comey could be fired because federal prosecutors exercise the president's "conclusive and preclusive" powers. He said the government's claim that Congress is barred from regulating the removal of federal prosecutors "flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent." Furman added: "Indeed, to accept Defendants' argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system." The firing violated the separation of powers, the Administrative Procedure Act and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, the judge ruled. Furman reserved judgment on Comey's First Amendment claim pending further arguments to be submitted by each side, though he said he was inclined to dismiss the claim because it was largely moot since she is now in private practice and no longer seeks actual reinstatement. The judge granted Comey retroactive reinstatement and back pay from the date of her firing through Dec. 20 to "make her whole" and ensure that she doesn't suffer adverse employment consequences for the "unlawful termination." Comey's lawyers, Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan, lauded the ruling. "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law," they said in a statement. "As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system.' This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law." The Justice Department didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment. The Justice Department during the Trump administration has fired scores of career employees, including prosecutors and FBI agents, who participated in investigations of President Donald Trump or who were perceived as opposed to the administration's agenda. Some of those firings have also resulted in federal lawsuits. The firing of Maurene Comey was seen as particularly personal, given her father's longtime adversarial relationship with Trump. The president fired James Comey as FBI director in May 2017 as the bureau was investigating ties between Russia and the Republican's successful 2016 campaign for the White House. Trump in the years since has repeatedly called for Comey to be jailed, and his Justice Department has worked with mixed success to make that happen. An earlier criminal case accusing James Comey of having lied to Congress in 2020 was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47," a case he has sought to dismiss that some legal experts have greeted with skepticism. 69a21532415c.text: TEL AVIV, Israel — Gadi Eisenkot is as low-key as Benjamin Netanyahu is bombastic. He's a political novice up against the longest-serving, most politically savvy prime minister in Israel's history. And yet, on the eve of Tuesday's elections, Eisenkot poses the most serious threat to Netanyahu's hold on power in years. Why it matters: A victory by the Yashar party leader would upend Israeli politics and could reset the country's strained relationships abroad. The intrigue: The contrast between the two top contenders could hardly be sharper. Their roots: Eisenkot, the son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants, grew up in Eilat, Israel's southernmost city. If he wins, Eisenkot will be the first prime minister of Moroccan descent in Israel's history. Their military backgrounds: Netanyahu served in the Israel Defense Forces' elite special forces unit "Sayeret Matkal" and later went into business and politics. Eisenkot joined the IDF Golani infantry brigade and rose through its ranks as a combat commander until becoming IDF chief of staff. He arrived at his rally on Sunday to the tune of the Golani brigade song from 1974. Their ties to America: Netanyahu is better versed in American politics — and more articulate in English — than many American politicians. Eisenkot is not an "American" politician at all, let alone a professional one. He speaks English with a heavy Israeli accent and doesn't deliver catchy soundbites. He does not enjoy being on TV. At his final campaign rally Sunday before about 1,000 supporters, Eisenkot was visibly uncomfortable being in the spotlight, even when the crowd cheered him on. Their trustworthiness: Netanyahu's credibility with the Israeli public has been battered by his long-running corruption trial, his political tactics, his refusal to take responsibility for the failures that led to October 7 and accusations of duplicity in his handling of the Iran war. Eisenkot is seen as a straight shooter, even among many of his opponents. Zoom in: The failure to prevent the October 7 attacks spurred Eisenkot to challenge Netanyahu. Eisenkot, who joined Nƒetanyahu's emergency cabinet shortly after the attacks, lost his son during the war. He later lost two of his nephews in the war. Zoom out: Netanyahu has cultivated a vast network of donors, lobbyists and supporters in American power corridors for the past half-century. Bibi is a household name in America — for better and worse. Eisenkot, on the other hand, is almost anonymous in Washington. Very few people know him personally, even within Jewish organizations. He did spend time in America in the 1990s studying for a master's degree at the U.S. Army War College. Eisenkot's main connection to the U.S. was through the military, particularly his relationship with former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Gen. Joseph Dunford. After retiring from the IDF in 2019, Eisenkot spent a year as a fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The numbers: Eisenkot is leading Netanyahu by 8 to 10 points in most pre-election polls. While Netanyahu is toxic among at least half of the voters, polls show Eisenkot enjoys high likability across the board. Netanyahu's efforts to publicly vilify him have been so far unsuccessful. The big picture: Eisenkot ran on a center-right platform. He did not make any sweeping foreign policy pronouncements and took pains to steer clear of any public positions that would allow Netanyahu to paint him as weak. Bibi tried to do it, anyway. Eisenkot has expressed opposition to a Palestinian state under current conditions. He has committed to taking strong steps to crack down on Jewish terrorism against Palestinians in the West Bank. He also pledged to end Hamas' control of Gaza within 18 months of taking office, either through diplomacy or military force. Eisenkot supported the war against Iran and strikes on its nuclear facilities. But he opposed Netanyahu's attempt to use military power to force regime change, calling it unrealistic. Eisenkot supports continuing economic pressure on Iran and building a regional alliance with the Arab world to curb Iranian influence. What to watch: Eisenkot has operated under the assumption that Netanyahu would be endorsed by President Trump. He tried to use his good relationship with GOP mega-donor Miriam Adelson to lobby Trump to stay on the sidelines. When Trump finally endorsed Netanyahu last week and again on Sunday, Eisenkot didn't criticize him, but rather praised the president's support for Israel. "I am convinced President Trump will work in full cooperation with any leader that will be elected by the Israeli people," Eisenkot wrote on X Monday.

Algeria is to send troops to Niger in its first foreign deployment since sending forces to Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war in 1973.
The deployment follows a visit to Algiers by Niger's defence minister, as the country seeks support against armed groups, some of which are linked to al-Qaeda or Islamic State.
Algeria has economic interests in Niger, including a planned gas pipeline that would carry Nigerian gas through Niger to Algeria. The troops are expected to protect energy facilities in northern Niger, near the Libyan border.
The deployment comes as the two neighbours rebuild ties after a diplomatic rift in 2025, when Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers.
Algeria's upper house of parliament held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on the proposed deployment. According to AFP news agency, 148 of the 174 senators voted in favour. It was later backed by the lower house of parliament.
However, the timing and number of soldiers to be deployed have not been announced.
The move would mark the first use of a 2020 constitutional provision allowing overseas military deployments and a significant shift in Algeria's long-standing policy against sending forces abroad.
"We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure," Algerian senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after the vote.
Algeria's state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has also signed an agreement with Niger's petroleum ministry to explore for oil in the Kafra region. Two exploration wells are estimated to contain 168 million and 100 million barrels, respectively, Reuters reported.
Relations between Algeria and Niger have not always been smooth in recent years.
Algeria condemned the 2023 coup that ousted Niger's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum, and brought Gen Abdourahamane Tchiani to power.
Tensions rose again in 2025 after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border. Niger recalled its ambassador to Algiers in solidarity with Mali, a close ally which is also under military rule.
Relations have since improved. Tchiani visited Algeria in February 2026, and in late August, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune sent fighter jets to Niger to help suppress a coup attempt and also donated four military helicopters.

26a29ec734c8.text: By — Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press By — Bernard Condon, Associated Press Bernard Condon, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/anthropic-files-for-potentially-the-biggest-ipo-ever-as-ceo-warns-of-ais-existential-risk-to-humanity Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Anthropic files for potentially the biggest IPO ever as CEO warns of AI's existential risk to humanity Nation Oct 26, 2026 12:40 PM EDT SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity. The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public in what is expected to be a pair of blockbuster stock debuts for the rival AI labs. READ MORE: Anthropic and OpenAI sound the alarm on AI safety — and seek to shape how it's controlled The filing comes weeks after CEO Dario Amodei argued in an essay for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models. An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price, but even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world's most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela, by billions of dollars. The 335-page document showed Anthropic's revenue is growing rapidly, but like many other tech companies going public, it has yet to turn a profit. The company behind the chatbot Claude reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, though its losses after taking out certain items were a fraction of that. In the same period a year ago, Anthropic lost $13 billion. Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world's most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla. As for money raised, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by one of Elon Musk's companies, SpaceX, earlier this year. In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT." Risks aplenty, but a big payoff to the founders In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals. Formed in 2021 by ex-OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company, and the two leaders, Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, are widely seen as bitter rivals. But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs in resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble. The need for cash may explain why Anthropic is rushing to tap public markets this year, and not waiting until next year, as is OpenAI's plan. Adding to the pressure is the possibility demand for AI shares could drop, or even collapse in the coming months. Investors have become increasingly jittery about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently. In addition to helping plug any cash shortfall, the IPO will shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic's seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. Collectively they own nearly 500 million shares, though it's unclear from the offering document how much that will represent of the company after the IPO. Dario, 43, and 39-year-old Daniela, who is Anthropic's president, are worth $15.5 billion each, according to Forbes, which ranks them as the 176th and 177th richest in the world. Reflecting AI's dangers, the document includes some unusual provisions, including granting those two and their five other co-founders 50.1% of shareholder votes through a special class of shares. Anthropic has also appointed independent, financially disinterested members of a so-called Long-Term Benefit Trust, holding power to appoint directors, that is designed to ensure the company doesn't put financial interests ahead of public safety. READ MORE: AI discovered a software vulnerability that could impact 70% of websites worldwide. The rush is on to patch it Another unusual feature of the filing is its long list of "risk factors," a required disclosure for every public company but in this case one that runs nearly 100 pages — and makes for riveting reading. Among the risks are the quotidian — the possibility it won't be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — and the horrific. The latter includes the prospect of "malicious actors" using AI models to build chemical weapons, authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens and, given the numerous hacking incidents from rogue AI agents recently, the possibility Anthropic's AI models could "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." Calls for an AI slowdown The IPO comes as reports emerge about AI's ability to solve problems beyond human capacity for good, but also to carry out harmful, life-threatening tasks while humans lose control. In September, Amodei said the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up.

More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks on Christians in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the country's Orthodox Church.
One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described it as an ambush. "We were completely unprepared and had no prior knowledge. They surrounded us from all four directions," he told BBC Amharic.
The regional government said that it would take action against those responsible.
A local official blamed the attacks on a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented but has denied carrying out previous such attacks.
A statement from the Holy Synod of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church said that 20 houses were burnt to the ground in the attacks. It did not say who was responsible.
Eyewitness told BBC Amharic that five of those killed were children.
A church official described the attacks on three areas in the Shirka district as a "massacre", saying security forces arrived at the scene but were unable to stop the assault.
Many residents have now fled the area.
Condemning the violence, the Orthodox Church said attacks against Christians had been increasing recently, and that "such actions undermine the country's values of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence".
In a statement posted on Facebook, the Orthodox Church said it had repeatedly raised concerns about insecurity with authorities at different levels of government, but that "so far there has been no solution".
The Ethiopian Human Rights Council, a non-governmental organisation, said in a report released in July 2026 that 458 people had been killed in attacks in that area over the previous four years.
But this is one of the most deadly attacks in that period.
The report said armed groups had repeatedly targeted local communities, particularly followers of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in what it described as religiously motivated attacks.
The government has previously blamed the OLA for the attacks, with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed saying violence targeting civilians and religious institutions was part of a plan to destabilise the country.
The group, which says it is fighting for greater rights for the Oromo people, denies these allegations.
Previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims in the area. Residents who spoke to the BBC on various occasions have described the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature.
About two-thirds of Ethiopians are Christians, mostly Orthodox, while one third are Muslim.

In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.
By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.
Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.
A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.
For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.
The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.
And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.
Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.
Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.
But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and the energy that flowed through it.
The Iran question
The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.
He has made new claims â without providing evidence â about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.
His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.
US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.
Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.
So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.
He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity â involving him â rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.
So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes.
'Legacy mode'
Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington.
"After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home."
In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks.
In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media.
Little wonder policymakers in Tehran have been following US opinion polls as closely as any analyst inside the Washington beltway. The risk, of course, is that any post-electoral strikes would plunge the Middle East into fresh chaos if Iran were to retaliate hard.
Publicly and privately, Iranian officials have threatened to hit airports, pipelines, undersea cables, energy facilities, desalination plants as well as US bases and warships.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote in the Financial Times that new attacks would put "civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk".
It's the economy
The two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz.
The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances.
Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanction

71a00aa2789b.text: By — Jake Coyle, Associated Press Jake Coyle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/eric-bauza-modern-voice-of-bugs-bunny-and-other-looney-tunes-characters-dies-at-46 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Eric Bauza, modern voice of Bugs Bunny and other Looney Tunes characters, dies at 46 Arts Oct 26, 2026 12:10 PM EDT Eric Bauza, the award-winning voice actor whose performances of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and many more characters made him the modern voice of Looney Tunes, has died. He was 46. Bauza died suddenly late Sunday, his family said in a statement. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner reported that he died at his home from hypertensive cardiovascular disease. READ MORE: Emmy Awards to move to Prime Video in 2027 Beginning in 2001, Bauza amassed more than 400 voice acting credits in a career that gave voice to beloved characters in animated Looney Tunes series including "Puss in Boots," "Muppet Babies," "Avatar: The Last Airbender," and countless others. He won three Children's and Family Emmy Awards, from 2022 to 2025. "Looney Tunes will always have a special place in my heart," Bauza said in an interview with The Associated Press this year. "I watched them on Saturday mornings originally. It's not just the voice but the overall aesthetic has influenced me as an artist." Raised in Scarborough, Ontario by Filipino immigrant parents, Bauza found his passion for voice acting as a teenager. In high school, he would deliver the P.A. system morning announcements in various cartoon voices. In voicing Looney Tunes characters, Bauza faithfully and reverentially channeled Mel Blanc. So great was his affection for Blanc that, in conversation, he would even toss out an impression of Blanc outside the recording booth. Bauza last year told The New York Times: "Mel Blanc is like the voice of God for me." Bauza's Looney Tunes work included such feature films as "Space Jam: A New Legacy" (2021), "The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie" (2024) and this year's "Coyote vs. Acme." That film, in which Wile E. Coyote takes the Acme Corporation to court for its defective products, became a modest cause célèbre after Warner Bros. opted not to release it. After an outcry from fans, partly stoked by Bauza, the film eventually found a distributor in Ketchup Entertainment and surpassed $100 million at the worldwide box office. While the film was in limbo, Bauza argued for its release at the 2024 Annie Awards, in the voice of Daffy Duck. "He's the go-to cartoon character above anyone else when it comes to begging and pleading," Bauza explained. "It seemed appropriate." As a voice acting professional, Bauza sometimes chafed at celebrities brought in to replace him in bigger-budgeted productions. Bauza occasionally voice-matched for stars including Bill Hader on "Bob's Burgers" and Antonio Banderas as Puss in Boots. "From my experience working several times in the feature film format, there's always the reminder that it is 'temporary dialogue' and 'Chris Pratt will be voicing all the Looney Tunes in this feature film' — no, just kidding," Bauza told The AP. But even in productions where A-list stars took the spotlight, Bauza said there was still room for "nine-to-fivers like me" to color in the scenery. Bauza, who seldom went more than a few minutes without slipping into the voice of Bugs or Daffy or some other character, was rarely anything but grateful at being part of the Looney Tunes legacy. "The Looney Tunes were here before I was born and they're definitely going to be here long after I leave this realm," he said shortly before the release of "Coyote vs. Acme." "I just feel like the luckiest guy." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 86a5fd2b6e60.text: Harvard economist Jason Furman told Axios that if he were to return to his old job as chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers today, he would rely on AI tools over staff economists for much of the council's day-to-day analytical work. The big picture: Unsurprisingly, this made some waves in the online discourse, particularly the loose-knit community formerly known as Econ Twitter. Many veterans of the economic policy trenches see real risks in future policymakers becoming overly reliant on AI — or at a minimum think that Furman is underestimating the importance of human economists in advising the nation's leaders. What they're saying: "CEA work, at least in my experience, is highly bespoke as you're explaining the data flow (and much else) to very busy people who don't want only market-shop analysis," Jared Bernstein, the CEA chair under President Biden, wrote on Substack . "Yes, they want and need that — what will the markets make of this CPI, jobs, GDP, etc. report — but more so they want to know how this report fits into our narrative, our agenda, the president's trip today to Iowa." He adds that within a White House, "the human skill of reading-the-room is paramount. I'm far from an AI expert, but my sense is it sucks at that and probably always will, a conclusion that derives in no small part from listening to its creators!" Zoom in: Claudia Sahm, a former Federal Reserve economist, raised an issue that we've often heard from senior people in fields like consulting and investment banking: If you get rid of junior positions, where will future senior leaders come from? Furman's staff "went on to found the Yale Budget Lab, run Treasury economic policy and a Fed institute, serve in later [administrations], and publish research on trade, environment, and taxes. That's what '20 staff' become," she wrote on X . "No model does that." Bloomberg chief U.S. economist Anna Wong argues that the "ability to now not depend on anyone, as a senior person, is very, very empowering. Now, with just the idea, a senior person can go far." Zoom out: "Entering into sci fi speculation," Wong wrote on X , "as humans [we're] not about to replace the aging experts due to low pipeline of young human experts, AI themselves, through the training over the years, became the one spawning the ideas." "That seems like a disaster waiting to happen that current social policy needs to address." Yes, but: Casey Mulligan, who served in President Trump's first-term CEA and now as chief economist at the Department of Health and Human Services, said that the implications of AI for human labor in policymaking are not so obvious. "I built AI tools at two federal offices," Mulligan wrote on X . "Able to do economic research better and more quickly, we needed more economists rather than fewer due to the added demand for what we do. This pattern is also evident in the small business sector." This concept — that labor-saving tools can actually increase demand for labor — is known as Jevons Paradox . The bottom line: "Be the labor-augmenting technological change you want to see in the world," wrote Stanford economist Neale Mahoney. "It's on us olders to build organizations where people and AI complement each other, and to prepare the youngers for a world with better and better AI," he adds.

c5e8947b91f7.text:
The News
Investors got a look for the first time at just how much money Anthropic is losing and how deeply entwined the frontier lab is with other players in the AI ecosystem.
The company is on the hook for more than $400 billion in future obligations for chips and data center leases, according to its long-awaited IPO document released on Monday. It lost $81 billion in the first half of this year, though most of that owes to accounting charges on derivative contracts that, ironically, grow alongside Anthropicâs valuation; operating losses narrowed to $700 million through the first six months of 2026.
Thereâs a lot riding on Anthropicâs trading debut. It will test investorsâ desire to keep funding an AI boom with no clear sight to profits, huge political risks, and an ambivalence toward traditional corporate governance rules that stands out even among founder-led tech giants.
Other companies, like Nvidia and Alphabet, offer safer ways to play the AI boom, and much of Anthropicâs pitch is that a company with a single product â one it admits is dangerously uncontrollable and unpopular â can justify a $1.5 trillion (or so) price tag.
Hereâs what else stood out to us in the filing.
The Filing
- The first-of-it-kind IPO has a novel governance structure to match. Anthropicâs seven co-founders will control the company through one golden share of supervoting stock â yes, just one share. A simple majority among the group of seven is enough to decide how that share is voted in most corporate matters. A separate council of âfinancially disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safetyâ will choose a majority of the board of directors, with the rest chosen by the founder group. Even compared with tech peers that afford their founders significant control, Anthropicâs setup stands out for how little say it gives shareholders whom the company is now asking to put up tens of billions of dollars. Amazon and Google, which were early investors in Anthropic, will receive nonvoting stock.
- The company owes a lot of people a lot of money. Anthropicâs compute liabilities could hamstring the company: As of June, it was on the hook for $417 billion in future compute and infrastructure leases. The company also expects to pay out $24 billion in stock-based compensation to its 5,300 employees â an average of $4.5 million apiece.
- A big key-man risk: US President Donald Trump. The filing calls out the February spat between Trump and CEO Dario Amodei over the use of Anthropicâs models in war. If the US government were to restrict its models again like it did with Fable and Mythos in June, or invoke export controls or the Pentagonâs Defense Production Act, it would limit its ability to do business. Anthropic said it doesnât plan to stand down from its positions, and that its own policy advocacy could be costly.
- The other key-man risks. Anthropicâs five largest customers represented roughly a quarter of revenue â and largely arenât locked into contracts. Nearly half its revenue comes from cloud service providers like Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Amazon Web Services.
- Skynet becomes self-aware. The self-appointed arbiter of AI safety warns of existential threats in its risk factors, highlighting that flags have been raised internally among its own staffers. âSufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.â
- Notably absent. China only made a few cameos in the 318-page document (11 times to be exact) despite competition between the two superpowers dominating the AI conversation around the world. Although the filing alludes to open-weight models âreleased by state actorsâ and frames distillation as a competitive and national security risk, Anthropic doesnât directly call out Chinese firms.
- Anthropicâs founders arenât meat proxies. An analysis from AI slop-detection tool Pangram found that the intro letter from the companyâs leadership is human-written, rather than Claude-authored. As Claude would say, itâs not just noteworthy â itâs striking.
J.D. Capelouto and Ellen DiMauro contributed reporting.

Israeli and American leaders have been sharpening their threats before elections in both countries, while Iranian leaders have remained defiant. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey's intelligence service, met with Iran's top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington. The war in Yemen and strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia were also topics of the talks, according to two regional officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak with reporters. Qatari mediators also traveled to Tehran on Sunday, working in coordination with the United States, as part of efforts to de-escalate regional tensions, according to a regional official speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks. Pakistan and Qatar helped broker an agreement in June aimed at having Iran fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, ending a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and opening negotiations on a broader settlement addressing Iran's nuclear program. The deal unraveled quickly, however, as both sides renewed attacks. "We made it clear that should Iran attack Israel, we would respond with great force." Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement.
Photos and video of the 22 October meeting show a group of bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.
Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity".
Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the administration's immigration policies. But Trump has typically enjoyed the support of Catholic voters.
In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons".
"In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said.
"I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added.
A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media.
Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump.
Grob said images of the meeting later caused concern among some of his congregants.
"I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he wrote.
"I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family have been harmed by the president's policies," he added.
Grob said none of the participants in the meeting gave permission for the public distribution or posting of video or photos of the event.
When contacted for comment by the BBC, the White House did not directly address questions regarding the meeting or subsequent comments by the two bishops.
"There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it," White House Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
According to Pew Research Center, which analyses religion in the US, opinions of Trump's performance have slipped among all major religious groups. In a survey this month, 30% of all US Catholics said they approved of his job performance, compared to 47% when he returned to the White House in 2025.
That could have an effect on the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. More Catholics in the survey, 42%, said they preferred the Democrats running in their local House of Representatives races, where slightly less, 39% favoured Republicans.
During his second term, Trump has had a tense relationship with the head of the Catholic church, Pope Leo, as he has moved aggressively to remove people believed to be in the US illegally.
Nine days before the Oval Office meeting with the bishops took place, Bishop Brendon Cahill and Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelicals, issued a statement urging "Christian compassion and wisdom in the immigration debate".
They said the immigration clampdown has led to the "sowing of fear, the fracturing of families, the deprivation of due process, and the vilification of our neighbors."
The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also recently condemned the Trump administration's plans to livestream a military execution, which were later scrapped.
Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are Catholics who have visited the Vatican during Trump's second term.
A Midwestern member of the bishops' conference, Robert Barron of Minnesota, agreed to serve on the president's Religious Liberty Commission last year, as did former New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan.

Police have arrested a teenager in connection with a shooting on Saturday that injured 12 people in Florida.
The incident took place at 20:00 local time (01:00 Sunday GMT), close to an American football stadium in the city of Tallahassee where a university game had recently been played.
Eleven people were injured by gunfire, local police said, while another hurt their ankle while fleeing the scene. Six of the victims were children.
Anthony Rivers III, 15, has been charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent.
Police said the shooting followed an altercation between people who knew each other and that additional arrests were possible.
None of the victims appear to have been the intended targets, they said in a statement.
"What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families," Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said.
"We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy."
Police said on Sunday that six people were in hospital, including one person who was in a critical condition. Five people had been released.
Revell told a press conference on Sunday that police had had to carry victims in their arms to get them to emergency responders because of the crowds from the football game.

A WhatsApp channel created to support Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva's re-election campaign is being credited by allies with helping deliver one of the most unlikely comebacks in recent Brazilian politics.
Brazil's left-wing president had been trailing right-wing challenger FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, but managed to turn the race around in just three weeks.
The rise of 'Lula's Army'
At a moment when many doubted Lula could reverse the result, a WhatsApp channel called Lula's Army emerged, and rapidly grew to 10.8 million followers.
Led by Congressman AndrÃ© Janones, the operation encouraged supporters to share videos, promote hashtags and recruit new voters.
Its dramatic growth between the two rounds was particularly notable because it appeared to reverse a long-standing imbalance in Brazilian politics.
For years, conservatives aligned with former President Jair Bolsonaro had been widely seen as dominating online political mobilisation, especially on platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram.
The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.
Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.
Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off".
"Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.
On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.
The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.
In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".
Social media's role in the comeback
Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult.
While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.
Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback.
Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.
According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights.
"It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."
By contrast, Holzhacker argues that FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.
Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media.
"It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."
In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement.
"Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.
She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration.
"I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."
Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.
In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed.
"We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

In the six years that she and her husband have been renting their home, Reeder said their rent had increased by hundreds of dollars. "Something's gotta give," she said. "It's like a dam — the pressure's too much, and it's going to break." Sandra Capell, 69, said she wants "to see some change" when it comes to the economy even though she voted Republican in Easley, which is part of South Carolina's conservative Upstate region. "I think everybody is kind of suffering when it comes to groceries, gas, everything really," she said. "I'm looking at the Republican Party to jump on the wagon, get in the saddle and let's bring it back." Beti Rosales, 47, said higher prices have taken a toll on her family's Mexican restaurant in Allentown, Pennsylvania, part of the Lehigh Valley that has seesawed between the parties in recent years. Limes and avocados cost more than before. So does the plumber who's occasionally needed. Two years ago, Rosales decided to give Trump and Republicans a chance, hoping for relief from inflation. "The reality now is that it actually didn't get better," she said. "It actually got worse. The prices of everything have increased." Rosales is now considering voting Democratic in the midterms. "Maybe fresh new faces might make a difference?" she said. Trump promised he'd bring prices down While running in 2024, Trump hammered President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris, his Democratic opponent in the election, for high inflation, which climbed as high as 9.1% in June 2022. He promised voters he would lower gasoline prices and unlock roaring growth. "With your vote in this election, I will end inflation," he vowed. In less than two years, Trump has aggressively remodeled the U.S. economy. He's slapped double-digit tariffs on many trading partners — including the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico — and sparked trade wars with allies. The U.S. government now holds stakes in several dozen private companies. He's signed broad income tax cuts into law. But the persistent challenge of inflation has continued, overshadowing the positives of continued economic growth and a low unemployment rate. Inflation was 3% when Trump took office and reached 3.7% last month. Part of Antarctica has been named after former BBC science correspondent Jonathan Amos.
A stretch of water between Rothschild Island and Alexander Island in the west of the White Continent is now called the Amos Channel.
Amos was given the honour for his "exceptional and influential role in bringing Antarctic research to the forefront of public understanding" during his 38-year career at BBC News, the naming committee said.
The channel is a new feature in Antarctica that appeared when a chunk of ice that connected Rothschild and Alexander Islands disintegrated.
The melting ice sheets of this remote continent are just one of many aspects of polar science that Amos reported on while at the BBC. He also covered colossal icebergs, the fate of penguin colonies and a BBC exclusive about the discovery of Ernest Shackleton's lost ship, the Endurance.
"It's absolutely incredible - what an extraordinary accolade. I'm so touched that there's a little bit of Antarctica named after me," Amos said.
Despite his fascination with the South Pole, he has not yet travelled to the continent.
"I've written about it so often, but always from my desk - this is quite the incentive to go and visit.
"Antarctica is the front line of the biggest news story on planet Earth - climate change," he added.
The naming of geographical features in Antarctica follows strict rules.
The Amos Channel was recommended by the UK Antarctic Place Names Committee, which looks after names for sites within the British Antarctic Territory, as well as South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.
Athena Dinar, from the British Antarctic Survey, said: "Jon's passion for Antarctica and engaging journalism offers something for every reader, viewer or listener.
"The naming of an Antarctic place in his honour is a fitting recognition of his outstanding contribution to the promotion of Antarctic research."
Amos joined the BBC in 1986 as a local radio reporter in Cambridge. He was part of the team that launched the BBC News website in 1997, and ran the online science desk for many years. He later worked as a BBC science correspondent across TV, radio and online, before leaving the organisation in 2024.
"Jon consistently highlighted the importance of Antarctic research, explaining not only what science is being done there, but why it matters for society, climate understanding and the global environment," said Fiona Fox, from the Science Media Centre.

Amazonâs Project Kuiper picked South Africa for its first African satellite launch, Microsoft is expanding its AI infrastructure, while Cisco is deepening its presence, too. National groups such as Indivisible and MoveOn are activating their own expansive networks. There are so many organizations working to protect the voting process — including many that cannot legally coordinate with each other — that some officials involved worry about unintentionally creating chaos outside polling locations. A US Marine has been indicted on suspicion of murdering and robbing a woman in Japan earlier this month in a case that has triggered protests, Japanese media reports.
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested on suspicion of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa.
Prosecutors have now indicted him for allegedly strangling Yagi with a telephone cord and then stealing her backpack and wallet on 3 October, media reports, citing the indictment document.
It wasreported Ballard had denied the allegations, but Asahi Shimbun and Kyodo News cited investigators saying he has made some statements suggesting involvement.
Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings.
Yagi's death has caused outrage in Japan, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi describing the crime as "brutal and heinous".
Earlier this month, the Marine Corps said it was "actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine" and extended condolences to the victim's family.
It is the latest case involving a US serviceman in Okinawa, which hosts the highest concentration of around 55,000 US soldiers stationed in Japan.
Previous criminal cases have sparked anger and protests, the largest of which took place in 1995, when tens of thousands took to the streets following the abduction, beating and rape of a 12-year-old girl.
In 2024 alone, there were four sexual assault cases involving US troops in Okinawa, including that of air force member Brennon Washington, who was given five years for the rape and kidnapping of an underage girl.
In 2025, US marine Lance Cpl Jamel Clayton was sentenced to seven years in prison for sexually assaulting a woman.
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline.
The prime minister said her government has registered a "strong" protest with the US and called for "strict disciplinary action against US military personnel and thorough measures to prevent a recurrence of such incidents".
People in Japan have been voicing anger, with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo earlier this month. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice, with one user saying: "Enough is enough."
