Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge ex-Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director James Comey with leaking national defence information, according to a court filing.
It marks the third time the justice department has moved to bring criminal charges against Comey, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump.
Few details are provided about the two counts in the three-page filing, but Comey's lawyers said in separate court papers that the case stemmed from an alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016, while he was head of the FBI.
Comey denied any wrongdoing in a video posted on Substack on Monday, calling the charges an "appalling abuse".
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the department of justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said in the clip.
"Nothing's changed with me - I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe the independent federal judiciary."
His lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that two different teams of prosecutors had investigated the alleged disclosure to the New York Times a decade ago during the first Trump administration.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.
The attorney said the court filing "purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit".
Comey was charged in Washington DC through a criminal information, which is a formal written charging document filed directly by a prosecutor.
This is different to a criminal indictment, which must be approved by a grand jury, a group of citizens sworn in to review if evidence is strong enough to prosecute.
Comey was fired by Trump during his first term, after the former FBI director opened an investigation into claims of Russian meddling in the US 2016 presidential election.
Since then, Trump has repeatedly called for his prosecution, and these charges are the administration's third attempt to do so.
Comey was first indicted by a federal grand jury in September 2025 on charges that he had lied to Congress during testimony and obstructed a congressional proceeding.
He pleaded not guilty the following month before the case was dismissed in November.
In April 2026, Comey surrendered to authorities to face charges alleging that an image he briefly shared on social media posed a threat to Trump's life.
The case stemmed from a 2025 Instagram post by Comey, which contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".
"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump, the 47th president.
Comey denies any wrongdoing, saying he did not know what the numbers meant, and accusing the prosecution of political motivation. That case is ongoing.

d5b7e39b8515.text: Former FBI director James Comey is facing new federal charges, according to a charging document made public on Monday. Why it matters: The charges mark the third time the Trump administration has charged Comey. He has been a subject of the president's ire since his dismissal from the first Trump administration in 2017. Driving the news: Prosecutors allege Comey directed the disclosure of national defense information to a reporter through one or more co-conspirators in October 2016, while he was serving as FBI director . He is charged with participating in the transmission of national defense information and conspiracy to transmit national defense information. The case has been ongoing under seal since early October. What they're saying: A DOJ spokesperson told Axios that the case is an "ongoing criminal investigation" and declined to comment further. The other side: Comey's attorney Patrick Fitzgerald said in a statement posted to Comey's Instagram account that the former FBI director "steadfastly maintains his innocence" and will fight the latest charges. Fitzgerald said the case concerns an Oct. 5, 2016, New York Times article that two separate teams of prosecutors investigated during Trump's first administration. Both teams decided not to bring charges, he said. He also welcomed U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden's decision to unseal the case. Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: Trump fired Comey in 2017 amid the FBI's investigation into alleged Russian interference in the 2016 election. His dismissal led to the appointment of Robert Mueller as special counsel, tasked with uncovering any links to Russian interference in the election. Mueller's investigation report — released in 2019 — documented extensive Russian interference in the 2016 election but did not establish a criminal conspiracy between Trump's campaign and Russia. Zoom out: The charges were made public the same day as a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration unlawfully fired Comey's daughter, Maurene Comey, a former federal prosecutor who worked on cases involving Sean "Diddy" Combs and Jeffrey Epstein . Go deeper: What to know about James Comey and his history with President Trump Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

Two new weather warnings have been issued as a third storm in a matter of days is set to batter Scotland.
It comes as thousands of homes across the country remain without power in the aftermath of Storm Boelo.
A yellow warning for wind, external covering the south-west of Scotland came into effect at 18:00 and runs until 03:00 on Tuesday.
A separate yellow wind warning, covering most of the country as well as parts of northern England and Northern Ireland, runs from 03:00 to 21:00 on Tuesday.
The Met Office said gusts of up to 65mph (105km/h) would hit coastal communities in the south-west on Monday evening and into the morning.
Forecasters added strong winds would be accompanied by heavy rain at certain points.
The latest weather system is unlikely to be as widely disruptive as Storm Boelo - or Storm Austen which came before it - and has so far not been named.
The next name on the storm list for the 2026/2027 season is Chloe.
Storm Boelo brought heavy flooding and wind gusts in some areas of up to 85mph (137km/h) on Monday.
A 60-year-old man died after being struck by a falling tree at Mid Kelton, near Castle Douglas, in Dumfries and Galloway on Sunday.
On Monday evening, Scottish and Southern Energy Networks (SSEN), which covers the north of Scotland, said work was ongoing to reconnect the supplies of about 15,000 homes that remained without power.
Meanwhile, Scottish Power Energy Networks (Spen) said all but a "very small number" of its 50,000 customers who lost power in Ayrshire and Dumfries and Galloway would have it restored by 02:00 on Tuesday.
Almost 100,000 homes had power restored in both areas across the weekend.
Rail and ferry disruption
ScotRail , externalsaid the "vast majority" of its services were running as normal.
However, it warned that speed restrictions would be in place on several routes until 16:00 on Tuesday due to heavy rainfall. They are:
- Glasgow Queen Street â Oban/Mallaig
- Inverness â Kyle of Lochalsh
- Glasgow Queen Street/Edinburgh Waverley â Inverness
- Aberdeen â Inverness
- Glasgow Central â Largs
- Glasgow Queen Street â Helensburgh Central
- Ayr â Stranraer
- Inverness â Wick/Thurso
West coast ferry operator CalMac, external said many its services remained liable to disruption or cancellation at short notice and urged travellers to check its website for updates.
Passengers on NorthLink Ferries, external were advised that there was the "possibility of disruption" to services until Thursday because of the weather.
School closures
All schools and nurseries in the Western Isles will be shut until Wednesday at the earliest.
Ellon Academy will remain closed on Tuesday after being shut on Monday as a result of damage caused by the storm.
It comes after more than a dozen primary schools in Aberdeenshire and Rothiemay Primary School, in Moray, were closed on Monday due to a lack of power.
Twelve primary schools and nine nurseries across the Highlands were also subject to full or partial closures, external.
The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa) said it had put an amber risk of flooding in place for the northern and Western Isles and Caithness and Sutherland.
Sepa said areas of the southwest and Argyll, including the Solway Firth and Firth of Clyde, would experience volatile conditions, with large waves and strong winds.
They said flooding of low-lying land was likely.
Highland Council said flood gates on the mile-long Caol and Lochyside flood protection scheme, near Fort William, had been closed following a warning from Sepa.
Police Scotland said a high risk of disruption remained with poor weather conditions expected on Tuesday.
Police Scotland Assistant Chief Constable Mark Sutherland said that, although the amber weather warning was no longer in place, disruption was "likely well beyond that due to further poor weather, fallen trees and other damage caused by the storm".
Social Justice and Housing Secretary Shirley-Anne Somerville told BBC Scotland News there were "challenges ahead" due to the prolonged nature of the conditions.
She urged councils to review their readiness, adding authorities were working to ensure that "everything that can be done is being done".
Somerville also said that everyone can play a part by getting "households as resilient as we can, as well as looking after neighbours and friends".

3eece4db405b.text: There has never been a company like Anthropic. It owes almost $650 billion for computing, generates eye-popping revenue per employee and wants every investor to know that its product poses existential risks to humanity. Why it matters : The future of the AI race, the market and the global economy rest within Anthropic's IPO prospectus, where some of Silicon Valley's most seasoned investors found new reasons to be bullish. They also found warning signs. A wager on Anthropic is a bet not just that AI will deliver on its enormous promise, but that customers will keep spending at a rate that keeps pace with massive computing costs. It's also a bet that Anthropic can continue to deliver models good enough to justify premium prices, even as competition intensifies and cheaper alternatives improve. What they're saying : Reaching a valuation of $2 trillion would require 50% growth, according to Theory Ventures. "What is Anthropic worth?" Theory's Tomasz Tunguz asked rhetorically. "The case for a very large number is simple," he said, noting that the company grew quickly on a high margin and generated an operating profit. "The case against is equally simple," he added, noting its $637 billion of computing commitments, non-cancellable contracts and no guarantee of customer loyalty. Catch up quick: Monday's filing offered the most detailed public look yet at Anthropic's business , finances and risks as it prepares for a potentially record-setting IPO. (See what Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT say about whether they'd invest). As Tunguz noted, the filing had fodder for a variety of perspectives. The good : Anthropic has nearly 2,000 customers with $1 million or more of revenue, and 250 with $10 million or more. Half the Fortune 500 pays the company $100,000 a year, and those customers spent less than 0.1% of their total expenses in the third quarter on Anthropic. "We are so early," Ben Bajarin, a longtime tech analyst, said on X. He pointed out that there are 300 million global businesses outside of China that spend almost $1.5 trillion on enterprise software annually. The company had more $130 billion in cash and short-term investments on hand as of June 30, about $10 billion less than the total it's raised, pointing to substantial financial discipline, some investors said. As noted, Anthropic had revenue per employee of $6.6 million as of the end of the third quarter, only slightly lower than Nvidia, which is typically seen as one of the most efficient operators in tech. Data: S&P Capital IQ Pro; Note: Calculated as trailing 12-month revenue divided by most recently reported annual headcount The bad (or maybe bad) : Anthropic's five largest customers accounted for approximately 25% of revenue during the first nine months of 2026. Many Anthropic customers pay by usage and don't make multi-year commitments. But the company's computing obligations extend for years and include minimum payments regardless of how much capacity it actually uses. Nearly 50% of Anthropic's first-half revenue came through cloud marketplaces operated by Amazon, Google and Microsoft — companies that are also investors, computing suppliers and competitors. That makes hyperscalers huge winners, since they collect revenue in multiple ways, once by providing compute and also as platform fee. The company said 5% to 7% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026 was from customers using Anthropic models in violation of its policies or against its terms of service. Some outside experts believe much of this is from distillation, the practice of querying a model an immense number of times for training purposes. The surprising/intruiging : Anthropic's deal with Elon Musk is expanding. According to Anthropic's paperwork, the company's payments to SpaceX are now seen reaching $3.1 billion a month and up to $120.5 billion on computing through 2029, up from $1.25 billion a month at the time of SpaceX's IPO filing. (Yes, but: Either side can cancel that deal with 90 days notice.) Anthropic has a ton of cash on its books. Its filing lists more than $134 billion in cash and similar securities. That represents nearly all the money the company has raised, leaving some to wonder if the company has been paying a lot of its bills with convertible notes. Others noted just how few of Anthropic's costs seem to be reflected in its so-called "cost of goods sold," which directly affects reported profit margins. CEO Dario Amodei received nearly $18 million in total compensation in 2025, while Anthropic disclosed millions in spending on personal security for its two top executives. And speaking of Amodei and his co-founders, the filing details an unusual succession plan in which they can nominate successors for their voting power, subject to approval from the other co-founders. The bottom line: Anthropic has demonstrated that demand for powerful AI can grow at a staggering rate. Its IPO will test whether investors believe that demand can remain strong enough, long enough, to pay for the enormous infrastructure being built to serve it.

On Monday, President Trump campaigned in ruby-red Mississippi, a state he won by almost 23 points two years ago. Over the weekend, the battleground state of Michigan saw a political heavyweight bout between Trump and former President Obama. Liz Landers reports. Amna Nawaz: It is crunch time for candidates across the country, as tomorrow marks exactly one week from Election Day. President Trump is spending today campaigning in ruby-red Mississippi, a state he won by almost 23 points two years ago. And it was the battleground state of Michigan that saw a political heavyweight bout this weekend between Mr. Trump and former President Barack Obama. Liz Landers reports. Liz Landers: Stumping in swing states this weekend, President Trump laid out what's at stake in the looming midterm elections now just eight days away. In the tight Michigan race that will help decide control of the Senate between former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, the president attacked El-Sayed's faith and said he would be a threat to national security. President Donald Trump: I'm here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator. And that's the fact. We're not going to let that happen. The people of Michigan are going to defeat Abdul Mohamed Sayed. Abdul El-Sayed (D): I don't care how he pronounces my name. I don't even care that he remembers my whole name, because he can just go on and call me senator after November. (CHEERING) Liz Landers: El-Sayed, who would be the nation's first Muslim Senator, said Trump's attacks were a distraction from voters' concerns about the economy. In a contentious interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," El-Sayed's opponent, Mike Rogers, dug in on his allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, even though there is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the group. Kristen Welker, Moderator: Is that up to your standard, calling... Mike Rogers (R): No, I don't. I have never called him a terrorist. I have never called him a terrorist. This election is about me versus Abdul. I mean, he's a Democrat Socialists of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don't like America. Liz Landers: Former President Barack Obama brought his own firepower to the trail, rallying Democratic voters in two Midwestern battlegrounds on Saturday, telling crowds in Michigan and Ohio that Trump was responsible for rising costs because of the war with Iran. Barack Obama: The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions. (CHEERING) Barack Obama: Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody has for -- nobody voted for. President Donald Trump: Washington, D.C., is looking so beautiful. Barack Obama: What's up with the gold? Everything more gold. He's got the white ass looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. I'm here for the future of this country, because I know we're at a crossroads. Sharday Barnwell, Ohio Resident: Education, health care, just general access and affordability. Life is just hard for everybody right now. Liz Landers: On that issue most important to Americans, the economy, President Trump had this to say while in Georgia: President Donald Trump: President Trump is talking about all the money they're making while people are suffering at the pump. That will be the headline. But I said, I don't give a damn. I'm going to say it. We're making a freaking fortune. Our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time. (CHEERING) Liz Landers: Vice President Vance had this to stay in Belgrade, Montana, today: Vice President J.D. Vance: As proud as I am of the last 18 months, we have done a lot, but there is still so much more that we can do together. Liz Landers: Mr. Trump cast his own ballot on Saturday in Florida, joining nearly 30 million Americans who have already voted early. The president has in the past called early voting ridiculous, one of his many lines of attack on elections in America. Meantime, the attorney general defended the Trump administration's preemptive lawsuit against Alaska state election officials, where the DOJ sued late last week to block the certification of the election if the Democrat wins. Blanche said there could be confusion over the incumbent Republican senator facing off against another candidate with almost the exact same name. Todd Blanche, U.S. Attorney General: If there is litigation -- there may not be, but if there is litigation brought by others after the election because of possible voter confusion, that the ballots are kept in a way that the Alaska state -- that the Alaska state election system can determine who the accurate winner is. Liz Landers: It's a move that the president says he directed. The Justice Department also defended another challenge to how states administer their elections in a legal battle playing out in California after the federal government asked state officials there to review and set aside more than 20,000 ballots that they believe were sent to noncitizens. In a rare Sunday argument session, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals appeared skeptical of the Justice Department's demand, questioning the timing and authority of the federal government's actions. b218f210f167.text: Israelis will go to the polls on Tuesday in what many describe as the most consequential election in years. It’s the first vote since the Oct. 7 Hamas attack and Israel’s war in Gaza. Prime Minister Netanyahu has been campaigning that he’ll keep Israel safe. But the opposition says Netanyahu failed to prevent the 2003 attack and is blocking an investigation into it. Nick Schifrin reports. Amna Nawaz: Israelis will go to the polls tomorrow in what many describe as the most consequential election in years. It's the first vote since the Hamas attack on Israel on 2023 and Israel's war in Gaza in response. Prime Minister Benajmin Netanyahu has been making the case that he will keep Israel safe. But the main opposition says Netanyahu failed to prevent the October 7 attack and is blocking an investigation into how warning signs were missed. Nick Schifrin reports from Tel Aviv. Nick Schifrin: In Tel Aviv this weekend, a clarion called for change. Gadi Eisenkot is the former Israeli military chief, son of Moroccan immigrants, and today leader of a coalition trying to unseat Prime Minister Benajmin Netanyahu. Gadi Eisenkot, Israeli Prime Minister Candidate (through interpreter): Israel and the Israelis will be able to start a new era, an era of growth, of real security, of taking action, an era without lies and manipulations. Lianne Pollak-David, Israeli Parliamentary Candidate: Gadi Eisenkot is the complete opposite of Benajmin Netanyahu. Gadi Eisenkot is a trustworthy, honest, pragmatic, and a leader that basically has the national interest at heart. Nick Schifrin: Lianne Pollak-David is a parliamentary candidate in Eisenkot's party, Yashar, Hebrew for Straightforward, a reference to both direction and integrity, that Netanyahu faces charges of corruption. Lianne Pollak-David: Benajmin Netanyahu speaks the most amazing English and how knows how to market himself, but basically has lost complete trust of not just the global arena, but also the U.S. general public. Nick Schifrin: This is the first vote since the deadliest day in Israel's history, the October 7 terrorist attacks, when 1,200 Israelis were murdered. It's also Israel's worst ever intelligence failure, for which Netanyahu has not been held accountable. Eisenkot vows, as his first action as prime minister, to launch an independent inquiry that he says Netanyahu has blocked. Devora Sharifian Bachar, Israeli Parliamentary Candidate: It's only because of him. It's only because of the Israeli prime minister, Benajmin Netanyahu, that we didn't investigate. Nick Schifrin: Devora Sharifian Bachar is a former Israeli intelligence official and a Yashar candidate for Parliament. Devora Sharifian Bachar: He wants to investigate himself. Please, we are not clowns, and we need to understand what to do better, where we go wrong, and we will do so. Nick Schifrin: After October the 7th, Eisenkot joined Netanyahu's War Cabinet, but resigned and accused Netanyahu of prioritizing politics over security. Now Eisenkot argues he can finish the wars that Netanyahu can't against Hamas in Gaza, against Hezbollah in Southern Lebanon, where Israel maintains an occupation for the first time in more than 25 years, and the war in Iran that has severely reduced Iran's traditional military, but installed an even harder-line regime. Devora Sharifian Bachar: In 20 years, I worked in the Israeli intelligence. If we see Iran still standing, they are rehabilitating their forces. They're starting to build again those crazy missiles that they throw on us. Nick Schifrin: And an Eisenkot government vows to crack down on extremist Israeli settlers in the West Bank who've recently attacked journalists and diplomats, as well as Palestinians as they harvest olives. Lianne Pollak-David: Extremist violent groups going out there every single night attacking honest and innocent, basically, civilians on the Palestinian side, but not only that, also diplomats and journalists, this is completely unacceptable. It does not reflect the Israeli people. And this government has done nothing to stop it, but also has even fueled that activity. Nick Schifrin: It is Palestinian violence in the West Bank that Netanyahu highlights, including a Friday attack that killed two Israeli soldiers. Netanyahu vowed a crackdown as part of his argument he alone can provide security. And Israeli bulldozers pulled down buildings where the attackers lived. On the campaign trail, Netanyahu's painted the opposition as dangerous because of a possible alliance with Arab parties. And Netanyahu has trumpeted his endorsement by President Trump and argued Eisenkot wouldn't maintain their relationship or be able to launch a joint U.S.-Israel attack on Iran. Netanyahu even reposted an AI image of an Iranian nuclear weapon exploding over Tel Aviv. Benajmin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister: Donald, we have a job to finish. You said it, and we will finish it together. Ophir Falk, Foreign Policy Adviser to Prime Minister Netanyahu: Israel and the American-Israeli alliance is stronger than ever. And Iran and the Iranian proxies are weaker than ever. Nick Schifrin: Ophir Falk is Netanyahu's foreign policy adviser. Ophir Falk: The prime minister, again, he promised on day two of the war that he will change the Middle East. And he has changed the Middle East. Has he completed, finished the job 100 percent? Not yet. He's done about 90 percent. He still needs to do 10 percent. He wants to finish the job. Nick Schifrin: Does that mean that Israel and the United States goes back to war after the U.S. midterm elections? Ophir Falk: Well, I can't comment on when the war will restart or if it will restart. There's great economic pressure on the Iranian regime. It might fall that way. But, as you said, President Trump, the leader of the free world, the leader of the United States, our number one ally, Israel's indispensable ally, sees us as a model ally and wants Netanyahu to win. This is not a political statement. It's a policy statemen

107d4d72e2b3.text: In a closely watched election, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated right-wing and Trump-aligned challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. Transport and weather disruptions in parts of Brazil led to a chaotic final stretch at the polls. Bolsonaro is refusing to concede, and President Trump called the outcome "rigged." Stephanie Sy reports. Amna Nawaz: In a closely watched election, Brazil's president, known as Lula, defeated right-wing and Trump-aligned challenger Flavio Bolsonaro last night by nearly 4.5 million votes. Transportation and weather disruptions in parts of Brazil led to a chaotic final stretch at the polls. Bolsonaro is now refusing to concede. And, today, President Trump said the outcome was -- quote -- "rigged." Stephanie Sy reports. Stephanie Sy: On the streets of Rio de Janeiro last night, rejoicing and cheers of relief rang out among Lula supporters. Brazilian voters narrowly reelected the leftist president, Luiz Inacio da Silva, the 80-year-old Lula beating right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro 51 to 48 percent. Lula addressed supporters in Sao Paulo after the win. Luiz Inacio Lula Da Silva, Brazilian President (through interpreter): I want you to know that everything I do, I do with you in mind. All public policies are designed with you in mind. And you have given me the distinction of being the first president of the republic to be elected four times through democratic means. This is a historic achievement that I owe to the Brazilian people. Stephanie Sy: It's historic in more ways than one. Lula was the underdog after he lost the first round of voting earlier this month to Flavio, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted for attempting to stage a coup. Millions of Brazilians who did not vote in the first round came out Sunday, with voters in Rio de Janeiro and the suburbs of Sao Paulo swinging their support to Lula. Ana Candida Cotrim, Lula Supporter (through interpreter): The feeling is that democracy resisted in the midst of authoritarianism, in the midst of the whole world, of the great powers like the United States against Brazil. And we managed to resist with the strength of the people in the streets and on social media. Stephanie Sy: Lula's victory broke a recent right-wing winning streak in Latin America. Now Brazil and Mexico, Latin America's two most populous countries, have bucked the trend. Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum reacted jubilantly today. Claudia Sheinbaum, Mexican President (through interpreter): It shows that, when the people decide to mobilize and defend their rights, they always win. And that is a lesson for Brazil, for Mexico, and for the whole world. Stephanie Sy: Lula's win was a loss for President Trump's influence in the region. And echoing Trump and his father, Flavio Bolsonaro refused to admit defeat last night, saying he planned to request an annulment of the election. Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazilian Presidential Candidate (through interpreter): What happened today was not normal. It was downright unacceptable. A Supreme Court justice for the first time in history, a former lawyer for Lula, with a simple stroke of the pen, at the request of a former partner, changed the rules of the game in the middle of the match. Stephanie Sy: Stormy weather and transportation troubles had led both candidates to request an extension of voting by two hours. But in the end, the country's Supreme Court granted Lula's request shortly before polls were set to close. Supporters of Bolsonaro are crying foul. Jeremias Oliveira, Brasilia, Brazil Resident (through interpreter): Flavio Bolsonaro has already said he will file to annul this election. I hope he manages to, because it's not normal, people. This is wrong. Stephanie Sy: Despite attempts to inject doubt, the results are official. And even right-wing leaders in the region are congratulating Lula. Flavio Bolsonaro will remain in the Senate through the end of his term, however, and with Congress still dominated by Brazil's right-wing. Lula's win, while decisive, is far from a mandate. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Stephanie Sy.

69cda18d8ca1.text:
Environmentalists worldwide are celebrating the re-election of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as a win for the Amazon’s future and global climate policy.
The three-term incumbent narrowly defeated right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who climate activists warned would have stripped away environmental policies and institutions protecting the world’s largest rainforest if elected.
The victory gives Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, another four years to pursue his pledge to end deforestation by 2030 after the greatest slowdown in forest loss in years. Between August 2025 and March 2026, deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon fell by 36 percent from the previous year.
This comes as nearly one-fifth of the Amazon has already been deforested. Coupled with climate change, the forest is nearing an irreparable tipping point, scientists say, and tree loss could dry out the region and further accelerate climate change.
Carlos Nobre, a professor of climate and sustainability at the University of São Paulo, said preventing the irreversible transformation of vast areas of the Amazon is still possible, but time is running out.
“The reduction in deforestation over recent years has been crucial, but much more needs to be done,” Nobre said in a statement. “The next four years will be decisive for the future of the world’s largest tropical rainforest and for climate stability in Brazil and around the world.”
Despite these warnings, governments across the Amazon, including Lula’s administration, continue to expand oil drilling, mining and industrial agriculture. It’s impacted local communities and environmental defenders.
Lula’s re-election also preserves Brazil’s role in international climate diplomacy after hosting COP30 in Belém in 2025. The government has pledged to implement its Paris Agreement commitments and accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels.
In November 2025, Lula’s administration formally recognized 20 Indigenous territories covering more than 6 million acres, and gave the communities firmer legal grounds to protect the forests on their land from exploitation or seizure.
Climate activists have called for Lula to speed up the recognition of other Indigenous territories, pressure agriculture businesses to stop using illegally deforested land, better protect environmental defenders and cancel oil and road projects that threaten the progress his administration has made.
“The Lula administration has shown that progress is possible, but much more remains to be done,” said Brad Adams, executive director of Climate Rights International.
Lula’s victory doesn’t shield the country from other political challenges, said Maurício Voivodic, the executive director of World Wildlife Fund Brazil. Voters elected Bolsonaro’s far-right Liberal Party to the most seats in both chambers of National Congress.
The newly elected Congress poses a significant risk to the president’s environmental and social agenda, Voivodic said in a statement. An analysis by the Brazilian climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima found that nearly 70 percent of elected lawmakers have low or very low alignment with environmental protection policies.
“This increases the risk of rollbacks in environmental and social legislation, with consequences for forest protection and deforestation,” Voivodic said. “Continued vigilance and public mobilization will be essential to defending the progress achieved.”
Meanwhile, Sen. Bolsonaro is continuing the populist movement built by his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.
Academic researchers report that Jair Bolsonaro systematically dismantled environmental regulations to enable corporate exploitation of natural resources while targeting Indigenous and traditional peoples, non-governmental organizations, scientists and other environmental defenders across Brazil.
In 2019, the first year of Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency, Brazil’s deforestation numbers spiked to the highest levels since satellite data became available. With Lula’s re-election, Adams said, Brazil’s forests and the people defending them have dodged a bullet.
“Flávio Bolsonaro could have brought back his father’s disastrous policies, which devastated forests and put communities and defenders in danger,” Adams said in a statement. “But the forests and their defenders are still at risk, and Lula should now double down on efforts to protect them.”

In Serbia, longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic lost a historic election that brought down his government. William Brangham discussed the results with Heather Conley. Amna Nawaz: Well, and Brazil isn't the only country with dramatic election results this weekend. In Serbia, longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic was defeated after an historic election on Sunday brought down his government. William Brangham joins us now with more. William Brangham: For more on the results from Serbia and how this result is echoing around the world, we turn again to Heather Conley. She served as deputy assistant secretary of state for European affairs during the George W. Bush administration. She's now a nonresident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and works with an international consulting company. Heather, great to have you back. Help us understand something. Your reaction to this? Because some viewers might think, Serbia is not that big of a nation, under seven million people. They're not in the E.U. They're not in NATO. So how important is this result? Heather Conley, American Enterprise Institute: Well, it's extraordinary because of how it came about and the focus of the concern of the protesters. First and foremost, this was led by students. It's a young persons' -- it's a movement that doesn't have a leader. It's decentralized. It's digitally savvy, and it brought down literally a strongman of Serbia who had all control over the powers, economic, political powers. And the focus of the protest was on corruption, government corruption, and we're seeing that issue become a real global issue. And certainly young people are taking to the streets and really, strongly seeking another solution from government. So I have to say, as a watcher of the Western Balkans, it was like I was watching October 2000, when the people poured out in the streets in Serbia to oust Milosevic. President Vucic was a member of Milosevic's Cabinet, and this was truly people power. And it sort of comes along -- we remember the Hungarian election not too long ago that brought in a new leader who also was fighting corruption. This is also a strike against Russia and China, two countries that were strongly influencing Serbia. And so it's certainly a win for the people of Serbia, but we will see how they govern from here. Big question marks to come. William Brangham: Right, because as you were saying, this wasn't Vucic against another candidate. This was a parliamentary election, and Vucic basically saw that his party was getting drubbed in the polls and conceded this race peacefully. Did that surprise you how quickly he came forward and said, we have clearly lost, time to move on? Heather Conley: Yes, I mean, we always think of the strongman with incredible control over economic powers, that they're not going to go quietly into the night. There was an hour where the Serbian government, the electoral commission, didn't release the results. I think they paused, saw how dramatically large it was, and said, look, we can't fight this now. But if the student-led movement is disorganized, if they cannot form a government, we have all the levers there. We will try to sort of fight this out another day. But I was surprised, and good for them for acknowledging this was a historic win. William Brangham: Did the tenacity of this student movement impress you? I mean, we have seen a lot of protests that have been bubbling up, often youth-driven. But this one lasted quite a while, and as you were saying, seems quite effective. Like, I -- when you look at this, the broad scope of what's happening in Europe, does this feel spiritually, philosophically connected to all these other protests that we're seeing? Heather Conley: Yes, I like to think we're starting to see some dots connected, particularly with youth movement. As you said, this started two years ago when a rail station in Novi Sad, Serbia, it was recently renovated and it collapsed, killing 16 people. It was clearly an example of, again, government corruption that didn't use the right building materials. There was no accountability. So these student protesters began to galvanize around, we want credit -- we want the government to be transparent. We want someone to be held accountable for this. Over time, though, it grew, and it grew about demanding greater things from government, greater accountability, and it and it grew across Belgrade. So there's something that they fought for two years and look at what they achieved. But we're seeing this historically elsewhere. In Albania very recently, students are now growing against a -- what they believe to be a corrupt investment in Albania that has links to President Trump's family. We see... William Brangham: This is the Kushner and his wife's investment in a luxury resort. Heather Conley: Exactly, in Albania. We're seeing that huge pressure on the government, whereas some we have seen in France in these -- in these protests. Now, some of them have become violent, but we're seeing where young people, just high schoolers, were saying, I cannot accept anymore. The fact that I don't have a teacher in my classroom, my classroom isn't working, I want something better. I demand the government take action. And now others are joining in that, unions, as well as the Yellow Vest movement. And even in the Brazil example that you just showed, what appears to be the difference between the first and the second round and the surprising victory by President Lula was a real empowerment, Lula's army of young people, that really were galvanized. So we're seeing young people taking part. Turnout is historically high. But the thing is, they're demanding something different from government, not the same old story. a50d5a4a5096.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-charges-former-fbi-director-james-comey-for-the-third-time Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration charges former FBI Director James Comey for the third time Politics Updated on Oct 26, 2026 6:47 PM EDT — Published on Oct 26, 2026 6:01 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director's lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment. The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents a clear escalation in the administration's targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year. The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week's midterm elections. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Well, they're back — again," Comey said in a video statement released after the documents dropped. "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me; I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary." The Justice Department, for its part, said it had filed what's known as a "criminal information" to extend the 10-year statute of limitations for bringing a case. "Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," a department spokesperson said. A criminal information is typically filed with a defendant's consent accompanying a plea deal, but Comey's lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid and barred by the statute of limitations. "For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence," his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement. The allegation was previously investigated The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing. Federal authorities, including then-Special Counsel John Durham, began investigating the FBI's Oct. 5, 2016, disclosure to The New York Times in early 2017. Durham wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey's attorneys said in a recent court filing. In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney's office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name "Tropical Vortex." But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020. "Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an "Information" against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit," Fitzgerald said. Trump and Comey have a long and uneasy history The first case against Comey was dismissed after the judge found that the prosecutor who brought the indictment was illegally appointed. Comey was charged in a separate case in April over a social media post depicting seashells on the beach that officials said constituted a threat against the president. Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush's Republican administration. But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum. Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump's campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration. At last, Army seeing progress in Pacific network
Recent exercises suggest the service and its foreign partners are moving closer to a single-screen data system.
WASHINGTON—After years of frustration, Army leaders are starting to see progress on upgraded networks designed to make it easier to communicate with allies and partners in a Pacific conflict.
“When I arrived at [U.S. Army Pacific Command], we had an exercise in Japan—and I'd only been in command a month. It was a trilateral exercise between the U.S., Japan, and Australia. And we literally couldn't pass voice data to each other. We couldn't create a common operating picture without physically putting icons into this system,” Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific, told reporters earlier this month.
“It was so frustrating to me because I just left working in the Pentagon where I had literally attended both the signing ceremonies for AUKUS…sharing our most sensitive defense technology. But we are using basically a swivel chair to have a conversation with regard to land forces.”
In recent years, the Army has been building and testing the telecommunications pipelines that allies and partner militaries would rely on in a war with China. U.S. Indo-Pacific Command has a broader Pacific Mission Network, previously known as the INDOPACOM Mission Network, which is used on a more strategic or operational level.
Earlier this year, the U.S., Australia, and Japan used the Pacific Mission Network during the large Balikatan exercise to get a “real-time picture of participating forces across the entire training area,” an Army spokesperson told Defense One.
Months later, the nations reconvened for Yama Sakura 91, an annual military exercise with Japan and Australia that ended Sept. 10.
“Yama Sakura 91 demonstrated the live sharing of simulated information in a command post exercise, while Balikatan 26 demonstrated the live sharing of real-time information across a physical training environment and multiple echelons,” the Army said.
That network, which connects dozens of nations, was the linchpin for USARPAC to test whether it could share and see the same information as allies and partners.
“The [mission partner] enclaves work, so we're able to pass and share data in a way that we had not been before,” Clark said, at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference, calling the network an “important and critical innovation” that addressed years of frustrations.
That means commanders can more easily send “target-quality data” and share a “common operational picture” without needing to swivel between workstations.
For example, Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington, who leads the Army’s Multi-Domain Command-Pacific and 7th Infantry Division, can gather information on “land-based long-range precision fires, sensors, space capability, [electronic warfare], cyber” and then share it with Pacific Fleet Commander Adm. Stephen Koehler, who led the exercise, and “can then integrate that [data] into a joint context in the fight,” Clark said.
The progress on the Pacific Mission Network comes as the Army looks to add more tech and sources of data—mostly drones—to its forces. That means being able to see, control, and learn from devices and the information they collect will become increasingly important on the battlefield.
Seventh ID recently finished an exercise called Bayonet Quest near Lake Huron, Mich., in which it was able to coordinate high-altitude balloons, and aerial and maritime drones, using a shared data connection, Harrington told reporters.
“We used multiple [unmanned aerial systems], multiple [unmanned surface vessels], long-range, one-way attack, and a high-altitude balloon,” he said. The division also collected and analyzed data from all of those systems using a single data layer.
During the exercise, which ended Oct. 6, the Army was also able to orchestrate the drones and coordinate simulated attacks with an “adaptive and agentic” command-and-control system.
“We were able to pull in a vast amount of data, make sense of it quickly, and then task those systems through a large language model, reducing the need for soldiers on individual ground control stations,” Harrington said in a statement to Defense One.
The exercise showed how unmanned systems could be used in the Pacific, particularly from different locations, which could help keep soldiers safe, he said.
The exercise wrapped earlier this month, but the division plans to keep training with the concept and employ it in future exercises with allies and partners.

755ac944b408.text: By — Sam Mednick, Associated Press Sam Mednick, Associated Press By — Natalie Melzer, Associated Press Natalie Melzer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/tens-of-thousands-of-israelis-living-abroad-are-expected-to-fly-in-for-pivotal-vote Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are expected to fly in for pivotal vote Politics Oct 26, 2026 5:44 PM EDT TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — For two decades since leaving Israel for Canada, Yael Natra said, she didn't consider returning to vote in her home country's elections. She felt it wasn't right to cast a ballot in a place she no longer lived. But now, after seeing the far right gain power, Natra, 61, said she believed she had no choice. Ahead of Israel's election on Tuesday — the first since the 2023 Hamas-led attacks and ensuing wars in the region — Natra spent thousands of dollars to travel nearly 6,000 miles from Toronto to Tel Aviv to be in the country and vote, she said. Natra said she plans to cast her ballot for parties not aligned with the current government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "The Israel that I grew up in is disappearing," she said in an interview from Toronto, citing an eroding democracy and deeply divided society. "If something won't change this time, I don't know what's going to be." Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are expected to fly in for this month's vote, according to AID Coalition, a U.S.-based nonprofit focused on strengthening Israel's democracy. The election is one of the most consequential in Israel in years, widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu's handling of the wars and the hard-right turn Israel has taken both domestically and on the world stage. Israel has more than 7.3 million registered voters, but polling suggests a tight race. Previous elections have turned on thin margins. It's unclear what effect these voters might have, but many liberal Israelis who don't support Netanyahu have left the country in recent years, suggesting that those returning to cast ballots would not support him. "Many Israelis who have left over the years — and especially since Oct. 7 — are exposed to the isolation and animosity toward the country much more palpably than those inside, and as such are likely to want to vote out Netanyahu," said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst with the International Crisis Group, a nonprofit think tank. The U.S. tops the list of voters traveling to Israel, one group's estimates show AID Coalition estimates that as many as 67,000 voters are returning to Israel, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data gathered for its "Fly&Vote" initiative. It says about half are flying in from the United States, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. "It doesn't matter what side of the political spectrum you're on, everyone views these elections as going to be critical," said Jonathan Barsade, AID Coalition's president. Israelis planning to travel from the U.S., United Kingdom and Canada told The Associated Press they felt a sense of obligation to try to preserve Israel's democracy. Hadar Susskind, 53, said he wants a new Israeli government to reverse course in the West Bank and Gaza, halting settlement activity and settler violence in the former and allowing for reconstruction in the latter. He and four relatives who live in the U.S. were flying back to "reaffirm Israel's democracy," he said. "This government is digging the hole deeper every day," he said. "The first thing the new government needs to do is put the shovel down." Dahlia Scheindlin, an American-Israeli political analyst, said the mobilization effort this year is notable, compared with past elections. And while many campaigns have focused on anti-Netanyahu sentiment, she said it's unclear overall how those flying in will vote. "There are also expats coming in to vote for the pro-Netanyahu side," Scheindlin said. Some voters previously supported Netanyahu but say their views changed Netanyahu's main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, is a centrist politician and former military chief of staff who has pledged to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the Oct. 7 attacks and Israel's conduct during the war. Eisenkot says he wants to restore the country's standing with international allies. Natra, who described her politics as center-right, said she voted for Netanyahu in the 1990s. But now, she said, his government's inability to take responsibility for the failures that led to the Oct. 7 attacks and his support for the ultra-Orthodox community have turned her away. Natra's younger sister, 57-year-old Tamar Ichilov, said the "horrible things" Israel is doing in Gaza and the occupied West Bank motivated her to travel to Israel to vote. She said Israel is consumed by a "vendetta" and intent to "destroy" after the Oct. 7 attacks, and she believes its actions have contributed to rising antisemitism. "People don't like us, and I can't blame them," she said in Tel Aviv, shortly after landing at Israel's main international airport. (AP) — Colorado and Washington are reliably Democratic states where elected officials have rejected moves to ban transgender women and girls from female sports competitions. Now activists have gone around lawmakers to put proposed bans on both states' ballots. At a time when some Democratic leaders nationwide are recalibrating their approach to transgender issues, particularly sports, and polls show Americans generally back the bans, supporters are optimistic they will pass and open the door to similar efforts in other places where lawmakers have blocked bans. Please check your inbox to confirm. Though the issue has been debated in many legislatures, this is the first time it's going to voters. "What is happening in 2026 is a testing ground for the future," said Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center, which supports LGBTQ+ rights. READ MORE: Abortion, taxes, trans rights are on the ballot this November. Here's what to know Twenty-seven states — including all where Republicans control both the legislature and governor's office — already have such laws. The efforts are billed as a way to protect women and girls and keep separate spaces for them, tapping into a concern that's gained momentum. President Donald Trump has taken steps to roll back transgender rights. The Supreme Court has upheld state sports bans. A June poll from Quinnipiac University found that about 7 in 10 registered voters think transgender women and girls should not be allowed to play on female sports teams. About one-quarter think they should. Democrats are divided, with about half saying transgender women and girls should be allowed and about half saying they should not. Robert Preuhs, a professor of political science at Metropolitan State University of Denver, said the absence of public polls on Colorado's ballot measure, which also covers college sports, makes it hard to predict whether it will pass. "It's probably going to get more support than some of the Republican candidates that will run," he said. Since transgender restrictions gained traction this decade, states with Democratic-led governors' offices and legislatures generally have rejected proposals such as banning transgender people from the bathrooms that match their gender identity and restricting gender-affirming care. Most Republican-led states have adopted those policies. In addition to the two blue-state questions, a measure in Arizona would broaden an existing ban to include private schools, and one in Nebraska would add an existing state law to the state constitution. The argument has been framed around fairness Let's Go Washington staff member Josh Johnson (left) helps a volunteer while phone banking in Bellevue on Oct. 19 in support of Washington State Initiative 638, which would prohibit transgender girls from competing in girls' sports. Photo by Photo/Lindsey Wasson/AP There's not a clear consensus on whether transgender women and girls have a competitive advantage. Factors include the age of the athlete, the sport, whether the athlete went through male puberty and how long they've received hormone therapy. But the idea that girls are being cheated is personal for some athletes. Ahnaleigh Wilson, a 17-year-old junior at Eastmont High School, about 150 miles (241 kilometers) east of Seattle, has been speaking out against allowing transgender girls to compete in girls' sports since she was in junior high. She said she'd won all her 1,600-meter races in seventh and eighth grade — until she finished second to a transgender athlete in a major meet. "I knew it wasn't right and it wasn't fair," she said. Wilson said three other transgender athletes she's competed against since then placed better in girls races than they would have with the same times against boys. "Women have fought for Title IX and our own categories and it's very important that we keep the dignity of that, and let women have their own sports and their own spaces to be safe and completely fair," she said, referencing the federal law that prohibits discrimination based on sex in education programs and activities, including athletics. Opponents say excluding transgender girls is also unfair. "They will say that they want to protect kids and in particular, young girls," said Nadine Bridges, executive director of One Colorado, which is leading the opposition to the measure there, "but I don't understand how you can protect kids and discriminate against kids at the same time." The number of transgender girls in school sports is believed to be a sliver of the total participants. Neither Colorado nor Washington has an official count. Let's Go Washington, which is behind the measure in that state, says it's counted 16 such athletes and that there could be more. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association has counted about 101,000 girls in sports that it oversees — a figure that double-counts girls who play in multiple sports. ba9aafacf2b1.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/following-post-surgery-checkup-pope-leo-will-proceed-with-latin-america-trip-vatican-confirms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Following post-surgery checkup, Pope Leo will proceed with Latin America trip, Vatican confirms World Oct 26, 2026 4:54 PM EDT VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will proceed with his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, after doctors determined there are no medical reasons preventing him from traveling three weeks after lung cancer surgery, the Vatican confirmed Monday. The Vatican press office said the pope's recovery continues to progress in line with favorable assessments from his medical team. It also confirmed the pope is keeping the already ambitious trip program with no announced changes. READ MORE: What is adenocarcinoma? Here's what to know about Pope Leo XIV's form of lung cancer Surgeons on Oct. 13 removed a lobe where the nodule later diagnosed as malignant was located, in the first major health event of Leo's 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Since returning to the Vatican, Leo has gradually resumed his activities while adjusting his schedule to prioritize recovery and periods of rest, the statement said. The pope's physician, Luigi Carbone, said there's no medical reason preventing Leo's trip to South America, which involves a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. Leo expressed gratitude for the prayers and support he has received during his recovery and said he was eager to return to a region where he spent important periods of his life. "I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," Leo said Monday. "May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy." The Vatican said the visit will provide an opportunity for the pope to strengthen ties with local churches, encourage the faithful and promote a message of faith, hope and peace in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. fc5210918beb.text: By — Dyepkazah Shibayan, Associated Press Dyepkazah Shibayan, Associated Press By — Mark Banchereau, Associated Press Mark Banchereau, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/1st-confirmed-ebola-patient-in-nigeria-evacuated-to-switzerland Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 1st confirmed Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland World Oct 26, 2026 4:46 PM EDT ABUJA, Nigeria (AP) — A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria was medically evacuated to Switzerland with her husband Monday, officials said, as Nigerian authorities continued monitoring 52 people who had been in contact with her. Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Pate said the woman, the country's first case in the current outbreak, left the capital, Abuja, early Monday with his approval. Her condition had improved significantly, and she was stable, conscious and able to communicate, he said. Please check your inbox to confirm. "This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place," Pate wrote on X. Her husband, a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria, has shown no symptoms. Switzerland's Federal Office of Public Health said the couple arrived Monday on a medical evacuation flight. The woman was being treated at Geneva University Hospital, while her husband was in isolation at Zurich University Hospital. The agency said both hospitals were equipped to care for them and that there was no risk to the Swiss public. The World Health Organization's regional director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, said the evacuation was arranged because the couple are Swiss citizens and that Nigerian medical teams had stabilized the woman after treating her through the acute phase of the illness. Nigeria will continue monitoring 52 other contacts, Janabi said. "With the evacuation of the patient and her husband, Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases," he said, stressing that vigilance remained critical. Pate said containment measures remained in place and urged Nigerians to remain vigilant. The woman tested positive after returning to Abuja from Uganda. Nigerian authorities said Friday they had yet to establish how she contracted the virus. Switzerland's foreign ministry told The Associated Press last week that she had not visited Congo and was believed to have been infected while traveling to Uganda with her husband. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had both traveled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on Oct. 3. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but later declared itself free of the virus. Kenya has recorded nine cases, including two deaths, since confirming its first case earlier this month. On Monday, Kenya released 20 people from quarantine following their exposure to the virus as contacts of the country's first case, while 98 others were expected to be released starting next Tuesday. "Each of the 20 contacts was assessed against the release criteria, including 21 days without any symptoms since their last exposure," the Kenyan Ministry of Health said in a statement. The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened longstanding fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus. The latest figures from Congo's health ministry show more than 9,900 cases, including more than 4,800 deaths, since the outbreak began in May. The WHO has said the outbreak is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is on track to surpass the death toll of the deadliest: West Africa's 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed 11,000 people. Nigeria was among the countries affected, recording 20 cases before its outbreak was declared over after three months. Banchereau reported from Dakar, Senegal. e8abb19575ec.text: President Trump will campaign with three football stars in Texas on Tuesday, leaning into America's favorite sport as Republicans scramble to turn out voters in the final week before the midterms, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Trump is trying to mobilize the lower-propensity voters who helped return him to the White House in 2024 — but who may be less inclined to vote when he isn't on the ballot. Driving the news: Former college football stars Johnny Manziel and Colt McCoy, along with two-time Super Bowl champion Danny Amendola, will join Trump for campaign appearances in Lubbock and Corpus Christi. The appearances bring some of Texas' biggest football names onto the campaign trail in a state where the sport commands an enormous following. Amendola starred at Texas Tech in Lubbock, Manziel won the Heisman Trophy at Texas A&M, and McCoy was a standout quarterback at the University of Texas. The big picture: Trump has made football a recurring feature of his campaign stops in recent weeks. He attended the Texas-Tennessee game in September and planned to attend the Georgia-Alabama showdown earlier this month before canceling because of a hurricane. Former NFL coach Jon Gruden joined Trump at an Ohio rally this month, while former Georgia and NFL star Todd Gurley accompanied the president on a stop in Georgia. Vice President Vance, a lifelong Cincinnati Bengals fan, visited the team's practice facility last week while campaigning in Ohio. Republicans are also pouring millions into ads during NFL and college football games. What they're saying: "Trump has many bases. And football is one of them, college and pros," said an adviser. "The response is good. And the president loves the atmosphere. So why not?" Between the lines: Football offers Trump a way to reach younger men who helped power his 2024 victory — a constituency Republicans are struggling to energize in the midterms. By the numbers: Polls suggest Republicans face a challenge holding onto Trump's gains among young men. Trump won men under 30 by 14 points in 2024, according to a Tufts University analysis . But a Harvard Youth Poll released last week found Democrats leading Republicans by 26 points among young men who say they will definitely vote in November. Marc Caputo contributed to this report.

a03d5facc91b.text: President Trump and MAGA-world influencers are echoing Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro's claims of a rigged election after the Trump-aligned populist fell to the incumbent president in Sunday's election. The big picture: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's runoff victory has been widely seen as a counterweight to the global right's surge in Latin America. But Bolsonaro, like his father , isn't accepting defeat. What they're saying: "It looked like another rigged election, frankly," Trump told reporters Monday. He added, "Elections have to be indisputable, and it looked very bad to me." The White House referred Axios to Trump's comments when asked to respond. Friction point: Bolsonaro told reporters it was "impossible to recognize the result of this election in the context of how these things have happened," according to a translation . He also vowed to ask for the results to be annulled. Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin's two-hour extension to Sunday's voting has fueled Bolsonaro's claims. Zanin previously served as Lula's lawyer. But both Bolsonaro and Lula's camps requested more time for voters. Lula's team requested the extension because of public transit issues, while Bolsonaro sought additional time in certain states because of weather, Bloomberg reported . The extension was reportedly given as many polling stations were already wrapping up. Multiple outlets noted that the decision risked setting the stage for candidates to dispute the results, despite Brazil's voting system being widely recognized for its reliability. Zoom out: Several prominent voices in the online MAGA movement backed Bolsonaro's refusal to accept the election results, and some urged the Trump administration to act. "The math just ain't mathin'," podcaster Benny Johnson said in a Monday edition of his show where he criticized the election results. He was joined by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, who argued Brazil looked like "a banana republic." Former Trump White House adviser Steve Bannon urged the administration to sever ties with Brazil on his "War Room" show, adding, "if we don't take action ... it's happening next Tuesday here in this country." Jack Posobiec echoed Bannon's unfounded claims, writing on X, "Look at what the Left is doing in Brazil in broad daylight. Do you really think they wouldn't in the United States?" Andrew Kolvet, who produced "The Charlie Kirk Show," said the U.S. should "quietly pressure them behind the scenes" and not accept the result. He further urged Bolsonaro supporters not to show up for work and "rally in the streets." What we're watching: The attention on Bolsonaro's loss comes as MAGA activists have pushed for Trump to take extraordinary measures, like martial law, if they think the U.S. election is rigged, Axios' Brittany Gibson reports . Trump has continued to stoke the coals of election denialism, while political opponents have accused his administration of trying to intimidate voters and election officials. Meanwhile, the Justice Department has waged an aggressive pre-election offensive, including a preemptive request that could delay certification of Alaska's Senate results and a lawsuit against California over alleged suspected noncitizens receiving ballots. Go deeper: Trump allies fall in two elections as Netanyahu faces next test

27638b3382ab.text: By — Thomas Adamson, Associated Press Thomas Adamson, Associated Press By — Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/france-pledges-new-university-admissions-to-quell-student-anger-but-only-after-macron-leaves-office Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter France pledges new university admissions to quell student anger. But only after Macron leaves office World Oct 26, 2026 4:32 PM EDT PARIS (AP) — France's government pledged on Monday to replace its national online university admissions platform in 2028, seeking to quell student anger after weeks of mass protests over education and living costs. Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste announced "substantial change" to the platform for 2027, before its replacement the following year. The concessions target the school grievances that helped ignite the unrest. But the movement has widened to include workers demanding relief from rising living costs, making the government's task broader than resolving a dispute over university admissions. The announcements followed France's worst unrest in years on Oct. 17, when demonstrations over school funding and rising living costs descended into rioting and looting across the country. Groups of protesters set fires, stormed public buildings — including Marseille's City Hall — looted shops and clashed with police. About 2,400 people were arrested over that weekend. READ MORE: From France to Albania, how social unrest is fueling protests across Europe Two high school student groups welcomed some concessions but called for protests to continue. Their representatives spoke after meeting with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu earlier Monday, before the ministers' news conference. Further demonstrations have been planned for Oct. 31, before nationwide strikes and protests called by labor unions for Nov. 5. The 2028 deadline puts a central concession to protesters beyond President Emmanuel Macron's time in office, leaving his successor's government to deliver it. Macron can't seek a third consecutive term in 2027, and far-right leader Marine Le Pen leads polling for the first round of the presidential election on April 18. A second round will be held May 2 if no candidate achieves a majority. The university admissions replacement system still has to be designed, and legal changes may be needed — leaving crucial decisions unresolved even as the government seeks to persuade students to end their protests. The system, called Parcoursup, handles applications to universities and other higher education courses. It has been a focus of the protests, with students criticizing unclear selection criteria and unequal access to their preferred courses. For the 2027 admissions round, institutions would have to publish more detailed selection criteria and explain rejections when applicants request reasons. The government also promised 15,000 additional places in higher education, introduced across 2027 and 2028, and increases in student grants linked to inflation from the start of the 2027 academic year. Another round of nationwide demonstrations on Saturday saw less violence. Authorities estimated turnout at more than 400,000, while organizers put it at nearly 800,000. Rapper Jay-Z will perform at the Super Bowl half-time show in February, the NFL has announced.
Jay-Z's company Roc Nation has produced the half-time show since 2019, and he plays a key role in selecting each year's performer but he has not performed before at the NFL championship game.
"Anticipation as to who Jay-Z might have guest star at halftime for the big game will now kick off," the NFL said in a statement. "Of course, his wife, BeyoncÃ©, will be atop the list."
Next year's Super Bowl LXI will take place on 14 February near Los Angeles.
The hip-hop star will follow in the footsteps of other recent half-time performers including Bad Bunny, Kendrick Lamar, Usher, Rihanna and The Weeknd.
The musical performance draws global attention while the sport is watched by tens of millions of people in the US.
Kendrick Lamar's 2025 performance was the most watched Super Bowl half-time show in history and won the Emmy award for outstanding music direction.
The announcement was made after Jay-Z, whose real name is Shawn Carter, performed two shows last weekend at the Los Angeles stadium where the Super Bowl will be played.
The LA shows were part of a tour to celebrate the 30th anniversary of his debut album Reasonable Doubt.
"From 'Reasonable Doubt' to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey," said Jay-Z, whose real name is Shawn Carter.
"Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."
NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said he "couldn't be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring".
"When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him," Goodell said.
The star's accolades include being the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame, 25 Grammy awards and being inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

The Duchess of Sussex has been confirmed as a co-host of the new season of Junior MasterChef Australia.
Meghan will join the 2027 series as a "special guest" with fellow host Poh Ling Yeow, according to Australia's Channel 10.
The duchess said she "can't wait" to take part in the programme after an appearance as a guest judge on MasterChef Australia last year. It was the show's largest Sunday audience since 2023, according to the statement from Paramount ANZ.
The announcement comes as Meghan faces increased scrutiny due to her father Thomas Markle being accused of child sexual abuse. He denies the allegations.
The BBC understands Meghan broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and authorities knew he had abused young girls.
Markle has strongly rejected the accusations as "lies" which are being used to destroy his reputation.
Meghan's return to Australia follows a four-day tour of the country she and Prince Harry undertook in April.
Meghan's MasterChef debut was announced on the second day of the tour, a Wednesday on which the duchess had been notably absent from public-facing appearances. That evening, it was revealed she had been filming an episode of the programme.
It is understood she was not paid for her appearance. Australia's Network 10, which airs the series as part of Paramount ANZ, did not respond to a question from the BBC about whether Meghan would be paid for co-hosting the Junior MasterChef season.
"I love cooking with my own kids, so seeing what these young stars create in the kitchen is going to be a lot of fun," Meghan said in a statement.
In August, the Sussexes announced they were moving back to the UK from California. The couple left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties in early 2020, before settling in California in March that year.
They embarked on media careers which included a high-profile interview with Oprah Winfrey and a deal with Netflix and Spotify.
Meghan's lifestyle and cookery show on Netflix, With Love, Meghan, ran for two series and a Christmas special but did not perform well with audiences.
She also launched lifestyle brand As Ever, which includes a food range, but in March it ended its partnership with the streaming platform.
Last year her trademark was registered in more than a dozen product categories in Australia, including cookware and table linen.
